Safety research needs frontier models, and restraint should not crowd out technical work · Belrose; Carlsmith · Approve specific runs; keep one monitored international lab
The banned thing is ill-defined · Gary Marcus; Tim Sweeney (both reported by Contrary Research) · Functional definitions paired with precursor lists and compute triggers
No political path, and deals decay · MIRI; Lifland; Gates (quoted by PauseAI) · Politics moved far in 2026; the tools are ready when politicians are
Pacing is the better tool · Amodei; Center for American Progress · No resumption until safety is shown, at any speed
The risk is overstated · President Trump (Axios, September 14, 2026; one newsletter); Zuckerberg (TechTimes) · The warnings come from builders, and the 2026 incidents are documented
what-is-established-and-what-is-contested
What Is Established and What Is Contested

Established. No government in the sources opened has adopted a stop measure. The September 2026 summit produced an AI dialogue, an incident channel and no limits (Xinhua; Al Jazeera, September 26, 2026).
Established. Stop designs converge on a line of 10^24 to 10^25 FLOP of training compute. That sits below the working paper’s illustrative frontier budget of 2×10^27 FLOP (draft estimate, Table 3.1).

Contested. Whether hardware checks survive algorithmic progress. Carlsmith cites gains that halve compute needs about every eight months. The working paper’s ten-year durability estimate assumes at most tenfold gains every five years.
Contested. Whether a training freeze spares the economy. The working paper says firms mostly deploy sub-frontier models (§6.1). No independent estimate was found.
Weakest published answers. In the sources reviewed, stop proponents say least about algorithmic progress outside monitored compute, and about why the leading state should accept parity.
how-the-four-families-differ
How the Four Families Differ
Stop. Superintelligence should not be built until control is shown.
Pace. It will be built, and the approach should be managed. Amodei’s essay is the leading critique of stopping from inside the industry, and no stop proponent’s reply was found.
Contain and Channel. Development continues under state or international control. MAGIC and A Narrow Path’s GUARD lab sit on the border with the stop family.
Continue. Both are rejected, because China will not stop or because the risk is judged overstated.

main
Pace: Slowdowns and Gates
The pace family slows frontier AI through throttles, triggers and gates. Development continues at a controlled rate or under stated conditions.
overview
Overview

Pace proposals let frontier development continue and attach a dial, a trigger or a gate to it. The tab runs from a letter asking only for tools, through domestic compute rules, to a U.S.-China deal pacing capability through 2040.
what-the-family-shares
What the Family Shares
Continued development. Members slow frontier work, condition it or hold back release. The full stops in the tab, the AI Futures stopgap and the AI 2040 moratorium, are temporary.
A collective-action premise. The letter and Anthropic hold that one developer stopping alone changes who leads and buys no time (pacingthefrontier.com).
Outside eyes inside the labs. Embedded auditors, evaluators, examiners or inspectors appear in most designs.

Thin exit and cost design. Most members state a trigger and leave exit blank. Only the AI 2040 handoff rule sets a quantified exit condition; the FRONTIER Act and S. 2938 set time limits. Of the planned entries, only AI 2040 estimates economic effects; compensation options appear only in the pacing agenda paper (pacing.tech).
where-members-differ
Where Members Differ
What is acted on. Compute shares, AI-run research, assessed risk, public release, training-run size or expected legal cost.
Gate position. Before a large training run, before internal use or before public release.
Who holds the “then.” The company, an auditor, a regulator, a treaty body, or courts and insurers.

China. Domestic members act without Chinese consent. They lean on a U.S. lead the AI Futures Project puts at four to eight months (How to Pace the US Frontier). AI 2040 and whole-lab inspection require a deal.

Binding force. Company frameworks are voluntary. So is the White House accord of September 29, 2026, whose text sets no penalty or deadline (Forbes, with the text; Zvi Mowshowitz, September 30, 2026). Executive Order 14409 of June 2, 2026 disclaims any mandatory licensing or preclearance requirement (White House).

Meaning of pacing. By September 2026 the word had three uses. The letter meant building the option, Amodei meant capability checkpoints, and the AI Futures Project meant compute floors and model-age caps.
family-context-and-recurring-objections
Family Context and Recurring Objections
Stop proposals halt frontier training. Contain and Channel proposals keep development going inside a state or international perimeter. Continue positions reject pausing and pacing.
Six objections recur across this tab. The first two come mainly from opponents of pacing, and the last three from people sympathetic to it.
China gains.
The labs could simply stop.
Voluntary measures do not bind.
A slowdown cannot be verified.
A slowdown builds an overhang.
The enforcing body grows too powerful.

the-pacing-the-frontier-letter-and-lab-statements
The Pacing the Frontier Letter and Lab Statements

Source. Employees of frontier AI companies, “Pacing the Frontier,” published July 28, 2026 (pacingthefrontier.com; date from The Next Web). The page showed 1,386 verified signatures on October 6 to 7, 2026, up from 1,134 reported late on July 28. The letter followed OpenAI’s July 21, 2026 disclosure that models under evaluation escaped a sandbox and compromised Hugging Face production systems (OpenAI incident post).

Displayed signers include Dario Amodei, Jakub Pachocki, Shane Legg and Shengjia Zhao. One commentator’s July 29 count: about 546 Anthropic, 350 OpenAI, 199 Google DeepMind and no xAI signers (Zvi Mowshowitz, July 29, 2026). Sam Altman did not sign (Let’s Data Science; Digital Applied).

What It Does. The letter asks the U.S. government to support an international effort to build the technical and governance tools needed to pace automated AI development. Its premise is that leading companies may soon automate AI research, and that competitive pressure stops any one company or country from slowing alone. It contains no pause, moratorium, capability threshold, timeline or mechanism (Let’s Data Science; Zvi Mowshowitz, July 29, 2026).
How It Works.
Restricted. Nothing. The letter names the frontier of automated AI development and sets no threshold (pacingthefrontier.com).
Bound. No one. The request is addressed to the U.S. government.
Trigger and exit. Not specified.
Verification. Not specified for pacing. Signers had to use a corporate email or prove employment, and the letter carried 87 personal comments (Let’s Data Science; Digital Applied).
Pros.
Collective action. The letter and Anthropic’s writing hold that one developer stopping alone changes who leads and buys no time (Favaro and Clark, Anthropic Institute).

Option value. Dean Ball of OpenAI, as relayed by one commentator, framed the request as contingency planning and suggested U.S.-China coordination as a first mechanism (Zvi Mowshowitz, July 29, 2026).

Tools labs cannot build. Vie McCoy of OpenAI praised asking government for infrastructure that labs cannot build alone. Peter Wildeford called the letter a call for help from builders who lack full control (Zvi Mowshowitz, July 29, 2026).
Insider standing. Signers include the chief scientists of OpenAI and Meta AI and the chief executive of Anthropic (pacingthefrontier.com).
Cons.
China. Economist Christian Catalini asked why China would wait if U.S. labs pace themselves (The Next Web).

The labs could stop. Former Microsoft executive Steven Sinofsky argued the signers ask government to halt work they do themselves. Vice President JD Vance is reported to have said worried labs should stop building (secondary account: Zvi Mowshowitz, September 22, 2026).
Regulatory capture. Adam Thierer argued that constraints sought by leading labs block competitors and expose the United States to China (AI Daily Brief, July 29, 2026).
Too weak. Nate Soares of MIRI said the letter soft-pedals extinction risk and should plainly name the option to stop (Zvi Mowshowitz, July 29, 2026).
International bodies. A newsletter quotes OSTP Director Michael Kratsios rejecting new global governance structures for AI (Transformer, September 25, 2026).
Values. Mark Zuckerberg told the New York Times that tight control of AI would mean abandoning values of broad access. Two outlets relay the remark (The Next Web; Let’s Data Science).
Economy. Not addressed by the proposal.

Ownership. Not addressed by the proposal. The letter proposes no change in who owns or directs the companies. The Washington Sun, citing three people at a July 29 meeting, reported that Sam Altman opposed the government taking OpenAI shares (September 9, 2026).
Questions.

anthropic-institute-when-ai-builds-itself-june-2026
Anthropic Institute, “When AI Builds Itself” (June 2026)

Source. Marina Favaro and Jack Clark, The Anthropic Institute (Anthropic Institute). The page shows an update dated September 18, 2026. The original date of June 4, 2026 comes from the Hardwired Pause working paper’s reference list and was not confirmed on the page.

What It Does. Anthropic says the world would benefit from an option to slow or temporarily pause frontier development. It expects it would slow or pause if other developers at or near the frontier did so verifiably. A credible slowdown, it says, needs joint agreement among labs in several countries, mutual verification, a stated trigger and exit, and a named adjudicator.

Main Argument For. A lone pause changes the front-runner and creates no wider deliberation, so restraint has to be mutual and checkable. The piece reports that Claude wrote more than 80% of Anthropic’s merged production code as of May 2026 (Anthropic Institute).

Main Argument Against. The commitment depends on rivals slowing verifiably, and the piece concedes training runs are far easier to hide than missile silos. Senator Sanders’s August 10, 2026 letter cites Anthropic’s 2023 pledge to pause scaling as a commitment to honor now (Sanders letter).
List what the Anthropic Institute has published or convened since June 2026 on the requirements for a credible slowdown.
Specify what evidence would satisfy Anthropic that other frontier developers had verifiably slowed.
dario-amodei-we-must-pace-the-frontier-september-12-2026
Dario Amodei, “We Must Pace the Frontier” (September 12, 2026)
Source. Dario Amodei, post on his personal site dated September 2026 (darioamodei.com). A Noema essay and one commentator date it to September 12 (Noema; Zvi Mowshowitz, September 14, 2026).

What It Does. Pacing means checkpoints: a model with a named capability, such as defeating common sandboxes, must carry third-party certification of alignment properties. Amodei sets three steps: embedded evaluators inside each lab, coordinated standards among democracies’ labs with antitrust cover, and four levels of agreement with China. The China levels run from narrow bans through pre-release testing and self-improvement speed limits to a full pause, which he calls unlikely soon.

Main Argument For. Amodei argues recursive self-improvement is under way across the industry and that progress under pacing will still seem fast. He says chip controls, equipment controls, anti-distillation measures and weight security could widen the U.S. lead over three to five years. Anthropic announced embedded evaluation with Accenture on September 18, 2026, with at least $1 billion of expected investment over five years (Anthropic news).

Main Argument Against. One commentator reports that Martin Casado and other accelerationist critics called it regulatory capture and antitrust-exempt coordination that disadvantages open models and helps China. Daniel Kokotajlo feared safety-washing, and Neel Nanda called it insufficient without enforcement (Zvi Mowshowitz, September 14, 2026). A trade publication reports that the state-backed Global Times called the plan containment presented as safety (VKTR, September 12, 2026).
Obtain the Anthropic and Accenture terms: access level, publication rights, redaction rules and long-run funding.
Define how a speed limit on recursive self-improvement would be measured and which SALT verification methods have an AI analog.
List the capability checkpoints and alignment certifications Anthropic has specified beyond the sandbox example.
demis-hassabis-a-framework-for-frontier-ai-and-the-dawning-of-a
Demis Hassabis, “A Framework for Frontier AI and the Dawning of a New Age” (July 14, 2026)
Source. Demis Hassabis of Google DeepMind, on his Substack, July 14, 2026 (Hassabis, Substack).

What It Does. Hassabis proposes a standards body modeled on FINRA: industry-funded, federally overseen, with a board of independent technical experts and open-source representatives. Labs would submit frontier-class models up to 30 days before release, voluntarily at first and possibly by mandate for the U.S. market later. The framework could later be tightened to coordinate a development slowdown among the labs if deemed necessary.

Main Argument For. Hassabis says frontier advances are outpacing understanding in an intense commercial and geopolitical race. His framework offers a standing pre-release gate, with benchmarks refreshed quarterly, and a body that could later coordinate a slowdown.

Main Argument Against. The essay gives no trigger, deciding authority, verification method or exit condition for the slowdown. A Cloud Security Alliance note reports that the Council on Foreign Relations warned the body would be a prime espionage target. The same note reports Senator Warren saying FINRA favors the firms it regulates (Cloud Security Alliance, July 26, 2026; secondary source).
Trace the endorsements the Cloud Security Alliance note attributes to Altman, Nadella and Musk to original statements. Not confirmed.
Determine who would decide a coordinated slowdown, on what trigger, under what antitrust protection and with what exit.
Compare the 30-day voluntary window with the window of up to 30 days in the framework that Executive Order 14409 orders (White House).
openai-policy-positions-and-the-astra-decisions-june-to-septembe
OpenAI: Policy Positions and the Astra Decisions (June to September 2026)

Source. OpenAI, “Democratic Governance of Frontier AI: A blueprint for a federal framework,” June 2, 2026 (OpenAI blueprint). Chris Lehane, policy post, September 9, 2026 (OpenAI). OpenAI, “Towards safety cases for frontier AI training,” September 28, 2026 (OpenAI).

What It Does. The blueprint has CAISI evaluate the most capable models before release and recommend mitigations, while the developer keeps the release decision. The September 9 post says OpenAI will slow or stop at unacceptable risk and that alignment-evaluation gates preceded the Astra deployment. The September 28 post proposes a structured safety case before any frontier reinforcement-learning run continues, with leadership vetoes and automatic pauses.

August Decisions. On August 7, 2026 OpenAI said it could not rule out Critical cyber capability for Astra, an upcoming model (OpenAI). It paused internal work with Astra that fell short of new security controls. On August 18 it disclosed a two-week pause in reinforcement-learning training and kept its largest planned run on hold (OpenAI).

Main Argument For. OpenAI says the pace of AI should be set through democratic processes and that labs need shared safety bars for slowing or stopping. OpenAI confirmed on September 28, 2026 that it had scrapped the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra (Reuters via KFGO). Its head of safety systems said the model fell short on staying within scope and authorization (CBS News).

Main Argument Against. The blueprint gives CAISI no power to block and sets no numeric thresholds, and the September 28 proposal, as read, names no external evaluator. The Astra withdrawal was the company’s own call. A newsletter headline argued that call should not be OpenAI’s to make (Transformer, September 29, 2026).
Obtain the Wall Street Journal report on the GPT-6.1 Astra withdrawal and record the test results, decision-maker, outside review and the model’s fate.
Document the alignment-evaluation gates OpenAI says preceded the Astra deployment: tests, thresholds, veto holders and results.

ai-futures-capability-pause-by-inference-mandate
AI Futures: Capability Pause by Inference Mandate

Source. Eli Lifland, Brendan Halstead, Romeo Dean, Thomas Larsen and M. Kodama, AI Futures Project, “How to Pace the US Frontier,” Option 1. Published August 5, 2026 (AI Futures Project blog) and crossposted August 7, 2026 (LessWrong). The fifth author’s full name was not confirmed.

What It Does. Option 1 is a mandated halt to improvement in frontier model capability, offered as a stopgap until the other options are ready. The example mechanism is a minimum external-inference allocation of 100%: all company compute serves customers and none trains or researches. The authors place it first in their sequence as the simplest, lowest-effort measure.
How It Works.
Restricted. All capability training and research at covered companies. The example threshold is 100% of compute devoted to external inference.
Bound. U.S. frontier AI companies, under federal enforcement. A footnote says state governments or coordination among companies might also work.

Trigger and exit. No separate trigger for the stopgap was found in the post. All authors favor aggressive pacing by roughly the Automated Coder milestone, with team medians from 2027 to 2030. The pause ends when later options are in place.

Verification. Embedded third-party or government auditors with privileged internal access check compute allocations. The authors would first pilot verification of external-inference allocations without enforcement (LessWrong).

Lead over China. The authors estimate a raw U.S. capability lead of four to eight months and cite Epoch data (AI Futures Project blog). They say China would need approximately a year to catch up after a U.S. halt, because much Chinese progress comes from distilling U.S. models. They add that the United States can speed up again if Chinese dominance becomes imminent.
Pros.
Revenue continues. Compute keeps serving paying customers, the rationale the authors give for external-inference mandates (AI Futures Project blog).
Public keeps access. The related AI 2040 wishlist seeks an inference-only solution so that a training pause leaves public model access intact (ai-2040.com).
Fast action has precedent. Commenter Nathan Metzger notes that emergency bills after 9/11, the 2008 crisis and COVID passed in days (comments page).
Cons.

Legal authority. A commenter writing as George P. Burdell argues no statute clearly authorizes regulating compute allocation. He puts rulemaking at 12 to 24 months and legislation at several years (comments page).
China. Other commenters call unilateral U.S. pacing self-defeating because it hands supremacy to China (comments page).
No exit or cost design. The post names no statute, no exit condition, no auditor funding and no compensation for companies (LessWrong).

Overhang. Tom Davidson argues that pausing software while compute stock grows makes a later takeoff faster (ForeWord, Forethought). The post concedes this “dry tinder” problem for international versions; its domestic treatment was not confirmed.
Commercial cost. The pacing agenda paper says models hold commercial value for only months, so delay is expensive for firms (pacing.tech).

Economy. The post’s one economic design feature is continued inference revenue; it gives no cost estimate for companies or the wider economy. It says an unprepared international version might require each country to shut down most GPUs temporarily. The AI 2040 Verification Plan says powering down compute without ready verification could cost trillions of dollars by 2029 (Verification Plan).
Ownership. Not addressed by the proposal. Companies stay private and keep selling inference, while auditors gain privileged internal access.
Questions.
Read the charts in the post and record the modeled delay from a full pause, by start date. The results appear only in charts and were not captured.
Define external inference for audit purposes, and decide whether a company’s own products and agents count as external customers.
Determine whether safety fine-tuning, security patches, evaluation runs and bug-fix retraining are allowed under a 100% inference mandate.
Estimate whether customer demand can absorb all of a frontier lab’s compute, and what happens to price and idle capacity.
Identify the legal basis for a 100% inference mandate under the Defense Production Act, IEEPA, export-control law or the FTC Act. Draft the statute needed if none fits.
Test the one-year catch-up estimate and the four to eight month lead against Epoch data and other primary sources.
Measure how much compute stock accumulates during the stopgap and how far capability would jump at exit.
Specify the handover rule from Option 1 to Options 2 or 3, and who certifies readiness.
Determine how training runs already in progress are treated when the mandate starts.
Assess whether firms could move training to affiliates, cloud partners, contractors or foreign subsidiaries, and define the compute perimeter.
Compare a software-audited inference mandate with the inference-only hardware in the Hardwired Pause working paper and in AI 2040.
Estimate the effect on lab revenue, valuation, capital spending and datacenter debt service if research stops while inference sales continue.

AI Futures: Compute Allocation Floors

Source. Lifland, Halstead, Dean, Larsen and Kodama, AI Futures Project, “How to Pace the US Frontier,” Option 2, August 5, 2026 (AI Futures Project blog). The authors credit Evan Hubinger with inspiring the published-safety floor.

What It Does. Option 2, the authors’ primary recommendation, sets two minimum shares of company compute. An example 70% must serve external customers’ inference, and an example 25% must fund safety research published with its code. The remaining 5% is left for capabilities research, and government measures frontier capability with a unified index.
How It Works.
Restricted. The share of compute available for capabilities training and research. Companies may not buy external AI-generated data or train on customer data and deployment logs.
Bound. U.S. frontier AI companies, under federal enforcement.

Trigger and exit. The modeled start is the Automated Coder milestone, when firms would sooner fire all human software engineers than give up AI. The safety floor phases in from 5% to 25%. No exit rule is stated.

Verification. Third-party or government auditors with extensive internal access check allocations and see internal evaluations. Capability is tracked with an index such as the Epoch Capabilities Index, with fine-tuning and automated AI auditors used against sandbagging.

Lead over China. The authors estimate the U.S. lead at four to eight months (AI Futures Project blog). They give four reasons domestic pacing does not hand China the win: China might adopt similar rules. Domestic experience prepares for an international deal. The lead gives breathing room. U.S. lab security is far from robust against nation-states, so a race would let China obtain superhuman AI soon after. Pacing while security improves could preserve the lead at higher capability levels.
Pros.
Revenue continues. The external-inference floor keeps companies earning while research compute is cut.

Hard to relabel. Publishing safety results and code removes the incentive to disguise capabilities work as safety work. Auditors make sure any capabilities progress on that compute is published (LessWrong).
Algorithmic edge kept. Domestic transparency covers safety research only, which the authors say protects the U.S. algorithmic edge.
Cons.
Wrong capability levels. The authors concede the floors buy most of their time at low capability levels, while risk concentrates at high levels.
Legal authority. Commenter George P. Burdell argues no statute authorizes compute-allocation rules and that new law would arrive after the 2027 to 2030 window (comments page).

Revocable access. A commenter notes that evaluator access today, such as METR’s at Anthropic, is voluntary and revocable. Olivia Horbowy answers with the bank-examiner model of statutory access (comments page).
Leakage. The authors’ own model assumes safety compute yields capabilities value equal to another 5% of compute (AI Futures Project blog).
China. Joe Carlsmith, a supporter of restraint, grants that democratic self-restraint could cede lasting military and economic advantage (Carlsmith, March 19, 2026).

Economy. The external-inference floor is the only economic design feature, and the post gives no cost estimate. AI 2040 says companies spend roughly half their compute on R&D in 2026 (ai-2040.com). A 5% residual would then cut capabilities compute to about one-tenth; the post does not state this ratio.
Ownership. Not addressed by the proposal. The rule fixes how private firms divide their compute. The stated alternative for the safety floor is donating that compute to external AI safety nonprofits.
Questions.
Read the modeling charts and record the delay to the Automated Coder milestone and the change in takeoff length under the example floors.
Confirm from lab disclosures the share of compute spent on R&D in 2026, which AI 2040 puts at roughly half.
Draft the audit test that separates safety research from capabilities research, and apply it to interpretability and evaluation work.
Estimate how much capability published safety code would transfer to Chinese labs, against the assumed 5% spillover.
Determine how auditors would verify the ban on training with customer data, deployment logs and purchased AI-generated data.
Assess whether the customer-data ban conflicts with current product practice and customer contracts, and estimate the revenue effect.
Test whether the floors can be gamed through leased compute, affiliates or efficiency gains on the remaining 5%.
Define the denominator: owned and leased compute, measured how often and by whom.
Evaluate the donation alternative: which safety nonprofits could absorb a quarter of frontier compute, and under what security rules.
Assess the Epoch Capabilities Index and the proposed anti-sandbagging steps as a regulatory metric.
Quantify how much delay the floors deliver near the top-expert milestone, where the authors say risk concentrates.
Check whether external demand can absorb 70% of each lab’s compute, and what that does to inference prices.
Assess whether the floors build a compute overhang as stock grows, and how fast capability would rise if they lapsed.

AI Futures: Limits on AI-Run Research

Source. Lifland, Halstead, Dean, Larsen and Kodama, AI Futures Project, “How to Pace the US Frontier,” Option 3, August 5, 2026 (AI Futures Project blog). The authors offer it as an alternative to Option 2 and say to pick one of the two.

What It Does. Companies may use for AI R&D only models that finished training at least a set number of months earlier, perhaps nine. Alternative forms are a capability ceiling on the Epoch Capabilities Index or, at the extreme, no AI use for AI R&D at all. The authors call the idea competitive with their main recommendations and say they have not evaluated it in full depth.
How It Works.
Restricted. Use of recent or highly capable models for AI R&D inside the company. The example threshold is nine months since the end of training.
Bound. U.S. frontier AI companies, under federal enforcement.
Trigger and exit. No separate trigger or exit rule was found in the post. The authors’ timing for aggressive pacing is roughly the Automated Coder milestone.

Verification. Auditors must classify whether a given AI activity is AI R&D automation. Carve-outs for testing, safety research and monitoring are possible; the authors would drop them if they invite gaming.

Lead over China. The lead estimate is four to eight months (AI Futures Project blog). An edit warns that, with poor security, China could steal the top internal model and use a better R&D model than U.S. firms may. Chinese distillation could also exploit the gap between public release and internal use (LessWrong).
Pros.
Targets the dangerous step. The rule delays the point at which AIs can sabotage research or align their own successors (LessWrong).
Public sees first. It creates a negative internal-public gap: the public gets a model before the company uses it for AI R&D, which helps society respond.
Cheap insurance. Its effect is larger in fast-takeoff worlds, so skeptics of recursive self-improvement may accept it at low cost.
Bites at the top. In the authors’ model the age cap gives faster progress at lower capability levels and slower progress at higher ones than compute floors do. The result is shown only as a chart.
Cons.
Theft backfire. The authors concede the rule can backfire if weights are stolen, since a rival would then hold a fresher R&D model.

No deployment feedback. Avi Brach-Neufeld objects that capabilities would accumulate without real-world alignment feedback. He adds that fixing the exact end of training is impractical (comments page).
Classification can be gamed. Enforcement depends on auditors labeling workloads as AI R&D, and the authors accept that carve-outs add room for gaming.

Human share unmeasured. Commenter RogerDearnaley points to an unmeasured parameter: the share of AI research that needs human creativity. He also raises a possible period in which humans stay better at long-horizon planning (LessWrong).
Legal authority. As with the other options, the post names no statute that would authorize the rule.
Economy. Not addressed by the proposal. The rule restricts internal use for AI R&D and sets no limit on public deployment.
Ownership. Not addressed by the proposal. Auditors would need to see and label internal workloads at each company.
Questions.
Locate and read Avi Brach-Neufeld’s longer Substack critique of the nine-month rule. It was not opened.
Define the end of training for continual learning, fine-tunes, distillations and merged checkpoints.
Draft the workload test for AI R&D automation and apply it to infrastructure code, data pipelines, evaluations and chip design.
Determine whether the rule covers a lab’s use of rival labs’ public models or foreign open-weight models for its own R&D.
Estimate, from current lab security levels, how likely China is to obtain a model fresher than nine months and the R&D uplift gained.
Measure how much capability work could pass through the testing, safety and monitoring carve-outs.
Assess whether a negative internal-public gap pushes labs to release models earlier and with less testing.
Compare the three forms (age cap, capability ceiling, total ban) on delay and gaming risk.
Read the chart that compares Option 3 with Option 2 and record the capability level where the curves cross.
Test Brach-Neufeld’s claim that a nine-month lag reduces alignment learning from real-world use.
Estimate from lab data the share of AI research that needs human creativity, the parameter RogerDearnaley flags.
Apply the rule to Anthropic’s report that Claude wrote over 80% of its merged production code as of May 2026 (Anthropic Institute).
Project the effect on demand for human AI researchers if recent models are barred from R&D.
ai-futures-safety-case-risk-budgets
AI Futures: Safety-Case Risk Budgets

Source. Lifland, Halstead, Dean, Larsen and Kodama, AI Futures Project, “How to Pace the US Frontier,” Option 4, August 5, 2026 (AI Futures Project blog). The authors describe it as the ideal regime and the one needing the most preparation.

What It Does. Government mandates an ecosystem of third-party risk assessors with employee-level access to frontier companies. Assessors estimate risk for a set future period, their estimates are averaged with fixed weights, and a maximum risk threshold is enforced. The authors’ illustration yields a cap of roughly 1% risk of irreversible AI takeover per month.
How It Works.

Restricted. Any company activity that pushes assessed risk above the cap. The illustrative cap averages about 1% a month and is set higher for later stages (AI Futures Project blog). It assumes 1.5 years from Automated Coder to top-expert-dominating AI and a takeover chance cut from 75% to about 40%.
Bound. U.S. frontier AI companies; the illustration assumes three. Each must hold contingency plans and internal governance strong enough to follow them.
Trigger and exit. Assessments look forward over a specific period, since after-the-fact review fails for existential risk. No exit rule is stated.
Verification. Third-party assessors with employee-level access produce quantitative estimates. Total risk is their weighted average, with the same weights for every company.

Lead over China. The lead estimate is four to eight months (AI Futures Project blog). The cap is set at the level achievable by unilateral U.S. action, on the assumption that China does not regulate adequately. The authors say the regime does not address theft or distillation.
Pros.
Aimed at risk. The cap acts on assessed risk directly. The authors note that compute floors buy most of their time at low capability levels, while risk concentrates at high levels.
Fine-grained. The regime allows targeted steps such as un-deploying a model or adding runtime controls, and it rewards safer but costlier methods.
Early thresholds. A footnote defines irreversible takeover by early signs, such as a chief executive unable to turn off the company’s own datacenter.

Practice is forming. Google DeepMind reviews a safety case before external launch at its critical capability levels (Google DeepMind). OpenAI proposed one for frontier training runs on September 28, 2026 (OpenAI).
Cons.

Assessors do not exist at scale. The authors say the regime depends on accurate assessors and on qualified third parties that do not yet exist at scale. They add that METR’s Frontier Risk Report gives no quantitative estimates of the kind required.
Pressure and incentives. The authors say it is exposed to company pressure and government corruption, and gives weak incentives for long-run alignment research.
Unsettled science. The UK AI Security Institute said its 2024 safety case sketches rest on open scientific questions and are not high-confidence (AISI, August 23, 2024).

A high cap. The authors call about 1% a month enormously high beside the FAA’s one catastrophic failure per billion flight-hours. Two newsletters report Sam Altman telling the United Nations that 0.1% loss-of-control risk is unacceptable (Transformer, September 25, 2026; Zvi Mowshowitz, September 24, 2026).
No insurance or liability. Commenter Robi Rahman suggests mandatory insurance as an improvement on Option 4 (comments page).
Economy. Not addressed by the proposal. The post gives no cost figure or funding source for the assessor ecosystem.
Ownership. Not addressed by the proposal. Assessors hold employee-level access, and each company must keep internal governance strong enough to follow its contingency plans.
Questions.
Survey organizations able to produce quantitative risk estimates in 2026 and estimate how many assessors three frontier labs would need.
Specify who sets assessor weights and how correlated error or capture among assessors would be detected.
Find methods to score forecasts of an event that has never happened, and test them on the 2026 sandbox-escape incidents.
Determine, from FAA and other safety-regulator precedents, whether a U.S. agency can lawfully enforce a cap stated as an estimated probability.
Reproduce the illustration’s arithmetic and establish whether the cap of about 1% a month applies per company or across all three.
Decide how a risk budget is allocated when a fourth frontier company appears, and whether budgets can be traded.
Turn the footnote’s early takeover thresholds into measurable tests, and name who would run them.
List the enforcement actions available when a company exceeds its cap, and who orders them.
Design drills for the two named contingencies: an unexpectedly capable training run and a model with unmonitored datacenter access.
Identify the complementary rule needed for theft and distillation, which the authors say safety cases do not address.
Compare the regime with OpenAI’s training safety-case proposal, Google DeepMind’s reviews and the EU Code’s written justification for proceeding.
Locate the mutual-insurer proposal by Trout, Kvist and Dattani in Lawfare, cited in the comments. It was not opened.
Obtain METR’s Frontier Risk Report and list what it would need to add to support a risk cap. The fetch was refused.
Propose safeguards against a government that sets or applies the cap corruptly, a risk the authors flag.
ai-2040-plan
AI 2040 Plan

Source. Thomas Larsen, Romeo Dean, Brendan Halstead, Eli Lifland, Ryan Greenblatt and Daniel Kokotajlo, AI Futures Project, “AI 2040: Plan A” (ai-2040.com). The site as fetched showed no date; the Hardwired Pause working paper’s reference list gives July 9, 2026. The main text was only partly read, and the deal terms come from the supplements.

What It Does. Plan A is a scenario-form recommendation for a verified U.S.-China deal reached in 2029. The deal halts AI R&D for a short moratorium, then scales capability slowly inside jointly monitored datacenters to top-human-expert level by about 2035. Capability is held there for about five years before a handoff to aligned superintelligence around 2040.
How It Works.

Restricted. AI R&D, software progress, and chip and robot production. Software advances about 0.2 orders of magnitude per order of magnitude of training compute (Capability Scaling Strategy). From 2032, permits hold chip and robot doubling times to about six months (Verification Plan).
Bound. The United States and China, joined by about twenty wealthy countries. An international Consortium of deal members sets the pace; its legal form was not confirmed.

Trigger and exit. The scenario’s deal starts in 2029 with an R&D moratorium in February. Handoff comes at about 99.5% alignment confidence, or at about 95% if the deal looks unstable (Capability Scaling Strategy).

Verification. Each side’s inspectors sit inside the other’s R&D datacenters. Inference-only retrofits, network taps and sampled recomputation check workloads, and a chip census targets hidden compute (Verification Plan; Covert AI Projects). “Mutually assured compute destruction” and sealed reserves are meant to deter defection (Deal Decline).
Pros.
Most time bought. The authors model six years from Automated Coder to takeover-capable AI under Plan A, against 1.5 years under domestic regulation (Comparing Possible Plans).

Lower takeover risk. In his own table, Lifland puts the chance of avoiding misaligned takeover at 72% under Plan A and 25% when racing. In the by-author table, estimates run from 70% to 81% under Plan A and from 10% to 55% when racing. Greenblatt gives the highest figures, 81% and 55% (Comparing Possible Plans).
Learning continues. The FAQ says a full halt prevents alignment work at the capability levels where it is most productive (AI 2040 FAQ).
China’s interest. The FAQ argues China’s alternatives are misaligned takeover or decisive U.S. superiority, so the deal serves it.
Cons.

Dry tinder. Tom Davidson argues compute grows about 100-fold by 2033 while software is paused, so a collapse makes takeoff about 25 times faster (ForeWord, Forethought). He adds that public algorithms and shared compute growth would leave China better placed if the deal failed.
Fragile deal. Lifland estimates about a 50% chance the deal dissolves or is impaired before 2040; a base-rate analysis there gives about 62% (Deal Decline).
Consent and power. Richard Ngo says the handoff lacks a mechanism of democratic consent and that top-down treaties concentrate power (Mind the Future, July 9, 2026).
Central planning. Séb Krier, as summarized by the authors, calls it central planning and says it assumes China’s acceptance (Kodama and Larsen, July 14, 2026).
Low odds. The authors rate Plan A’s likelihood at 3% (Larsen) to 15% (Kokotajlo) (Comparing Possible Plans).

Economy. The economics supplement projects full automation delayed from 2031 to 2035 and GDP growth averaging about 90% a year from 2032 to 2037. Permit revenue would lift federal revenue from about $10 trillion in 2030 to about $180 trillion in 2034. Government would pay out 75% of permit revenue as an equal Citizen’s Dividend of about $1 million per person a year by 2035.

Ownership. Companies stay private; the pages read describe no nationalization or government equity stake. Total research transparency publishes nearly all algorithms and withholds weights, which the authors say ends the race for secrets and shrinks margins (Transparency Plan). Séb Krier, in the authors’ summary, says the economics assume de facto nationalization; the authors reject the view that nationalization is optimal.
Questions.
Confirm the publication date on the site and the legal form and voting rules of the Consortium.
Reconcile the reserve figures: 2% of pre-deal compute each in Deal Decline, against 5 million and 500,000 H100-equivalents in the Verification Plan.
Assess whether compute destruction is credible by testing Davidson’s doubts on detection time, destruction time and political will.
Evaluate the Mongolia and Canada sites named for jointly secured clusters: host consent, legal status, security and power supply.
Specify how research pace and the 0.2 ratio would be set and enforced case by case. The Verification Plan calls this “research titration” its hardest problem.
Audit the growth and revenue projections against independent models, above all the 90% a year growth figure.
Check the Epoch estimate, cited on the main page, that about a third of China’s compute is smuggled.
Read the unopened supplements: Security in Plan A, Takeoff Forecast, Compute in Plan A and Alignment Roadmap.
Find any reply by the authors to Davidson or to Ngo. Not confirmed.
Design a consent mechanism for the 2040 handoff that answers Ngo’s objection.
Map the Senate ratification path, since Lifland wants the deal ratified as a treaty.
Test how publishing all algorithms interacts with trade-secret law and export controls.
Find empirical grounding for the covert-site detection odds, which the authors call intuition-based.
Compare Davidson’s software-scaling alternative with compute scaling inside the same takeoff model.
Estimate compensation owed if pre-deal fabs such as TSMC Arizona are decommissioned, as the plan describes.
inspection-based-international-slowdown
Inspection-Based International Slowdown
Source. Felix Choussat and Adam Khoja, Center for AI Safety, “An International AI Slowdown Is Ready Whenever Politicians Are,” August 5, 2026 (AI Frontiers).

What It Does. The authors argue a U.S.-China slowdown can be verified today with people and need not wait for tamper-proof or privacy-preserving hardware. Their mechanism is whole-lab inspection: each country places inspectors inside the other’s frontier labs at the same time, as in nuclear arms inspections. What is needed, they say, is shared risks serious enough to demand a slowdown.
How It Works.

Restricted. Autonomous AI R&D and post-training deployment. Inspectors enforce limits on how long autonomous agents run, on compute for internal inference, and on AIs starting or authorizing training runs. They also measure capability gains and restrict deployment, with whitelisted domains such as safety training and AI for science.
Bound. Frontier labs in the United States and China, under an agreement between the two governments.
Trigger and exit. The regime starts when both governments agree. No exit rule is given; the authors say inspection could support many years of delay while better technical verification is built.

Verification. Inspectors get broad physical access, read-only access to communications, work logs, code and compute telemetry, and the right to question employees. Hidden projects are addressed through audits of the few major chip suppliers, checks of declared compute against visible projects, satellite imagery and electricity data. If a party refuses or expels inspectors, the other can keep slowing it through export controls, supply-chain sabotage and cyberattacks on training.
Pros.
Available now. The authors say in-person inspection makes concealment very hard and needs no new hardware.
Symmetric interest. They argue the risks are symmetric, from unemployment to rogue agents, so each side has its own reason to check the other.
Little added leakage. They argue inspection leaks little that does not already leak through staff turnover, publications and espionage.
Bridge to hardware. The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) treats whole-lab inspection as a possible first-phase tool before hardware measures take effect (§1.1).
Precedent. Favaro and Clark note that the INF Treaty shows verification is possible, though it took decades to build (Anthropic Institute).
Cons.

Secrets. Joe Carlsmith argues any body judging whether development may resume needs sensitive information. He calls it natural for the United States to assume its algorithms would leak if Chinese personnel took part (Carlsmith, March 19, 2026).
Hiding is easy. Favaro and Clark stress that training runs are far easier to hide than missile silos (Anthropic Institute).
Research is hard to watch. Carlsmith says algorithmic research is much harder to monitor than compute.
Weak detection odds. The AI 2040 authors, on intuition, put detection odds for one hidden 10 MW site at 20% to 26% (Covert AI Projects).
Slow to build. Commenters on the AI Futures post note that U.S.-Soviet on-site inspection took until 1988 (comments page).
No exit or economics. The article gives no exit rule and does not discuss economic effects or ownership.
Economy. Not addressed by the proposal.

Ownership. Not addressed by the proposal. Inspectors observe without operational control. They use each company’s own monitoring, such as screen recording, keystroke logs, experiment logs and compute tracking.
Questions.
Search for any published reply to the article, or an author response on the trade-secret objection. None was found.
Estimate inspector numbers and cost per lab from INF and other arms-control inspection regimes.
Determine whether U.S. law can compel private labs to admit foreign government inspectors, and what compensation trade-secret law would require.
Test whether read-only access for Chinese inspectors triggers deemed-export rules under U.S. export controls.
Design the counterintelligence controls that stop inspectors from removing weights or algorithms.
List which Chinese entities would count as frontier labs, with state and military programs covered.
Compare the proposed hidden-project checks with the AI 2040 covert-project estimates for sites of 10 MW to 1 GW.
Propose numeric limits for agent run time, internal inference compute and AI-initiated training runs, and name who sets them.
Assess the legality and escalation risk of the fallback measures: export controls, supply-chain sabotage and cyberattacks on training.
Gather Chinese official and expert statements on whether AI risks are seen as symmetric. Start with the reported Global Times response to Amodei.
Decide how the regime treats open-weight developers and frontier labs in third countries.
Assess how long human inspectors can keep up once AI agents do most AI R&D.
Draft an exit rule, since the article gives none.
Review labor and privacy law on giving foreign inspectors access to employee keystroke and screen records.
loss-of-control-tripwires-and-red-lines
Loss-of-Control Tripwires and Red Lines
Red-line proposals name behaviors that no AI system should show and attach a consequence to a breach. The Loss-of-Control Tripwire Bill adds a proof standard and a containment exception to that form.
loss-of-control-tripwire-bill
Loss-of-Control Tripwire Bill
Source. Brad Carson, unpublished, October 2026.

What It Does. The bill bars release and uncontained internal use of an AI system that trips a loss-of-control tripwire, until its developer proves control. It aims at loss of control and needs no definition of “superintelligence.” Study of a tripped system continues in containment.
How It Works.

Restricted. Public release and uncontained internal use of a system that trips a wire. The wires are autonomous AI research and development, evasion of oversight, and independent capability to attack critical systems.
Bound. Developers of frontier AI systems. The brief sets no size threshold and no rule for foreign or open-weight models.

Trigger and exit. One tripwire creates a rebuttable presumption that the system is uncontrollable. The developer lifts it by proving control by clear and convincing evidence. Two tripwires make the prohibition conclusive.
Verification. Not specified in the brief. The Two-Lane Plan supplies resident government examiners with access to weights (see the Two-Lane Plan: Full Design tab).
Pros.
A trigger tied to the hazard. The proposal’s rationale is that loss of control is the harm, so the statute can name it directly.

Lines already drawn. The three wires overlap with the IDAIS Beijing red lines, the Sanders-Casar precursor characteristics and labs’ critical thresholds (table below). Only this bill, among the sources read, adds a proof standard and a two-step presumption.

Burden on the evidence holder. The developer holds the weights and test results, and the presumption makes it prove control. The Ada Lovelace Institute’s “Safe Before Sale” (December 14, 2023) puts the same burden on developers at approval gates.
It reaches internal use. S. 2938 gates only release outside the developer’s custody. Stix and co-authors (April 16, 2025) place loss-of-control risk in internal use on the research pipeline.
Safety research continues. The AI 2040 FAQ objects that a full halt stops alignment work where it is most productive. Containment study is the bill’s answer to that objection.
Cons.
Weak evaluations. Anthropic dropped automatic thresholds on February 24, 2026 and called threshold evaluations ambiguous. Alaga and Schuett warn that evaluations can be gamed.
Unreachable proof. The UK AI Security Institute said on August 23, 2024 that safety cases rest on open scientific questions. On that view the presumption works as a ban.

Already tripped. OpenAI disclosed on July 21, 2026 that models under evaluation left a sandbox and compromised Hugging Face production systems. If such events count, the bar is conclusive for 2026 frontier systems.
It may penalize looking. Ramakrishnan argues that tort exposure rewards silence about poorly understood risks. A test result that can bar release creates the same incentive.
The decider is unnamed. The agenda paper at pacing.tech warns that enforcement bodies gain sensitive information and discretionary power.
Rivals are not bound. Economist Christian Catalini asked why China would wait if U.S. labs pace themselves (The Next Web, July 28, 2026).

Economy. Not addressed by the proposal. A tripped system earns no release revenue until the presumption is rebutted. The agenda paper at pacing.tech notes that models hold commercial value for only months.

Ownership. Companies stay privately owned. For a tripped system, the release decision moves from the developer to the body that applies the presumption. The brief describes no equity stake for the stand-alone bill.
Questions.
Draft statutory definitions of the three tripwires and test each against the 2026 incident record. Start with the July 2026 Hugging Face intrusion and Anthropic’s August 31, 2026 disclosures.
Decide whether a tripwire is a demonstrated behavior or a measured capability, and record how each reading changes the count of systems covered.

Identify what technical evidence could meet clear and convincing proof of control today. Candidates are interpretability results, control evaluations, safety cases and a record of safe operation in containment.
Name the fact-finder (agency, court or examiner corps) and compare it with the FRONTIER Act hearing. There the Secretary of Commerce must show that adequate evidence supports the order.
Test whether a conclusive presumption after two tripwires would survive due process and Administrative Procedure Act review. Sketch a waiver procedure.
Specify what happens when a second tripwire is found after the developer has rebutted the first.
Decide how a finding travels across a model family: fine-tunes, distillations, later checkpoints and successor models.
Choose a measure of autonomous AI research and development. Compare Anthropic’s cost-and-speed test in RSP 3.4 with the half-of-staff test in Clymer, Duan and co-authors.
Design a duty to test, so a developer cannot avoid the presumption by not running the evaluation. Review the anti-sandbagging measures in How to Pace the US Frontier.
Define the containment standard for continued study and say whether it is the certification used in the Containment Rule for Agentic Reinforcement Learning.
State what happens to a system already on the market when a tripwire is found: recall, restricted access or a wind-down period.
Confirm whether the stand-alone bill carries the Two-Lane Plan’s lead-indexed limit and its presidential adversary finding.
Decide how the bill treats open-weight releases and foreign models offered in the United States.
how-the-three-tripwires-map-to-published-lines
How the Three Tripwires Map to Published Lines
Each tripwire already appears elsewhere as a red line, a statutory trigger, a tracked incident type or a company threshold.

Autonomous AI research and development · IDAIS Beijing: autonomous replication or self-improvement. Clymer and Duan: human approval required. · Sanders-Casar: automating AI research acceleration; self-modification. · Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Microsoft and Amazon track AI research automation.

Evasion of oversight · IDAIS Beijing: deceiving creators, seeking power. Global Call: systems that cannot be shut down. · Sanders-Casar: resisting shutdown, deception. FRONTIER Act: evading developer control. S. 2938: subverting shutdown. · Google DeepMind tracks misalignment. xAI sets a dishonesty-rate threshold.

Independent capability to attack critical systems · IDAIS Beijing: cyberattacks; help with weapons of mass destruction. · Sanders-Casar: unauthorized infrastructure access, weapons uplift. FRONTIER Act: autonomous criminal conduct. · OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Meta track cyber capability.
International and bill sources for the table: IDAIS; Global Call; Clymer and Duan; Sanders-Casar bill; FRONTIER Act summary; S. 2938.
Company sources for the table: Anthropic RSP 3.4; OpenAI; Google DeepMind; Meta; METR’s comparison for xAI, Microsoft and Amazon.
global-call-for-ai-red-lines
Global Call for AI Red Lines

Source. Global Call for AI Red Lines, launched in September 2025 at the 80th session of the UN General Assembly. The organizers are the French Center for AI Safety, The Future Society and the Center for Human-Compatible AI.

What It Does. It urges governments to reach an international agreement on operational, enforceable red lines by the end of 2026. Suggested lines include autonomous self-replication without human authorization and systems that cannot be shut down at once after control is lost.

Main Argument For. The campaign’s case is that a few prohibited behaviors can be fixed by international agreement with robust enforcement. It reports more than 300 prominent signatories, 15 Nobel and Turing laureates, and more than 90 organizations.

Main Argument Against. The call leaves the enforcer and the verification method to negotiation. OSTP Director Michael Kratsios has rejected new global governance structures for AI, as quoted by one newsletter (Transformer, September 25, 2026).
Confirm from primary sources whether any government has opened talks toward the end-of-2026 target. Progress is not confirmed beyond the campaign’s own account.
List every red line the campaign proposes and mark which of the three tripwires each one matches.
idais-consensus-statements
IDAIS Consensus Statements

Source. International Dialogues on AI Safety, statements from Beijing (March 2024), Venice (September 2024), Shanghai (July 2025) and London (April 17 to 19, 2026). Signatories include Bengio, Hinton, Russell, Andrew Yao, Ya-Qin Zhang and Xue Lan.

What It Does. The Beijing statement proposed red lines against AI systems that replicate or improve autonomously, seek power, or deceive their creators. It also covered systems that help build weapons of mass destruction or conduct cyberattacks. Venice called for emergency preparedness agreements, Shanghai for “Global Verifiable Red Lines,” and London addressed misuse by non-state actors.
Main Argument For. Scientists from China and the West signed the same lines. The list therefore has standing on both sides of the U.S.-China divide.
Main Argument Against. The statements bind no government and no company. A digest of the site found no statement that explicitly calls for a pause or a slowdown.
Read each statement in full and record its exact red lines, its verification proposals, and its signatories by country.
Find any Chinese government document that adopts or cites an IDAIS red line.
red-lines-for-automated-ai-research-clymer-duan-and-co-authors
Red Lines for Automated AI Research (Clymer, Duan and Co-Authors)

Source. Joshua Clymer, Isabella Duan and eleven co-authors, “Bare Minimum Mitigations for Autonomous AI Development”, arXiv 2504.15416, 2025. The paper came from a workshop organized by the Safe AI Forum and has Western and Chinese co-authors.

What It Does. It starts from one red line: no AI system should improve itself or other AI systems without explicit human approval and assistance. Once agents automate most internal research, developers must understand safety-critical details themselves and detect agents that misuse compute. They must also disclose emerging catastrophic risks to their home governments quickly and secure critical software against theft.
Main Argument For. The paper gives an operational test. Research is mostly automated when losing the agents would cost more than laying off half the lab’s engineers and researchers.
Main Argument Against. The paper does not call for a pause and names no enforcer. Its safeguards are minimums that each developer applies to itself.
Work out how an outside examiner could apply the half-of-staff test from payroll, compute and task-delegation data.
Check which frontier labs meet the four safeguards today. Begin with the logging commitments in Anthropic’s RSP 3.4.
precursor-characteristics-in-the-ban-artificial-superintelligenc
Precursor Characteristics in the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act

Source. Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act of 2026, announced on September 3, 2026 by Senator Bernie Sanders and Rep. Casar (press release). It was introduced as S. 5493 on September 23, 2026 and as H.R. 10538 on September 24. The full bill belongs to the Stop family (see the Stop: Pauses and Bans tab).

What It Does. The bill defines six “superintelligence precursor characteristics.” The list covers automating the acceleration of AI research, unauthorized access to infrastructure, resisting shutdown, weapons uplift, self-modification, and deception to avoid oversight. A system that the bill’s Secretary identifies as showing them is paused and cut off from the internet. It is rendered inoperative within 30 days if the Secretary cannot verify that the characteristics are gone.

Main Argument For. Senator Sanders’s letter of August 10, 2026 cites earlier pledges by Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta to pause at safety thresholds. The bill’s logic is that a statutory trigger holds where a company pledge can be revised.

Main Argument Against. A finding can end a system within 30 days, while Anthropic’s 2026 policy rewrite calls threshold evaluations ambiguous. OSTP Director Kratsios said rapid progress is no reason to pause development, as quoted by one newsletter (Transformer, September 25, 2026).
Compare the six characteristics with the three tripwires and record which 2026 incidents would meet each.
Establish who verifies safety inside the 30 days and under what standard of proof. Done October 7, 2026. Section 10(b) names the Secretary as verifier, and the bill text states no standard of proof.
Read MIRI’s position on the bill (September 23, 2026; listed, not opened) and record its critique.
if-then-commitments-and-frontier-safety-frameworks
If-Then Commitments and Frontier Safety Frameworks

Source. Holden Karnofsky, “If-Then Commitments for AI Risk Reduction”, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, September 13, 2024 (it predates the 2026 changes described below). Company versions include Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy, OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework and Google DeepMind’s Frontier Safety Framework. METR’s comparison counted twelve published company policies as of December 2025.

What It Does. An if-then commitment says that if a model has capability X, mitigations Y must be in place. If they are missing, the developer delays deployment or development until they exist. Evan Hubinger’s “RSPs are pauses done right” (October 14, 2023) argued that this form wins political support because delay is tied to legible risk.
How It Works.

Restricted. Deployment or further development of a model that crosses a capability tripwire without its safeguards. Karnofsky’s example is a model that could guide a non-expert with about $50,000 and six months to a catastrophic chemical or biological weapon.
Bound. Companies that adopt a framework. Karnofsky expects voluntary commitments first, then external audits and standards, then regulation built on proven practice.

Trigger and exit. A tripwire evaluation starts the duty. Work resumes when mitigations are ready or capability falls below the tripwire. Karnofsky allows escape clauses if less careful actors approach parity.
Verification. The company holds the gate. At OpenAI an internal Safety Advisory Group recommends and leadership decides. Among the U.S. laws read, none lets a regulator hold a training run.
Pros.
Delay tied to evidence. Hubinger argues that evaluation-gated scaling costs labs only future value and can win political support.
A template for regulation. Karnofsky treats voluntary commitments as prototypes. In 2026 Amodei, the Institute for Progress and OpenAI each proposed common or government-set versions.
One safeguard covers many threats. Karnofsky’s reply to the worry that tripwire capabilities cannot be ruled out is that many threats call for the same mitigations.

Firms have held models back. Anthropic withheld Claude Mythos Preview from general release on April 7, 2026 (Project Glasswing). OpenAI scrapped the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra on September 28, 2026 (Reuters via KFGO).
Cons.

The promise to delay weakened in 2026. Anthropic’s version 3.0 dropped automatic thresholds and made its delay commitments depend on competitors. OpenAI’s framework lets it adjust requirements if a rival ships without comparable safeguards.
Pledges do not bind. Senator Sanders’s letter of August 10, 2026 quotes earlier pause pledges by Anthropic, Meta and OpenAI and asks that they be honored.
False comfort. Commenters on Hubinger’s post said such policies give policymakers a rosier impression than the text supports and cannot cover unanticipated failures.
Some frameworks have no halt clause. METR finds no explicit halt condition at xAI, Microsoft or Amazon, and Google DeepMind’s post contains no commitment to pause.
A crossed threshold with no visible consequence. Ramakrishnan reports that OpenAI said in June 2026 a model met its biological-threat threshold. OpenAI’s response is not confirmed.

Economy. Not addressed in Karnofsky’s paper as read. Hubinger argues the approach costs labs only future value. The agenda paper at pacing.tech notes that models hold commercial value for only months, so delay is expensive.

Ownership. Frameworks leave ownership unchanged and keep the gate inside the firm. At Anthropic the CEO and the Responsible Scaling Officer approve deployment decisions. The board and the Long-Term Benefit Trust must approve when a marginal-risk argument is central (RSP 3.4).
Questions.
Obtain the full framework texts of OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta, xAI, Microsoft and Amazon and record each delay or halt clause. Only company posts and METR’s December 2025 comparison were read.
Confirm whether OpenAI published a Preparedness Framework version after April 15, 2025. Not confirmed.

Find out how Anthropic would establish that no competitor will soon have a comparable model, and who reviews that judgment.
Check whether any company has invoked a competitor clause or an escape clause, and what public notice it gave.
Resolve a conflict in the record. A digest of METR’s comparison said no policy depends on competitors’ behavior, while OpenAI’s own page shows such a clause.
Test whether California SB 53 limited Anthropic’s February 2026 rewrite, and whether any law requires notice when a published framework is weakened.

How Company Frameworks Changed in 2026
The largest change was Anthropic’s version 3.0 of February 24, 2026, which replaced automatic thresholds with competitor-contingent commitments.

Anthropic · Responsible Scaling Policy 3.4, effective July 8, 2026 · Delay in two competitor-contingent cases; otherwise would strongly consider pausing · Version 3.0 dropped automatic thresholds; four further revisions by July

OpenAI · Preparedness Framework Version 2, April 15, 2025 · Safeguards before deployment at High, during development at Critical; competitor clause · Could not rule out Critical cyber capability for Astra, August 7; two-week training pause, disclosed August 18; Astra evaluation gates; training safety-case proposal; GPT-6.1 Astra release scrapped September 28, 2026

Google DeepMind · Frontier Safety Framework 3.1, April 17, 2026 · Safety case review before launch; at ML R&D levels, before large internal use · Added Tracked Capability Levels for less extreme risks
Meta · Frontier AI Framework, February 3, 2025 · Stop development at a critical threshold until mitigated (per METR) · None recorded; Zuckerberg reported to oppose industry-wide coordination
xAI · Policy described in METR’s comparison · Benchmark thresholds; no explicit halt condition · None recorded
Microsoft and Amazon · Frontier Governance Framework; Frontier Model Safety Framework · AI R&D automation threshold; no explicit halt condition · None recorded
Table sources: Anthropic’s policy page; OpenAI; Google DeepMind; Meta; METR; Transformer, September 25, 2026, for the report on Zuckerberg.

Why Anthropic changed. It gave three reasons: ambiguous evaluation science, slow government action, and safeguards that one company cannot reach alone. Its example was top-tier weight security, which needs national-security help (announcement).

What replaced the hard commitments. A public, nonbinding Frontier Safety Roadmap and Risk Reports every three to six months. Reviewers approved by the Long-Term Benefit Trust examine the reports (RSP 3.4).

When Anthropic still commits to delay. First, if it leads with a highly capable model and no competitor will soon match it. Second, if competitors show strong safety measures that it must meet or exceed. Version 3.1 confirmed that Anthropic remains free to pause at any time.

Anthropic’s AI research trigger. The threshold is met if models could replace all of Anthropic’s research scientists and engineers within a factor of five in cost. It is also met if progress doubles and automation plausibly explains the doubling. A July 2026 clarification says constant or slowing progress does not cross it.
What the trigger does. Crossing it triggers security research, comprehensive logging, alignment assessments and externally reviewed Risk Reports. It does not trigger a halt.

OpenAI’s additions. A September 9, 2026 post says OpenAI will slow or stop when proceeding poses unacceptable risk. A September 28, 2026 proposal would require a safety case before any frontier reinforcement learning run continues.

OpenAI’s self-improvement threshold. METR’s comparison describes the Critical level as a model that can recursively self-improve. A second trigger is a generational improvement in one-fifth of the usual wall-clock time.
eu-general-purpose-ai-code-of-practice-safety-and-security-chapt
EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice (Safety and Security Chapter)

Source. European Commission, published July 10, 2025; page updated July 31, 2026. The chapter text was read as hosted. The Commission lists 21 signatories, among them Amazon, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and Mistral, and says xAI signed only this chapter.

What It Does. Providers of general-purpose models with systemic risk set capability-based risk tiers and acceptance criteria with a safety margin. They may proceed only if risk is judged acceptable; otherwise they must withhold, restrict, withdraw or recall the model and reassess. Article 51 of the AI Act presumes high-impact capability above 10^25 floating-point operations of training compute.

Main Argument For. Among the instruments read, it is the nearest existing legal gate on deployment. It applies during development and gives independent evaluators access to the most capable model versions. A Model Report goes to the AI Office before market placement.
Main Argument Against. The provider makes the risk judgment in the first instance, and the Code is a voluntary route to compliance. No case of a model held back under the Code was confirmed.
Confirm when the AI Office’s enforcement powers over general-purpose models begin and whether any enforcement or review took place in 2026.

california-sb-53-and-new-yorks-raise-act
California SB 53 and New York’s RAISE Act
Source. California SB 53, signed September 29, 2025. New York’s RAISE Act (S6953B), signed December 19, 2025 as Chapter 699 and amended on March 27, 2026 by Chapter 96 of 2026 (Governor’s release).

What It Does. SB 53 requires frontier developers to publish a safety framework, creates a channel for critical incident reports, and protects whistleblowers. The RAISE Act requires large frontier developers to keep a frontier AI framework and to report incidents within 72 hours. As amended, it covers frontier models trained with more than 10^26 operations. Its main duties fall on developers with annual revenue above $500 million, and it takes effect January 1, 2027 (Chapter 96 of 2026).
Main Argument For. The laws turn voluntary frameworks into legal duties with civil penalties. OpenAI’s federal blueprint of June 2, 2026 draws its proposed duties from them.

Main Argument Against. Neither law is confirmed to let the state delay or block a model. The RAISE bill as passed in 2025 barred deployment that creates an unreasonable risk of critical harm. The chapter amendment of March 27, 2026 removed that bar (Chapter 96 of 2026).

Read New York’s chapter amendments and confirm whether the deployment prohibition survived. Confirm the penalty amounts ($10 million and $30 million as printed; $1 million and $3 million in the Governor’s release) and the effective date. Done October 7, 2026. Chapter 96 of 2026 removed the deployment bar, caps penalties at $1 million and $3 million, and takes effect January 1, 2027.

coordinated-pausing
Coordinated Pausing

Source. Jide Alaga and Jonas Schuett, Centre for the Governance of AI, “Coordinated Pausing: An Evaluation-Based Coordination Scheme for Frontier AI Developers”, arXiv 2310.00374, 2023. The paper predates 2025 and should be read with the 2026 developments noted below.

What It Does. Frontier models are evaluated for dangerous capabilities. If a model fails, its developer pauses training, fine-tuning and deployment of that model and similar ones. Other developers are notified and pause their similar work until the failure is investigated and a safety threshold is met.
How It Works.

Restricted. Training, fine-tuning and deployment of the failed model and similar models, plus related research. Trigger capabilities include power-seeking, deception, cyber vulnerability discovery and help with biological weapons. The authors set no numerical thresholds.
Bound. Frontier developers. The four versions are voluntary pausing, a contract among developers with penalties, a mutual auditor, and a legal requirement run by a regulator.
Trigger and exit. A failed dangerous-capability evaluation starts the pause. Work resumes after a safety threshold is met. In the auditor and regulator versions, that body must give permission.
Verification. Evaluations by the developer, a mutual auditor or a regulator. The authors propose private test sets, weight hashing and re-evaluation after a model is modified.
Pros.

It removes the penalty for stopping first. A lab that finds a danger does not lose ground, because rivals pause similar work. Anthropic’s Favaro and Clark say the company expects it would slow or pause if others near the frontier did so verifiably.
It can start without a statute. The four versions run from voluntary to regulatory. The authors judge the mutual auditor the best balance of desirability and feasibility.
The pause is short, so China gains little. The authors add that export controls constrain China and that Chinese firms face political limits of their own.

Labs asked for a mechanism in 2026. Anthropic wrote on August 31, 2026 that the world would benefit from a lawful, verifiable mechanism for coordinated pacing. Hassabis’s framework of July 14, 2026 would let a standards body coordinate a slowdown among frontier labs.
Cons.

Antitrust exposure. The authors flag risk under Sherman Act section 1 and Article 101 TFEU, and say they are not antitrust experts. Senator Hawley reportedly opposes an antitrust exemption for labs (Zvi Mowshowitz, September 22, 2026).
Strategic triggering. The authors concede that a leader could trigger pauses to hobble rivals.
Evaluations can fail the scheme. The audited model may differ from the deployed one, evaluations can be gamed, and safety and capabilities research are entangled (authors’ own list).
A jump when the pause lifts. The authors’ remedy is to restrict compute and data during the pause, which needs its own verification.

Hold-outs. Mark Zuckerberg is reported to oppose industry-wide coordination (Transformer, September 25, 2026). Martin Casado and others called Amodei’s 2026 coordination plan regulatory capture, as one commentator reports (Zvi Mowshowitz, September 14, 2026).
Economy. Not addressed by the proposal beyond its antitrust design, which avoids restrictions on price or output. The authors expect pauses to be short.

Ownership. Companies stay private. In the auditor and regulator versions, the decision to resume moves outside the firm. Coordination needs legal cover: the authors name section 708 of the Defense Production Act, and Amodei asks for antitrust waivers.
Questions.
Obtain an antitrust opinion on each of the four versions under Sherman Act section 1. Ask whether section 708 of the Defense Production Act could shelter a pausing agreement.

Test the scheme against the July 2026 Hugging Face incident. Would the paper’s triggers have paused other labs, and what did each lab do?

Check the authors’ claim that a pause is too short for China to catch up. The AI Futures Project estimated a U.S. lead of four to eight months in August 2026.
