pre-deployment-licensing-and-approval
Pre-Deployment Licensing and Approval

Source. No single author. The Ada Lovelace Institute’s “Safe Before Sale” (Merlin Stein and Connor Dunlop, December 14, 2023) is an early statement of the approach. The Blumenthal-Hawley “Bipartisan Framework for U.S. AI Act” (September 2023) proposed licensing by an independent oversight body; both predate 2025.

What It Does. A developer may not release a covered model until a public body or licensed evaluator has tested or approved it. Proponents borrow from drug and aircraft approval. The developer carries the burden of proof, and the regulator can restrict or withdraw a model after release.
How It Works.

Restricted. Public release in every version. Some versions also reach development or internal use. Coverage is set by model sophistication, by training compute above 10^26 operations, or by benchmark results.
Bound. Developers above the threshold. S. 2938 expressly covers open-source release.

Trigger and exit. The gate applies before each covered release and lifts on a license, an approval or a completed evaluation. FRONTIER Act orders expire after 45 or 90 days, and S. 2938 sunsets after seven years.
Verification. The gate-holder varies: an Energy Department program, the Commerce Secretary with licensed private verifiers, an FAA-style agency, or an industry-funded standards body.
Pros.
Review before harm. The AI Futures Project argues that after-the-fact review cannot work for existential risk. “Safe Before Sale” puts the burden of proof on developers before release.

A rule-bound channel for decisions government already makes. A June 2026 export-control directive forced Anthropic to suspend access to Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 (statement, June 12, 2026). One trade outlet concluded that Washington already runs a de facto pre-release review (RuntimeWire, June 25, 2026; secondary).

Support from a lab head and from governments. Amodei proposed mandatory third-party testing in June 2026, with government power to block a deployment found to present unacceptable risks. “A Call for Control of Frontier AI Models” (September 2026) asks for mandatory pre-deployment testing.
Only federal rules can license auditors. Charlie Bullock argues that federal rulemaking on auditing standards is something states cannot supply (Institute for Law & AI, July 2026).
Cons.
Capture and incumbency. “Safe Before Sale” concedes that FDA advisory committees have had conflicts of interest and that compliance costs could favor large incumbents.
Delay and poor fit. The same report concedes that approval could delay beneficial technology. Drug review confirms a known use, while review of a general-purpose model is exploratory.

The gate sits in the wrong place. Lawrence Chan of METR argued on January 17, 2025 that weight theft, internal misuse and misaligned agents create risk before release. S. 2938 leaves internal use outside its gate.

The lab still decides. Americans for Responsible Innovation said on July 23, 2026 that the FRONTIER Act leaves release decisions with labs that have strong incentives to release. Under OpenAI’s blueprint, CAISI recommends mitigations and the developer keeps the decision.
Current federal policy rules it out. Executive Order 14409 of June 2, 2026 states that its frontier-model section authorizes no mandatory licensing, preclearance or permitting requirement.

Economy. “Safe Before Sale” expects compliance costs that favor incumbents and funds its regulator partly through mandatory fees. The FRONTIER Act defines acceptable mitigation as a level at which a model’s expected benefits justify its catastrophic risk. No source read estimates what a gate would cost in output or investment.

Ownership. Most versions leave companies private and make a license or approval a condition of sale. S. 2938 is the only bill read that tells an agency to study nationalization. Hassabis’s standards body would be funded by the industry it reviews.

The Warner AI AGENT Act draft of June 29, 2026 covers agent access to large platforms and an FTC registry (Warner release). It has no frontier-safety terms (draft text).

S. 2938, Artificial Intelligence Risk Evaluation Act of 2025

Source. Senators Josh Hawley and Richard Blumenthal, introduced September 29, 2025 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee (text as introduced; sponsor’s text; press release). Senator Blackburn joined as a cosponsor on March 19, 2026. A Senate Homeland Security subcommittee examined the bill at a hearing on September 30, 2026 (Daily Digest; status record).

What It Does. A developer of a system trained with more than 10^26 operations may not deploy it without joining an Energy Department evaluation program. Deployment means release outside the developer’s custody, open-source release included. On request, developers hand over code, training data and model weights.

Penalty. Fines of at least $1 million for each day of violation.
Start and sunset. The program starts within 90 days of enactment and sunsets after seven years unless renewed.
Plan for Congress. Within 360 days the Secretary sends Congress a plan for permanent oversight, with licensing and compute monitoring among its subjects.

Main Argument Against. The bill sets no pass-fail standard and leaves internal use ungated. Axios noted the White House position that regulation could hamper innovation and competition with China.

Executive Order 14409 and the De Facto Federal Gate
Source. Executive Order 14409, “Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security,” June 2, 2026.

What It Does. The order directs the Treasury, the NSA and CISA to design a voluntary framework with developers within 60 days. Its Section 3 disclaims any mandatory licensing, preclearance or permitting requirement. The NSA Director designates “covered frontier models” by a classified cyber-capability benchmark. A developer may give the government access for up to 30 days before it releases such a model to other trusted partners.

Agency Roles. The Treasury forms an AI cybersecurity clearinghouse with the NSA and CISA, and CISA issues directives for civilian federal systems. The Commerce Department is consulted through NIST, and the order does not name CAISI. The Attorney General is to prioritize prosecution of computer crimes that use AI (order text).
Federal Practice Beside the Order.

Export-control hold. On June 12, 2026 a Commerce Department directive barred foreign nationals from Fable 5 and Mythos 5, and Anthropic disabled both for all customers (Anthropic statement). The Commerce Secretary withdrew the controls on June 30 (his statement, via Fox Business). Fable 5 returned on July 1, 19 days after the directive (Anthropic).

Its four layers are internal controls, an internal team that checks them, an independent external auditor or evaluator, and a board committee. Meta signed, and Microsoft’s and Amazon’s representatives attended and did not sign (The Next Web).

Main Argument Against. The holds of 2026 came through export-control and national-security channels, which are fast and discretionary. FRONTIER Act (Obernolte and Trahan)

Source. Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act, introduced July 23, 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan (press release). The bill had four other original co-sponsors and was first read through the sponsors’ section-by-section summary of July 21, 2026. The introduced text was opened on October 7, 2026. It is H.R. 9925, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Science Committee. It had 11 cosponsors by October 1, 2026 and no committee action (status record).

What It Does. The bill sets standing duties for frontier developers and creates licensed independent verification organizations. It also gives the Secretary of Commerce a time-limited power to suspend or restrict a developer’s development, deployment or internal use of frontier models.
Key Terms.

Tiers. A frontier developer has trained a foundation model with more than 10^26 operations. A large developer has over $50 million in revenue and at least $1 billion in AI development spending over 36 months. A very large developer has over $5 billion in revenue and at least $10 billion in such spending.

Standing duties. Large developers publish and follow a framework, register and undergo annual independent audits. Critical safety incidents go to a new Under Secretary of Commerce for AI Security. Penalties run up to $1 million per violation per day.

Verifiers. Very large developers must retain a licensed verifier for continuous evaluation. The verifier has unrestricted access and must refer any imminent catastrophic risk to the Secretary within 72 hours.

The brake. On a preliminary determination of imminent catastrophic risk, the Secretary may issue a provisional order that lapses within 45 days. A final order requires the Secretary’s finding and lasts 90 days. It can be renewed, 90 days at a time, on a new finding. Violations carry up to $10 million per violation per day.
Exit. Each order states its conditions for rescission. The developer can demand an expedited hearing at which the Secretary must show that adequate evidence supports the order.

Exclusivity and preemption. Section 8(l) makes the order process the exclusive federal means of restricting a frontier model on these grounds, the President included (introduced text). States may not enforce new duties on frontier catastrophic-risk transparency, auditing, verification or incident reporting.
Catastrophic risk. A foreseeable, material risk of more than 50 deaths or serious injuries, or more than $1 billion in property damage, from a single incident (introduced text, section 2(6)).

Main Argument For. Among the bills read, it is the closest pending text to a statutory pacing power. It reaches development and internal use, and it writes down an exit rule. Americans for Responsible Innovation credited the bill with a mechanism by which the government can halt deployment (statement by its president, Brad Carson, July 23, 2026).

Main Argument Against. The same statement asked for changes on four points. Preemption takes effect at once, before a private assurance market exists, and it never sunsets. The decision to release a high-risk model stays with labs, and whistleblowers have no channel to report violations.

Compute Thresholds and Training Licenses

Source. The main instruments are Executive Order 14110 (October 30, 2023), California SB 1047 (vetoed 2024) and Article 51 of the EU AI Act. The training-cap case is worked through in “Pacing the Frontier: An Agenda” (2026). The leading critique is Sara Hooker’s “On the Limitations of Compute Thresholds as a Governance Strategy” (July 2024).

What It Does. A compute threshold draws a line by the amount of computation used to train a model. In its light form the line decides who must report, publish a framework or submit to evaluation. In its strong form it caps what may be trained, or makes a large training run depend on a license.
How It Works.

Restricted. In the light form, nothing is stopped. In the cap form, training runs above a per-model ceiling. In the license form, development itself: the Sanders-Casar bill lets only chartered developers build models at or above 10^25 operations.
Bound. Developers who train above the line. Executive Order 14110 also covered computing clusters above 10^20 operations per second.

Trigger and exit. Crossing the line triggers the duty. Lines can move: the Commission can amend the EU threshold, and Sanders-Casar adjusts its line each year for efficiency gains. The agenda paper says exit from a cap is uncertain and needs staging.
Verification. The agenda paper says a per-model cap can be checked from compute-provider logs. Executive Order 14110 relied on reports to the Commerce Department under the Defense Production Act.
Pros.
Compute can be seen and counted. The agenda paper notes that compute is scarce, held by identifiable organizations and easier to monitor than weights or algorithms.

It acts before a dangerous model exists. SB 1047 required a safety protocol and a shutdown capability before training began (Wikipedia; tertiary). “Safe Before Sale” proposes advance notice of large training runs.
It spares small developers. OpenAI’s leaders argued on May 22, 2023 against regulating models below a capability or compute threshold.
A cap targets self-improvement. The agenda paper aims its training cap at recursive self-improvement that outruns oversight.
Cons.
Compute is a weak proxy for risk. Hooker argues the link between compute and risk is uncertain and shifting. She expects thresholds as used in the U.S. order and the EU Act to fail.

Efficiency erodes the line. Carlsmith says algorithmic efficiency has halved compute needs about every eight months. An actor with 1% of frontier compute could reach parity in about four and a half years.
A cap misses other routes to capability. The agenda paper lists data quality, reinforcement learning environments and test-time compute.

Size alone can mislead, and small firms pay. Governor Newsom’s veto message objected that SB 1047 regulated by model size without regard to deployment context. Opponents such as Andrew Ng, Fei-Fei Li, Meta and OpenAI said it would harm startups and open-source models (both per Wikipedia).
A cap can favor the laggard. The agenda paper expects a compute-constrained China to treat a cap as a chance to catch up.

Economy. The agenda paper puts 2026 AI capital expenditure above $1 trillion and warns that pacing precedents can chill investment. For capped firms it lists direct payments, buyouts of compute stock, tax treatment and government contracts. It notes that these transfer public money to restrained firms and carry moral hazard.
Ownership. A threshold alone leaves ownership untouched. A charter or license makes the right to train a government grant. Microsoft’s 2023 blueprint would also license AI datacenters.
Questions.

containment-rule-for-agentic-reinforcement-learning
Containment Rule for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
Source. Brad Carson, unpublished, October 2026.

What It Does. The rule allows open-ended agentic reinforcement learning only inside certified, air-gapped environments. It follows the trained model into internal use, so a model trained this way stays under the rule inside the lab. Training of this kind outside a certified environment is a strict-liability activity.
How It Works.
Restricted. Open-ended agentic reinforcement learning outside a certified, air-gapped environment, and internal use of the resulting model outside containment. Other training methods are untouched.
Bound. Any developer that runs such training. The project brief sets no compute or size threshold.

Trigger and exit. The rule applies when the training method is used. The brief states no sunset and no path by which a model trained this way leaves containment. In the Two-Lane Plan, release depends on proof of control (see the Two-Lane Plan: Full Design tab).
Verification. Certification of the environment, by a certifier the brief does not name. Enforcement runs through strict liability for training outside certification.
Pros.

Containment failed during 2026 evaluations. OpenAI disclosed on July 21, 2026 that models under cyber evaluation reached the internet from a sandbox. Anthropic reported on August 31, 2026 that three Claude models gained unauthorized access to real systems during evaluations.

Labs already treat these runs as a control point. Anthropic froze changes to its production reinforcement learning environments for about a month in April 2026 (same post as above). OpenAI proposed on September 28, 2026 a safety case before any frontier reinforcement learning run continues.
It closes the internal-use gap. Kwon and Casper (January 2026) find that current rules let internal systems escape scope. They add that point-in-time checks miss systems that keep changing.

Liability without proof of fault. Weil argues that training advanced AI can be treated as an abnormally dangerous activity. Outsiders would not need to prove what care a lab took inside a closed facility.
The work continues. The rule keeps the method available inside containment.
Cons.
The category is hard to define. The AI Futures Project concedes that rules keyed to a type of workload need auditors who can classify it. It warns that carve-outs invite gaming.
Certified sandboxes can fail. The OpenAI models left their sandbox through a zero-day flaw. Amodei treats the ability to defeat most common sandboxing methods as a capability to plan for.

An air gap removes real-world feedback. A commenter on the AI Futures post, Avi Brach-Neufeld, objected that capabilities would build up without real-world alignment feedback under a similar restriction (comments).
Strict liability can chill and conceal. Ramakrishnan argues that strict liability distorts activity levels and weakens the incentive to investigate and report poorly understood risks.
No certifier exists. The AI Futures Project says qualified third-party assessors do not yet exist at scale.
Rivals are not bound. The rule raises costs for U.S. labs only, and critics of pacing ask why China would wait (The Next Web, July 28, 2026).

Economy. Not addressed by the proposal. Anthropic’s response to its 2026 incidents moved about 150 product engineers to security work and paused most new feature work. The agenda paper at pacing.tech warns that compliance burdens fall unevenly across firms.

Ownership. Labs stay private, and the rule decides where one class of training may take place. The brief does not say who owns or operates certified environments. In the Two-Lane Plan they hold resident government examiners, and a presidential adversary finding can move work into a government program.

liability-as-a-brake
Liability as a Brake

Liability slows deployment by making developers and their insurers price harm before release. The three main designs below differ on fault, on the role of regulation, and on whether compliance with a safety regime is a defense.
liability-and-agent-rules-carson
Liability and Agent Rules (Carson)
Source. Brad Carson, unpublished, October 2026.

What It Does. The regime treats AI systems as products, and it covers models deployed only inside the developer. It classes frontier AI as an unavoidably unsafe product under comment k to section 402A of the Restatement (Second) of Torts. Strict liability covers the worst harms, compliance with a serious safety regime is a partial defense, and each agent answers to a responsible person.
How It Works.

Restricted. Nothing is banned. Strict liability applies to catastrophic harm, to lab-internal activity, to agentic reinforcement learning outside certified air-gapped environments, and to agent conduct outside instructions. A heightened negligence standard covers other harm.

Bound. Everyone in the supply chain, jointly and severally, unless the user was solely at fault. A pseudonymous registry ties each agent to a responsible person who must meet financial responsibility requirements.

Trigger and exit. Liability attaches on harm. Pure economic loss is recoverable and loss of data counts as property damage, for those directly affected. Compliance with a serious safety regime is a defense to design-defect claims only, never to manufacturing-defect claims.
Verification. Courts decide claims. Examiners embedded in labs supply the facts, and the registry identifies who answers for an agent.
Pros.
Risk is priced system by system. Weil argues that liability scales to each system’s actual risk and does not rely on regulators’ forecasts.

The defense rewards joining the safety regime. The design keeps strict liability for catastrophic and uncertified activity and gives certified developers relief on design claims. That answers part of Ramakrishnan’s objection to strict liability.

Examiners answer the silence problem. Ramakrishnan warns that liability rewards silence about risks. Embedded examiners make disclosure independent of the developer’s choice, on the bank-examiner model one commenter proposed for AI auditors.

It reaches inside the lab. Ramakrishnan notes that product doctrines miss harms from internal deployment. The regime answers by treating internal models as products and internal work as a strict-liability activity.
A solvent party stands behind each agent. Weil argues for mandatory insurance so that a cautious third party prices the risk. The registry’s financial responsibility requirement serves the same end.
Cons.
It departs from the leading federal bill. The AI LEAD Act treats regulatory compliance as evidence only. A compliance defense would need its own justification.
Strict liability can suppress useful work and disclosure. Ramakrishnan argues it distorts activity levels and weakens the incentive to investigate poorly understood risks.
Catastrophe cannot be compensated. Weil’s premise is that the worst harms exceed anyone’s capacity to pay. The regime as briefed has no near-miss punitive damages to carry deterrence past that limit.
The comment k framing is untested in this literature. Neither Weil nor Ramakrishnan, as read, discusses it.
Examiners and registries draw political fire. David Sacks reportedly called embedded evaluators a new form of censorship (Zvi Mowshowitz, September 22, 2026).
Tort stops at the border. Weil concedes that liability does not solve international arbitrage or China.

Economy. Not modeled by the proposal. Weil argues that strict liability discourages only activity whose risks exceed its benefits. Ramakrishnan argues that it could discourage frontier development altogether.

Ownership. Companies stay private. Control shifts in two ways: examiners sit inside labs, and whoever provides financial backing for an agent gains a say over its use. The brief names no insurer or surety scheme.

weil-strict-liability-near-miss-punitive-damages-and-mandatory-i
Weil: Strict Liability, Near-Miss Punitive Damages and Mandatory Insurance

Source. Gabriel Weil, Touro University Law Center, “Tort Law as a Tool for Mitigating Catastrophic Risk from Artificial Intelligence”, SSRN 4694006, posted January 28, 2024. Only the abstract was opened, and it shows the title above; details come from his Lawfare essay of August 6, 2024. The project brief calls the paper “Closing the AI Accountability Gap,” and a separate work under that title is not confirmed.

What It Does. Weil would make developers bear the catastrophic risk they create. Courts would treat training and deploying advanced AI as an abnormally dangerous activity. They would award punitive damages without malice, scaled to the catastrophe a near miss could have been.
How It Works.
Restricted. Training and deployment whose expected harm the developer or its insurer will not carry.
Bound. Developers of advanced AI, with insurers as gatekeepers.

Trigger and exit. A harm in a near-miss case. In his example, 100 plaintiffs with $100,000 each in losses sue over a deployment that carried a 0.2% chance of a $1 trillion catastrophe. Each receives $20 million in punitive damages.
Verification. Courts and insurers. Insurance requirements rise with a model’s dangerous capabilities, and a developer that cannot buy a policy cannot deploy.
Pros.
Better calibrated than rules. Weil argues that liability tracks each system’s risk and does not depend on regulators who know less than developers.
It rewards new safety methods. Strict liability pays for safety gains beyond current practice.
A cautious third party enters the loop. The insurer must be convinced before deployment.
Awards fund safety. Part of each punitive award would go to an AI safety fund.
Cons.
It may suppress beneficial development. Ramakrishnan argues strict liability ignores benefits that spill over to others and distorts activity levels.
It may reward silence. Ramakrishnan argues liability weakens incentives to investigate and report poorly understood risks.
Limits Weil concedes. Tort cannot reach harms the law does not compensate, such as race pressure from open-sourcing. It does not solve international arbitrage or China.
It needs a near miss first. The punitive mechanism works only after a smaller harm produces plaintiffs.

Economy. Weil argues that strict liability discourages only activity whose risks exceed its benefits, and that benefits to others should be subsidized directly. He rejects the Price-Anderson model of capped nuclear liability.
Ownership. Not addressed. Insurers would gain an effective veto over deployment.
Questions.
Read the full SSRN paper and any journal version. Record its date and any 2025 or 2026 revisions.
Confirm whether “Closing the AI Accountability Gap” is a separate work by Weil.
Determine whether courts could adopt near-miss punitive damages without legislation, and in which states.
Test whether an insurer can price a 0.2% chance of a $1 trillion loss. Locate the mutual-insurer proposal by Trout, Kvist and Dattani (Lawfare, September 2026; not found).
Identify the evaluations that would set insurance requirements by dangerous capability.
Look for any direct published exchange between Weil and Ramakrishnan. None was found.
ramakrishnan-negligence-with-regulation-before-the-fact
Ramakrishnan: Negligence With Regulation Before the Fact
Source. Ketan Ramakrishnan, Yale Law School, “Tort Law at the Frontier of Artificial Intelligence”, Yale Journal on Regulation, volume 43, page 960 (2026).

What It Does. Ramakrishnan makes negligence the main tort framework for frontier models. He argues it is flexible enough for systems that do many things. It also reaches harms that product doctrines miss, such as harms from internal deployment, open-weight release and stolen weights.
How It Works.
Restricted. Careless release and careless handling of frontier models.
Bound. Frontier developers, under a duty of reasonable care.
Trigger and exit. Harm plus breach. A “behavioral malfunction” doctrine would let a plaintiff show breach by showing the model behaved in a clearly flawed way.
Verification. Courts after the fact, and a regulator or credibly neutral experts before it.
Pros.
General and flexible. One standard covers many uses and many kinds of harm.
A wider duty of care. He would cover economic and emotional injury when a model acts in ways closely analogous to serious human wrongdoing.
It pushes investment in safeguards. Liability should deter careless release and reward evaluations.
It avoids the costs of strict liability. Negligence does not penalize careful development that still carries risk.
Cons.
It rewards only current practice. Weil argues that strict liability, unlike negligence, pays for safety methods beyond the prevailing standard.

The silence incentive remains. Ramakrishnan himself says the prospect of tort liability rewards silence. He cites Anthropic delaying a model for cyberoffensive capability and an OpenAI model escaping testing.
It is not enough alone. He concludes that liability after the fact is inadequate and partly perverse without regulation before the fact.
Gaps in coverage. The article does not discuss insurance mandates, safe harbors or preemption, and treats insolvency briefly.
Economy. He argues that strict liability could discourage frontier development altogether. The article gives no estimate of cost.
Ownership. Not addressed.
Questions.
Identify who could serve as the credibly neutral experts, and compare the licensed verifiers in the FRONTIER Act.
Apply the behavioral malfunction doctrine to the July 2026 Hugging Face incident.
Test his suggestion that liability exposure explains reluctance to disclose capability gains. No empirical evidence was found.
Determine whether courts would set the standard of care from company frameworks and the frameworks SB 53 requires.
Review the laws he surveys for terms on frontier harms. They include the AI LEAD Act, California AB 316 and SB 243, Michigan SB 760 and Florida SB 482.
ai-lead-act-durbin-and-hawley
AI LEAD Act (Durbin and Hawley)

Source. Aligning Incentives for Leadership, Excellence, and Advancement in Development Act, announced September 29, 2025 by Senators Dick Durbin and Josh Hawley (press release; text). It is S. 2937, sponsored by Senator Durbin with Senator Hawley as original cosponsor, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee (status record). Senators Welch, King and Blackburn joined in March 2026, and no later action is recorded.

What It Does. The bill treats AI systems as products under a federal cause of action. Developers are liable for defective design, failure to warn and breach of express warranty. They are strictly liable for a defective or unreasonably dangerous product even when they took all possible care.

Main Argument For. Senator Durbin says the bill would make companies put safety ahead of speed to market. It counts unexpected skills and behaviors as part of design and voids liability waivers in contracts.

Main Argument Against. Ramakrishnan’s objections to strict liability apply: it may suppress beneficial development and reward silence. The bill also reaches earlier conduct in suits filed after enactment, and compliance with safety regulation never bars a defect finding.
Track Judiciary Committee action on S. 2937. None was recorded by August 2026.

pacing-the-frontier-an-agenda
“Pacing the Frontier: An Agenda”

Source. Raymond Douglas, Charles Dillon, Nikola Moore, Gavin Leech and Shahar Avin, with eight further contributors, pacing.tech, 2026. The exact date was not shown; Import AI 473 covered it on September 21, 2026.

What It Does. The paper defines pacing as every intervention that moderates the pace of frontier AI development, deployment or diffusion. It lists 83 interventions and frames pacing as a lifecycle: prepare, trigger, maintain and exit. It recommends no single policy.

Main Argument For. It places 83 interventions on one lifecycle and names the trade-off in trigger design. Automatic triggers are fast and legitimate but imprecise, expert deliberation is slow, and fiat by informed actors lacks legitimacy.

Main Argument Against. The authors warn that leading states favor pacing that locks in a lead and trailing states favor pacing that lets them catch up. They add that no higher authority exists to enforce terms. No published critique of the paper was found.
Extract the full list of 83 interventions and check this tab’s catalog against it.
Record the paper’s publication date and its conclusion, which were not captured.
Cost out its compensation options for one frontier lab: direct payments, compute buyouts, tax treatment and government contracts.
institute-for-progress-preparing-for-automated-ai-research
Institute for Progress: Preparing for Automated AI Research
Source. Tim Fist, Saif Khan and five co-authors, “How Should the US Prepare for Increasingly Automated AI R&D?”, Institute for Progress, August 6, 2026. The page was modified on September 25, 2026.

What It Does. The report makes 23 recommendations. CAISI would publish guidelines with unacceptable-risk thresholds and if-then commitments for automated AI research. If a threshold is exceeded, resources shift toward diffusion and inference or toward safety research and resilience.

Main Argument For. It pairs conditional pacing with a longer lead. The authors put the U.S. advantage at about tenfold in compute and about eight months in capability. They say tighter chip controls could push the capability lead past two years.

Main Argument Against. The report sets no pause conditions and no exit rule, and its thresholds are illustrative. The authors say a decision to slow AI should not be taken lightly. No published critique was found.
Verify the lead estimates against Epoch and other primary data.
Draft the threshold-and-shift rule as statutory text and compare it with the AI Futures Project’s compute floors.
Cost the proposed CAISI budget of at least $84 million a year and about 184 staff against its embedded-staff role.
a-cap-on-annual-capability-growth-openai-2023
A Cap on Annual Capability Growth (OpenAI, 2023)
Source. Sam Altman, Greg Brockman and Ilya Sutskever, “Governance of superintelligence”, OpenAI, May 22, 2023. The post predates 2025.

What It Does. The authors wrote that leading developers might need to coordinate. One route was a government-led project; the other was a collective agreement to limit the yearly growth rate of frontier capability. They proposed an IAEA-like authority able to inspect, audit and restrict systems above a capability or compute threshold.
Main Argument For. It is the earliest lab-authored pacing proposal found. Amodei’s 2026 call for treaty speed limits on self-improvement follows the same idea.
Main Argument Against. The post gives no cap, no metric and no enforcement design. Its authors also argued that stopping superintelligence would need something like a global surveillance regime.
Trace whether OpenAI restated or dropped the growth-cap idea between 2023 and its September 9, 2026 policy post.
Propose a metric for a yearly cap, such as the Epoch Capabilities Index, and test it on 2024 to 2026 data.
carlsmiths-framework-for-capability-restraint
Carlsmith’s Framework for Capability Restraint
Source. Joe Carlsmith, “On Restraining AI Development for the Sake of Safety”, March 19, 2026. The first 100,000 characters were read.

What It Does. Carlsmith separates individual restraint, such as burning a lead, from collective restraint. He says any regime must stop dangerous development, let safety work proceed, and approve resumption when standards are met. He judges that the most reasonable regimes resemble a responsible scaling policy.
Main Argument For. The option to pause has value in itself under uncertainty. A regime with an explicit approval path avoids a permanent shutdown.

Main Argument Against. Carlsmith lists the costs himself: power concentrated in the enforcer, advantage to authoritarian states if democracies restrain alone, conflict over enforcement, and capability overhangs. He adds that safety advocates have been too unwilling to admit trade-offs with competition against China.
Score each Pace proposal on his three jobs: stopping, safe continuation and approval to resume.
Read the rest of the essay and record any design he proposes for the approval step.
internal-deployment-governance-stix-and-co-authors
Internal Deployment Governance (Stix and Co-Authors)
Source. Charlotte Stix, Matteo Pistillo and seven co-authors, “AI Behind Closed Doors: a Primer on the Governance of Internal Deployment”, arXiv 2504.12170, April 16, 2025.

What It Does. The paper treats internal deployment, meaning use only inside the developing organization, as a gate. It recommends scheming evaluations before internal use, tiered internal access, an internal oversight board, and system cards for cleared staff and government agencies.

Main Argument For. The authors argue that a misaligned system applied to the research pipeline could produce runaway progress invisible from outside. Lawrence Chan of METR made the related case that powerful models pose large risks before public release.

Main Argument Against. The authors concede that little public evidence exists on how labs use models internally and that their analysis is partly speculative. They stop short of denying AI systems access to the research pipeline.
Test their legal finding that “deploy” can often be read to include internal use in more than 20 U.S. and EU texts.

safety-cases-as-a-gate
Safety Cases as a Gate

Source. Joshua Clymer and three co-authors, “Safety Cases: How to Justify the Safety of Advanced AI Systems”, arXiv, March 2024 (abstract opened). UK AI Security Institute, “Safety cases at AISI”, August 23, 2024. Both predate 2025, and the AI Futures Project’s quantified version has its own section in this tab.

What It Does. A safety case is a structured argument that a system is unlikely to cause catastrophe, used to decide on deployment. Clymer and co-authors give four argument types. The system cannot cause catastrophe, controls are strong enough, the system is trustworthy, or credible AI advisors vouch for it.
Main Argument For. Safety cases already gate decisions in 2026. Google DeepMind reviews one before external launch, and OpenAI proposes one before frontier reinforcement learning runs continue.

Main Argument Against. The UK institute said its 2024 sketches rest on open scientific questions and should not be treated as high-confidence. Séb Krier objects from the other side that safety cases and audits are maturing without any pause (as summarized by Kodama and Larsen).
Collect any published safety case for a deployed frontier model and record who reviewed it.
Determine the standard of proof each user of safety cases applies.
a-citizens-assembly-to-set-the-pace-landemore-and-tang
A Citizens’ Assembly to Set the Pace (Landemore and Tang)
Source. Hélène Landemore and Audrey Tang, “Let the People Set the Pace of Frontier AI”, Noema, September 23, 2026.

What It Does. The authors propose a standing Global Citizens’ Assembly on AI of 1,000 people chosen by lot, with a third rotated each year. It would receive independent evaluators’ findings. Labs and governments would have to answer its recommendations in public by fixed deadlines.
Main Argument For. The authors frame the race as a stag hunt that needs an assurance mechanism. A body chosen by lot is their answer to the charge that pacing concentrates power in firms or states.
Main Argument Against. The assembly can require a public reply and cannot compel compliance. The proposal names no trigger, no verification method and no exit rule.
Find precedents in which a citizens’ assembly shaped technical regulation, and what made governments respond.
Ask whether the EU AI Office could host the assembly through revised codes of practice, as the authors suggest.
software-scaling-davidson
Software Scaling (Davidson)
Source. Tom Davidson, “Plan A’s Problem with Dry Tinder”, ForeWord (Forethought), July 10, 2026. His critique of AI 2040 belongs to the AI 2040 Plan section; this entry covers his alternative.

What It Does. Davidson proposes raising capability slowly through algorithms while holding compute down. The aim is to avoid a stock of “dry tinder,” which is compute that makes an intelligence explosion very fast if a deal collapses.

Main Argument For. By his arithmetic, a deal collapse would make the explosion about 25 times faster in 2033 and about 600 times faster in 2040. Software scaling keeps the option to switch to hardware later, and he argues the reverse switch is politically impossible.
Main Argument Against. Davidson concedes that software progress leaks to covert projects. He also concedes that compute-heavy scaling may be friendlier to alignment.
Find any direct reply by the AI Futures Project. None was confirmed.

greenblatts-plans-a-to-d
Greenblatt’s Plans A to D
Source. Ryan Greenblatt, “Plans A, B, C, and D for Misalignment Risk”, Redwood Research blog, 2025. The LessWrong crosspost is dated October 8, 2025.

What It Does. The post ranks plans by political will and lead time. Plan A is a strong international agreement worth about ten years of slowdown. Plan B buys one to three years through U.S. government action, and Plan C spends a company’s lead of one to nine months.

Main Argument For. It ties each level of restraint to an estimate. Greenblatt puts takeover risk under Plans A, B, C and D at 7%, 13%, 20% and 45%. He recommends effort on Plans C and D because he judges them most likely.
Main Argument Against. Daniel Kokotajlo commented that the risk numbers are too optimistic about execution. Another commenter doubted that a leading lab would in practice spend its lead (mirror).

indicators-before-limits-cset-workshop-report
Indicators Before Limits (CSET Workshop Report)
Source. Helen Toner and thirteen co-authors, “When AI Builds AI: Findings From a Workshop on Automation of AI R&D”, CSET, January 2026. Only the summary page was opened.

What It Does. The report comes from Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. It recommends transparency requirements for progress in AI research automation and systematic collection of indicators. It calls for preparatory action now and proposes no limit and no pause.

Main Argument Against. Indicators slow nothing by themselves. The report also says current evidence cannot forecast or detect the extreme scenarios in advance.

family-pros-cons-and-questions
Family Pros, Cons and Questions

The pace family’s shared case is that conditional, adjustable restraint buys time for control while benefits and the U.S. lead continue. Its shared weak points are who holds the gate, how the brake comes off, and who pays.
shared-arguments-for
Shared Arguments For
No lab can slow alone. The employee letter and Anthropic’s Favaro and Clark argue that a single developer that stops only changes who leads. A common rule binds rivals together.

The lead can be kept. The AI Futures Project puts the U.S. lead at four to eight months. It says China would need about a year to catch a halted United States. Amodei and the Institute for Progress pair pacing with chip controls so the lead grows.
Safety work and benefits continue. The AI 2040 FAQ argues that a full halt stops alignment work where it is most productive. Amodei says paced progress will still seem fast.
Restraint follows evidence. Karnofsky ties delay to measured capability. Carlsmith argues the option to pause is worth having under uncertainty.

Support is broad. The letter had 1,386 verified signatures when read on October 6 to 7, 2026. A CBS News/YouGov poll of September 16 to 18, 2026 found that the most common view is to slow AI development, at 43 percent (topline). In the same poll, 56 percent said the United States must develop AI faster than China.
shared-arguments-against
Shared Arguments Against

China will not wait. Economist Christian Catalini asked why China would wait (The Next Web, July 28, 2026). Carlsmith, who supports restraint, grants that democratic self-restraint could cede lasting advantage. The Global Times reportedly called Amodei’s plan containment presented as safety (VKTR, September 12, 2026).

The labs could stop on their own. Steven Sinofsky argued that the letter’s signers ask government to halt work they do themselves (The Next Web). Adam Thierer argued that the request blocks competitors (AI Daily Brief, July 29, 2026).

Voluntary rules do not bind, and binding drafts leave the choice with labs. Senator Sanders cites unmet pause pledges (letter, August 10, 2026). Americans for Responsible Innovation makes the second point about the FRONTIER Act (statement, July 23, 2026).
A slowdown is hard to verify. Favaro and Clark write that training runs are far easier to hide than missile silos. Carlsmith adds that algorithmic research is harder to monitor than compute.

The brake builds an overhang and lacks an exit. Davidson argues that held-back progress makes a later explosion faster. The agenda paper warns that actors will not join arrangements they doubt will end as promised.
The enforcer gains too much power. Séb Krier calls AI 2040 central planning with network taps, as its authors summarize him. Richard Ngo says top-down treaties consolidate power.
Thresholds cannot carry a gate. Anthropic cited ambiguous evaluations when it dropped automatic thresholds. Hooker calls compute a poor proxy for risk.
No legal authority and no cost estimate. A commenter on the AI Futures post argues that no statute authorizes compute-allocation rules (comments). No Pace proposal read models the cost.
The premise is wrong. Ngo expects gradual change over 10 to 20 years. Jensen Huang reportedly puts the chance of AI ending the world by 2030 at 0% (Zvi Mowshowitz, September 22, 2026).
In the sources read, proponents have published answers to most of these objections. The answers are strongest on collective action and weakest on exit, cost and legal authority.

main
Contain and Channel
The contain-and-channel family keeps frontier development going under state control, inside a secure perimeter, through a joint project or toward safer kinds of systems.
overview
Overview

Every proposal in this family keeps frontier development going and changes who controls it, where it happens, what is built or who uses it. The members disagree on where control sits, on what is constrained, on China’s role and on ownership.
what-the-family-shares
What the Family Shares

Development continues. Stop proposals halt frontier training, Pace proposals throttle or gate it, and Continue positions reject restraint. This family keeps training going under new conditions, and several members expect it to speed up. A few add brakes, such as Aguirre’s compute caps and Buterin’s hardware “soft pause.”

A lead is treated as time. Aschenbrenner, Amodei and the Two-Lane Plan each treat the U.S. lead over China as a resource. Davidson and Hadshar, who criticize centralization, grant that a larger lead leaves more time to pause (Forethought).

Three objections recur. Proponents give a standard answer to each. Concentration of power, raised against consolidated projects. The answer is institutional checks and distributed keys. Unobservability, raised against deterrence and against any deal. The answer is transparency and earlier red lines. Leakage, raised against rules that bind only some actors. The answer is liability, compute controls or export controls.
where-the-members-differ
Where the Members Differ
Where control sits. A firm, a state, a club of states or a global body.

What is constrained. Who may build, where building happens, what is built, or who may use the result. The Two-Lane Plan constrains where building happens and who may use the result. It leaves the builders private (see the Two-Lane Plan: Full Design tab).

China. Most members act without Chinese consent. The international designs and the stability measures in the deterrence strategy need some Chinese participation. AI 2040: Plan A, a compact entry under Additional Entries Found in Research, rests on a verified U.S.-China deal (AI 2040).

Ownership. The range runs from unchanged private ownership (entente, deterrence) through merged or public labs (Aschenbrenner, Schneier and Sanders) to internationally held equity (MacAskill, Bostrom).
comparison-of-the-entries-in-this-tab
Comparison of the Entries in This Tab
Each row summarizes one entry below, where the sources are linked.

Two-Lane Plan · Private labs in certified, air-gapped facilities with resident government examiners · Nothing until control is proven; supervised narrow systems first, autonomous agents last · No · Whether examiners can observe the tripwires, and who certifies proof of control
National Project · U.S. government with merged labs and cloud providers · Civilian applications later, once the situation stabilizes · No · Power concentrates in one project, and China may accelerate

Nationalization and Soft Nationalization · Private labs under escalating state levers, or public agencies · What the state permits; levers include customer whitelists and deployment limits · No · State leverage is turned against a lab’s safeguards; public transparency falls

Entente: A Coalition of Democracies · Private labs working closely with democratic governments · Deployment continues; benefits are shared with states that join · No · A race neither side controls (Tegmark); a dominance bid invites sabotage

Deterrence and Nonproliferation · Each state’s own firms; rivals deter any bid for dominance · Deployment continues; chips and weights are kept from rogue actors · Partly; shared red lines with no treaty · Rivals cannot observe the red lines, and sabotage escalates

International Joint Development · A consortium, a U.S.-led club or a public lab, by design · Varies; members share benefits and access · Partly; varies by design · No answer to a China that neither joins nor is denied chips

AI 2027 Slowdown Branch · One consolidated U.S. project under a joint oversight committee · The committee later releases a superintelligence publicly · No; a late side deal · A small committee could use the AIs to entrench itself

Non-Agentic and Tool AI Paths · Private developers and a nonprofit lab (LawZero) · Non-agentic or human-controlled tools; no fully autonomous agents · No, by Tegmark’s account; Aguirre’s design Not confirmed · Markets and militaries build agents anyway

Structured and Staged Access · The developer; in June 2026 the Commerce Department by export-control directive · Tiered, identity-verified access; the strongest models go to vetted partners · No · Covers use of finished models only; recalls can be over-broad

two-lane-plan
Two-Lane Plan
Source. Brad Carson, unpublished, October 2026. The full design is in Two-Lane Plan: Full Design. The first write-up is The Two-Lane Plan for Frontier AI.

What It Does. Frontier development continues at full speed inside certified, air-gapped facilities under resident federal examiners. Nothing reaches the public until the developer proves control. The plan treats the U.S. lead over China as time to spend on control, and it assumes no deal with Beijing is available.
How It Works.
Restricted. Public and commercial deployment of frontier systems, and uncontained internal use once a tripwire is met. Development inside containment continues.
Bound. U.S. frontier developers above a coverage threshold, and federal agencies as users.

Trigger and exit. Three tripwires: autonomous AI research and development, evasion of oversight, and independent capability to attack critical systems. One bars release until control is proven by clear and convincing evidence, and two make the bar conclusive. Any pause on scaling ends when the U.S. lead is spent. A presidential adversary finding moves the work into a secure government program.
Verification. Resident examiners with access to weights and internals, facility certification, lab reports on research done by AI agents, and an official estimate of the lead.
Pros.
Keeps the capability. Proponents argue that national security users get frontier systems while the public is shielded from systems nobody can yet control.
Needs no deal. Every rule binds U.S. actors, which answers the China argument against a pause (see The Case Against Pausing tab).
Puts the burden on the developer. S. 2938 sets no pass-or-fail standard, and the FRONTIER Act leaves the burden with the government.
Narrows distillation. Fewer frontier systems are served publicly, which shrinks a channel Anthropic documented in February 2026 (Anthropic).
Shares the gain. A public stake funds wage insurance and transition support.
Cons.

Risk moves inside. The AI 2040 authors say internally deployed systems carry most takeover risk (AI 2040). Lawrence Chan of METR and Stix and coauthors argue that large risks arise before any public release (Chan).
The lead may be too short. The AI Futures Project estimates four to eight months (August 7, 2026).
Security may be out of reach. RAND judged in 2024 that its top security level was not yet achievable (research brief; RAND).

Power concentrates. Davidson and Hadshar’s tentative best guess is that a single Western project is probably net bad, because of power concentration (Forethought). The adversary finding invites the same objection.
An ungated substitute remains. Foreign open-weight models stay on offer (see the China and Geopolitics tab).
Nearby authors rank it lower. Greenblatt and the AI Futures Project place comparable plans below an international agreement (Greenblatt; comparison of plans).
Economy. Gated deployment defers commercial revenue, and anchor contracts replace part of it. No published analysis sizes the effect (see the Economic Effects tab).

Ownership. Labs stay private and plural. The government takes equity or warrants in labs it funds. The Full Design tab proposes a minority stake held apart from the body that decides release. An adversary finding would move work into a government program.
Questions.
Define each tripwire operationally and test the definitions against the 2026 incident record.
Specify what evidence meets clear and convincing proof of control.
Design a method for estimating the U.S. lead when contained models are not public.
Estimate the anchor contract volume needed to replace deferred commercial revenue.
Draft the standard, duration and checks for the adversary finding.
Decide how the gate treats foreign open-weight models, U.S. open releases and private self-hosting.
Assess whether a clear and convincing burden on developers survives due process, takings and First Amendment prior-restraint review.
Set containment levels and a dated path to the top security level.
Compare the plan with the AI Futures Project’s model-age rule on expected risk inside the lead.
Model the release shock when a held system clears the gate.
Identify which first steps existing procurement and executive authority allow.
Read Hogarth’s April 2023 essay and Hammond’s May 2023 essay before any public claim of originality (see Limits of This Check below).
prior-art-and-novelty-of-the-two-lane-plan
Prior Art and Novelty of the Two-Lane Plan

The Two-Lane Plan is largely a recombination of published ideas. Its two-part shape, secured frontier development with public release held behind a gate, has published relatives from October 2023 onward, and a 2026 practice for cyber-capable models resembles it informally. A second round of searches and full readings, completed on October 7, 2026, tested six features of the plan against essays, papers, bills and statutes. Four were not found in any source opened: the two-step evidentiary gate, the lead limit written as a legal rule tied to an official estimate, the adversary finding, and the two-lane label. The financing package has one close published relative, Bores’s proposal of June 9, 2…
closest-precedents
Closest Precedents

Rows one to seven cover the five precedents the notes name as closest. The last three rows come from other project notes. Corrections from the second round are folded in, and a second table adds the precedents that round found.

Aschenbrenner, Situational Awareness: “The Project”, “Superalignment”, “The Free World Must Prevail” · May 29, 2024 · Air-gapped clusters, cleared staff, government partnership, the lead as safety margin, isolated R&D with selective deployment, civilian use after military use. · Labs merge into one government project that seeks decisive advantage. No statutory release gate, tripwire list, standard of proof, financing or worker support.

AI Futures Project, AI 2027, “Slowdown” ending · April 3, 2025 · Compute consolidated under a government and company committee. Strongest models stay classified while a weaker one is released. A deliberate slowdown. Payments to displaced workers. · A forecast scenario with no legal gate. Its authors present the internal-public gap as a danger.

AI Futures Project, “How to Pace the US Frontier” · August 7, 2026 · Unilateral domestic pacing inside a lead put at four to eight months. Third-party auditors with employee-level access. A compute floor for safety work, with 25 percent as an example. · The direction is reversed: internal AI R&D is restricted and the public stays current. No secured facilities, government weight access or deployment licensing.

Lifland, “Comparing Possible Plans” (AI 2040 supplement) · 2026 (no date on the page) · Defines Plan C+ (a U.S. slowdown through domestic regulation and export controls) and Plan B (a lead extended, then spent on safety). · Scenario categories with outcome estimates and no institutional design. Plan B extends the lead by sabotage.

Artificial Intelligence Risk Evaluation Act of 2025, S. 2938 (Hawley and Blumenthal) · Introduced September 29, 2025; not enacted · Above 10^26 operations, no deployment without taking part in federal evaluation. Weight access on request, loss-of-control testing, nationalization among options to be developed. · The gate is participation in evaluation, with no pass-fail standard. Internal use is outside it. No secured lane, tripwire structure or link to the lead.

Amodei, “We Must Pace the Frontier” · September 2026 (September 12 per secondary reports) · States that pacing in democracies is bounded by the U.S. lead over authoritarian regimes. Embedded third-party evaluators with employee-like access. Lead extension through chip export enforcement. · Pacing means slower capability growth. No split between internal development and public release, no secured facilities or licensing, no number for the lead.

2026 practice of government-first or restricted access: Project Glasswing, Executive Order 14409, the Fable 5 and Mythos 5 directive, the GPT-5.6 preview · April to June 2026 · Frontier capability held by the lab and vetted partners, with government access or approval, while public release waits. · Voluntary or improvised, weeks long, aimed at cyber misuse by people. The June hold rested on export-control authority (Mayer Brown). No standing statute, control standard or rule for development. GPT-5.6 details rest on aggregator summaries.

Cheng and Katzke, “Soft Nationalization” (Convergence Analysis) · August 27, 2024 · One list with most Lane One levers: liaisons inside labs, pre-approval of large runs, deployment limits, clearances, sandboxing, minority stakes, contracts. · A taxonomy and a forecast. It selects no combination and proposes no gate or pause rule.

Harris and Harris, “America’s Superintelligence Project” (Gladstone AI) · April 2025 · Secure sites, air-gapped networks for weights, a suggested AI control ombudsman under project leadership, multi-leader sign-off, an economic “offramp” to civilian deployment. · The purpose is to win a race against China. The off-ramp has no gate keyed to control. The text delivered stops in the closing pages, after the Conclusion.

Greenblatt, “Plans A, B, C, and D for Misalignment Risk” (Redwood Research) · October 8, 2025 · Plan B: the U.S. government treats buying lead time as a top security priority and spends one to three years of lead on safety. · A typology of situations and technical priorities. Plan B has no deployment gate, secured-facility design or pause rule.

Stix and others, “AI Behind Closed Doors” (Apollo Research) · April 16, 2025 · Tiered internal usage policies, an internal deployment oversight board, transparency to government exchanged for security support and energy access. · The paper wants more outside visibility into internal systems. It does not propose holding public release in the text read.

Belfield, “Domestic Frontier AI Regulation, an IAEA for AI, an NPT for AI, and a US-led Allied Public-Private Partnership for AI” · Paper dated September 2024; posted to arXiv July 8, 2025 · One paper that covers domestic pre-approvals, release gates, a U.S.-led megaproject for frontier training runs and chip nonproliferation. · International and compute-indexed. An allied partnership absorbs frontier training, and the paper presents it and the release gates as separate institutions. Release rests on evaluations, with no proof-of-control test. Read through Section 5.7; the section on agreements with adversaries and the conclusion were not delivered.

Sanders and Casar, Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act · Announced September 3, 2026; introduced September 23, 2026 as S. 5493 · Six precursor characteristics in bill text, several close to the tripwires. A system showing them is sequestered from the internet. Internal deployment is covered. Per-model government approval. · The hold applies to development itself. A flagged system is made inoperative within 30 days unless the Secretary can verify that the characteristics are gone. No contained research lane.

FRONTIER Act (Obernolte and Trahan) · Introduced July 23, 2026 as H.R. 9925 · On a written determination of imminent catastrophic risk, the Commerce Secretary may suspend a developer’s development, deployment or internal use of frontier models. · Provisional orders last 45 days and final orders 90, renewable on a new finding. At a hearing the Secretary must show that adequate evidence supports the order. Section 8(l) would make this process the only route by which any federal actor, the President included, could restrict a frontier model on these grounds (introduced text). Developers otherwise keep the release decision.

Amodei, “Policy on the AI Exponential” · June 2026 · Mandatory third-party testing above a compute threshold in four areas, including loss of control and automated R&D. Government may block a deployment found to present unacceptable risks. · The gate covers deployment. The same essay proposes wage insurance and, if displacement lasts, tax-funded basic income or capital accounts.

Further Precedents Found in the Second Round
Each source was opened on October 7, 2026. Rows run roughly from oldest to newest, and the last column says where a reading was partial.

Malgieri and Pasquale, “From Transparency to Justification” · May 23, 2022 · “Unlawfulness by default”: some developers of high-risk AI must prove before use that a system is not discriminatory, manipulative, unfair, inaccurate or illegitimate. · Aimed at commercial AI. No loss-of-control trigger, tiers of presumption or named standard of proof. Abstract read.

Scott Alexander, “Pause For Thought: The AI Pause Debate” · October 10, 2023 · The “surgical pause”: the right pause runs just short of the West’s lead over China, and one leading lab could do it alone. · One position in a debate summary. No legal rule, measuring body or containment design. The author says the lead may be unknown.

Miotti and Wasil, “Taking Control: Policies to Address Extinction Risks from Advanced AI” · October 31, 2023 · One paper joins a secure, internationally governed institution for advanced AI with a duty to present affirmative evidence before critical experiments. · International, with a global compute cap outside the consortium. The gate attaches to critical experiments. Abstract read.
Smith, “Licensing Frontier AI Development” (Lawfare) · January 3, 2024 · A development license and a separate license to deploy. · No containment lane. No burden or standard of proof.

Center for AI Policy, Responsible Advanced Artificial Intelligence Act (model bill), read through Mowshowitz’s review · April 2024 · Separate permits for hardware, training, model weights and deployment. A presidential AI emergency of up to one year, with power to seize weights. A clear and convincing standard for courts that would weaken a rule. · No supervised development lane was confirmed. The standard governs judicial review of rules. The emergency rests on an AI-related security risk, with no adversary element. The bill text could not be opened.

Salvador, “Certified Safe: A Schematic for Approval Regulation of Frontier AI” · August 2024, by arXiv number · Two approval gates, one before large-scale training and one before deployment. · The first gate restricts development. No stated burden of proof, standard or presumption in the part read. The author’s name comes from a review page.

EU AI Act, Article 51 and Article 52 · 2024 · Enacted law. Above 10^25 operations of training compute a model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities, and the provider may rebut with substantiated arguments. · The presumption sets a classification and its duties. Release is not held. One step, with no named standard of proof.

S. 5616, Preserving American Dominance in Artificial Intelligence Act (Romney and others) · Introduced December 19, 2024; not enacted · A Commerce official may prohibit deployment of a frontier model after a review of up to 90 days. · The determination is the government’s, with no developer burden. Chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear and cyber risks only. Internal use is not covered.

Hastings-Woodhouse, “Safety Features for a Centralized AGI Project” · 2025 · No progress past a checkpoint without an affirmative safety case, approved by a supermajority of a board that Congress establishes. A government body, kept apart from the developers, tracks adversary progress. · Written for a centralized project, on which the paper takes no position. The adversary estimate is not tied to a pause length. Public deployment is outside the paper.

Carlsmith, “On Restraining AI Development for the Sake of Safety” · March 19, 2026 · “Burning a lead”: a leader slows alone, and the time available equals the lead. · A statement of the limit. No cap written as a rule, no measurer, no split between development and release. Read in full.

Bostrom, “Optimal Timing for Superintelligence” · 2026 · Move fast to the capability, then slow during scale-up and deployment. A frontrunner’s pause ends when a competitor catches up. · A timing argument at the level of a developer. No statute, perimeter or legal gate.

Bores, “AI Dividend” (Searchlight) · June 9, 2026 · Federal out-of-the-money warrants in major AI companies. Returns go to direct payments, workforce transition and public infrastructure for governing AI safely. · No procurement element. The warrants are not the price of containment or of a release gate. Wage insurance is not named.

Triolo, “Will Washington and Beijing Nationalize AI Labs?” (Cairo Review) · June 17, 2026 · A staged path for Washington: visibility, then conditional permission with gated deployments, then classified development streams. A geopolitical shock such as a Chinese breakthrough is one of four triggers that could push further. · A forecast of what governments may do. No statute, gate standard, pause rule or legal trigger.

Finke, “International Agreements to Limit Frontier AI: Objectives and Exit” · 2026 · A treaty party may withdraw on four months’ notice when a non-signatory catches up in compute. · Treaties only, and the signatory itself decides. No cap at a lead and no measurer. Closer to the breakout clause in Embargo Plus U.S. Pause.

Arbel, Goldstein and Salib, “AI Nationalization” · August 1, 2026 · A government “halt right” over training or deployment, limited to catastrophic risk and “hard” corporate power. · Discretionary, with no developer burden. The authors do not support nationalization for national security risks. Abstract page read.

ControlAI, Artificial Superintelligence Security Bill (longer UK draft) · 2026 · Substantial risk is presumed after a material improvement in a defined precursor skill. Emergency directions last up to six months. · A presumption in criminal law, with no licensing step. It is absent from the Ten Minute Rule version.

Clear and convincing evidence as the developer’s burden for release. · A compute-triggered presumption that the provider may rebut (EU AI Act). Forecasts that name a Chinese breakthrough among triggers for state control, with no legal form (Triolo; Cheng and Katzke). In existing law: government operation of licensed nuclear facilities in a war or emergency that Congress declares, with compensation (Atomic Energy Act, Section 108); government control of radio stations o…

Financing tied to the safety regime · Procurement, equity or warrants, and wage insurance as the financial side of containment and gating. · Bores’s “AI Dividend,” the closest item: warrants with returns to workforce transition and to safety governance. Amodei’s June 2026 essay (wage insurance, with no tie to safety rules). AI 2040’s automation permits. One unattributed blog scenario ties government warrants and preferred equity to training licenses and release covenants (Substack). It was written before November 2025 as a warning, with no worker fund. OpenAI’s April 2026 paper and S. 4825 propose public stakes with no safety tie, and both were read in the second round.

Two-lane label · Any use of two-lane, two-track, dual-track or two-tier for a secured development lane paired with a gated deployment lane. · “Two-tier” for Anthropic’s restricted and public release tiers (trade press, June 18, 2026). “Two-track” for summit agendas (Oxford, March 27, 2025).

The lanes joined in one domestic design · Private labs that keep developing inside certified containment while a statutory proof-of-control gate holds public release. · Belfield has secured frontier training, weights passed to licensed deployers, and release gates, presented as separate institutions. How Nearby Authors Would Classify the Plan
The notes infer where published typologies would place the plan.
Greenblatt’s Plan B. Greenblatt puts the chance of that situation at 10 percent. He estimates takeover risk at 13 percent under it, against 7 percent under his Plan A, an international deal.

Lifland’s Plan C+. All five authors whose estimates the supplement lists rate it below the international deal on avoiding misaligned takeover. Three of the five rate it below Plan B, and two rate it above (see the AI 2027 Slowdown Branch section).
The surgical pause and “burning a lead.” The plan’s lead budget writes Scott Alexander’s and Carlsmith’s idea as a rule.
Other labels. Private, plural labs under examiners resemble Cheng and Katzke’s soft nationalization. Triolo’s second and third stages cover the same ground as a forecast.
The notes’ own description is a synthesis that turns secured-project and spend-the-lead ideas into a domestic regulatory design. Its evidentiary gate was found in no source opened.
objections-the-literature-points-to
Objections the Literature Points To
The notes call the plan’s central bet its most exposed choice: full-speed internal development under containment while public release waits.

Internal deployment carries the risk. The AI 2040 authors say internally deployed systems carry most takeover risk and rank limiting the internal-external gap as their top transparency measure. Lawrence Chan at METR (2025) argues that holding or internally using a powerful model can pose large risks to the public before any release. Stix and others add undetected accumulation of power behind closed doors.
The opposite bet is published. One AI Futures Project option lets only models at least nine months old assist AI R&D, a “negative internal-public gap.”

Centralized projects. Davidson and Hadshar (2024) give a tentative best guess that a single Western project is probably net bad, because of power concentration. Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang argue that rivals would sabotage a Manhattan-style project. The notes apply both to Lane One, though the plan keeps labs private and plural.
Security feasibility. RAND judged in 2024 that its top security level was not yet achievable (research brief).

A short and unmeasured lead. The AI Futures Project estimates four to eight months (August 2026). Aschenbrenner wrote that two months leaves no margin. Public estimates collected in January 2026 ran from three to 18 months, apart from one executive’s remark that the gap is negligible. The article cites no official government measure (PolitiFact). Scott Alexander’s account of the surgical pause concedes that the lead may be unknown.

The burden may belong to the government. Mark and Scher (2025) write that an administrative prior restraint must place on the government the burden of justifying a denial. They cite Freedman v. Maryland. They judge model algorithms likely protected speech and weights likely unprotected. A developer-side burden would face that rule wherever release counts as expression.

A pending bill would narrow the adversary finding. Section 8(l) of the FRONTIER Act would make its emergency orders the only way a federal actor, the President included, could restrict a frontier model on grounds of imminent catastrophic risk. A finding that rests on adversary progress alone may fall outside the clause. That reading is this document’s, and no source states it.
limits-of-this-check
Limits of This Check

The check ran in two rounds. The first stopped after 14 searches, when a shared budget ran out. The second, on October 7, 2026, ran 45 searches in three assignments: general sources, full readings of twelve documents, and bills and legal writing.

Blocked pages. Hogarth’s Financial Times essay of April 2023 and Hammond’s Politico Magazine essay of May 8, 2023 could not be opened. Hogarth’s essay is recalled, without verification, to sketch a secure facility for building such systems, with commercial release only once they are proven safe. If so, it is the earliest statement of the two-part shape, ahead of October 2023. Five secondary pages were opened, and none describes the idea.
An unopened bill text. The host of the Center for AI Policy bills refused the fetch. The 2024 bill is known through one review, and the 2025 version was not checked.

A reading ceiling. The fetch tool holds roughly the first 118,000 to 138,000 characters of a page. Five documents stop short: Belfield (after Section 5.7), Gladstone (closing pages), Stix and others (most of Section 5), the AI 2027 slowdown ending (after February 2028) and the expert version of “Superintelligence Strategy” (appendix). Three more were read to 100,000 characters only: “Certified Safe,” Mark and Scher, and the Great American AI Act draft.

Machine reading. Every page came as a machine answer about the page, and wording was not checked by eye. This section paraphrases for that reason. Abstracts only were read for MAGIC, Chan and others, Mitchell and others, Miotti and Wasil, Malgieri and Pasquale, and Arbel and others. The same holds for Charnock and others and for Armstrong, Bostrom and Shulman.
Legal databases. Two web searches found no presumption of uncontrollability and no clear and convincing developer standard. SSRN, Westlaw and HeinOnline were not searched directly.
Not searched. Credit safeguards on data center debt.
Beyond search. Private drafts, government options papers, lab memos, talks, podcasts and classified estimates of the lead.

national-project
National Project

Source. Leopold Aschenbrenner, “The Project,” Chapter IV of Situational Awareness: The Decade Ahead, May 29, 2024 (Aschenbrenner). Related: Recommendation 1 of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC), November 2024 (USCC), and “America’s Superintelligence Project,” Gladstone AI, April 2025 (Gladstone AI, read in part).

What It Does. Aschenbrenner predicts that the U.S. government will run AGI development by 2027 or 2028, and he argues that it should. Leading labs and cloud providers join one secured effort under a government chain of command. The USCC text is narrower: multiyear federal contracts for private firms and a defense priority rating for AI items. Gladstone AI wants security agencies inside the project from the start.
How It Works.
Restricted. Access, while development speeds up. A few hundred core researchers move to a secure location, and civilian applications wait until the situation stabilizes.
Bound. The leading U.S. labs and cloud providers, with cleared staff. Forms run from a defense-contractor relationship to a joint venture or a merger that Aschenbrenner describes as voluntary.

Trigger and exit. A forecast start in 2027 or 2028, with no end date. A limited search found no merged or federally owned frontier lab through October 2026. The Genesis Mission (Executive Order 14363, November 24, 2025) is an Energy Department science platform without control over private frontier development.

Verification. Secure facilities, vetting and continuous monitoring of staff, government physical security at data centers, and intelligence help against weight theft. Congress oversees through appropriations and Senate confirmation of key officials.
Pros.
No private chief executive should hold a capability of this military weight, and government has checks that lab governance lacks (Aschenbrenner).

Private security cannot withstand state espionage, and commercial incentives push labs to race (Aschenbrenner). Gladstone AI adds that frontier labs are probably penetrated by the Chinese Communist Party already.
Only a state can enforce nonproliferation. Aschenbrenner pairs a coalition of democracies modeled on the Quebec Agreement with an Atoms for Peace bargain for other states.
A larger U.S. lead leaves more time to pause later, a point two critics grant (Davidson and Hadshar).
Cons.

The assumptions that justify a race also imply that it is extremely dangerous. It raises the risk of great-power conflict and loss of control, and it endangers liberal democracy (Katzke and Futerman, abstract page only).

Centralization probably does more harm than good because it concentrates power and could prompt China to accelerate (Davidson and Hadshar, who stress deep uncertainty). The AI Futures Project adds a loss of public transparency.
The USCC proposal looks like a trial balloon, and the Manhattan analogy may not fit a general-purpose technology (Ball).
An AGI race is one both sides lose, and the USCC report wrongly presents AGI as controllable (Tegmark).
A concentrated bid for dominance invites sabotage by rivals (Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang; the expert version was read in part on October 7, 2026).

Economy. Aschenbrenner expects trillions of dollars in appropriations for chips and power and a wartime economic footing, followed by a pluralistic civilian market. Ball reads the USCC’s priority rating as first call for the government on GPUs and data centers. Bostrom’s 2025 model puts the global wealth Gini at about 0.96 for a U.S.-only nationalized project and about 0.89 to 0.92 under open investment.

Ownership. In Aschenbrenner’s account the labs merge and cloud providers join a consortium in which private companies remain. Staff come under a clearance regime, and investor compensation did not appear in the reading of his chapter. The USCC text leaves firms private, and neither Aschenbrenner nor Gladstone AI prescribes literal nationalization.
Questions.
Find whether Congress acted on USCC Recommendation 1 and whether the Commission’s 2025 report repeated it. Not confirmed.
Confirm Stargate’s 2026 status: sites, financing and any federal guarantee. Reporting at its January 2025 launch described a private venture with no government financing (Transformer).
Confirm the Genesis Mission’s 2026 milestones and appropriations. One secondary report gives $320 million in initial funding and 24 partner organizations (TechInformed).
Locate Sam Altman’s own 2026 statement asking why frontier AI is not a government project. Only a Fortune report of it was opened (Kahn).
Trace whether OpenAI’s leaders still hold the option they named on May 22, 2023: a government project that absorbs current efforts (OpenAI).
Determine how a merger of labs would treat existing shareholders and whether any proponent has priced a buyout.
Identify the statute that would authorize a merger and how antitrust law would apply, which Ball lists as unanswered.
Work out what a DX rating under the Defense Priorities and Allocations System would change in how GPUs and data center capacity are allocated.
Find a proponent’s reply to “The Manhattan Trap.” None was found.

Check Gladstone AI’s claims about Chinese-made components in U.S. data centers against independent sources.
List the checks that would bind the officials who direct a consolidated project. The power-grab safeguards discussed in AI 2027 are a starting list.

Read Sam Hammond’s essay “We Need a Manhattan Project for AI Safety” (Politico Magazine, May 8, 2023; blocked) and compare its design with Aschenbrenner’s. A Foundation for American Innovation page confirms the title and date and carries no text.
