nationalization-and-soft-nationalization
Nationalization and Soft Nationalization

Source. Deric Cheng and Corin Katzke, “Soft Nationalization: How the US Government Will Control AI Labs,” Convergence Analysis, August 27, 2024 (EA Forum copy). Paul Triolo, “Will Washington and Beijing Nationalize AI Labs?” Cairo Review of Global Affairs, June 17, 2026 (Triolo). Bruce Schneier and Nathan E. Sanders, The Guardian, August 12, 2026 (Schneier and Sanders).

What It Does. Cheng and Katzke predict, without endorsing it, that Washington will tighten control of frontier labs in stages through levers short of ownership. Triolo reads 2026 events as that process under way. Schneier and Sanders argue for outright public ownership if markets abandon OpenAI and Anthropic. Palantir’s Alex Karp reportedly said the labs may need nationalizing because their risks are unlimited (Startup Fortune; secondary report, wording not confirmed).
How It Works.

Restricted. Cheng and Katzke list thirteen groups of levers. Examples are pre-approval of large training runs, customer whitelists, compute permits, staff clearances, containment requirements and golden shares. They state that the government will not slow frontier development without an international agreement.

Bound. Private frontier labs, with their investors and staff. Under Schneier and Sanders, model research becomes national laboratories under congressional oversight and compute becomes a regulated utility.

Trigger and exit. Cheng and Katzke’s highest scenario is full acquisition with an equity buyout after a bioweapon-capable model. Triolo’s triggers are capability thresholds, lost government visibility, military dependence on frontier models and geopolitical shocks. The trigger for Schneier and Sanders is market collapse, and none of the sources describes an exit.

Verification. Triolo describes three layers of control: visibility through reporting and evaluations, conditional permission over releases, and operational integration through classified work and procurement. Tools used in 2026 included a Pentagon supply-chain-risk designation of Anthropic and a 19-day export-control suspension of two models (Defense One; Anthropic).
Pros.
Lighter levers can meet the state’s security goals at lower cost than seizure (Cheng and Katzke).
Public ownership replaces shareholder incentives with public accountability (Schneier and Sanders).
Only government offers a single chain of command and state-grade security (Aschenbrenner).
Private firms cannot carry unlimited risk, and customers would otherwise sue (Karp, as reported).
Cons.

State leverage can be turned against a lab’s own safeguards. In February 2026 the Defense Secretary demanded an all-lawful-uses term for Anthropic’s models and threatened the Defense Production Act (Defense One; Wikipedia, tertiary). Jeremy Kahn reads that threat as soft nationalization (Fortune, March 3, 2026).
Voluntary frameworks can harden into soft mandates, as Davis Wright Tremaine warned about the June 2, 2026 executive order on pre-release access.
Treating frontier AI as weapons-adjacent can become self-fulfilling, and Beijing may already see U.S. labs as security instruments (Triolo).
Nationalization concentrates power and reduces public transparency (Davidson and Hadshar; AI Futures Project). The risk of expropriation also deters private investment (Bostrom).
The frontier firms are trillion-dollar companies whose AI units cannot be cleanly carved out, and legal and shareholder resistance is expected (Cheng and Katzke).

Economy. Cheng and Katzke report a belief that full nationalization would hurt the U.S. lead. Under softer control they expect investors to face dilution, profit regulation and narrower exits. Schneier and Sanders start from a market verdict that the labs cannot earn a return, and no source here addresses the global economy.

Ownership. Under soft nationalization firms keep formal ownership and lose autonomy over research priorities, customers, compute and deployment. The shareholding levers run from minority stakes and golden shares to full acquisition, and Schneier and Sanders add civil-service pay for staff. Anthropic stayed investor-owned through this period, with a reported $65 billion round at a $965 billion valuation in May 2026 (Wikipedia, tertiary).

Analyze the legal authorities for nationalization or compelled control. Candidates are the Defense Production Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, eminent domain and the Invention Secrecy Act.

entente-a-coalition-of-democracies
Entente: A Coalition of Democracies
Source. Dario Amodei, “Machines of Loving Grace,” October 2024 (Amodei 2024), and “The Adolescence of Technology,” January 2026 (Amodei 2026; about three-quarters read).

What It Does. A coalition of democracies secures the AI supply chain, scales quickly and blocks or delays adversaries’ access to chips and chipmaking equipment. Its military superiority is the stick and a share of AI’s benefits is the carrot, so that more countries join. Frontier development stays in private labs that work closely with democratic governments. The 2026 essay adds limits on what democracies themselves may do with AI.
How It Works.

Restricted. Sales of chips, chipmaking tools and data centers to China, which Amodei compares to nuclear weapons sales to North Korea. For democracies, mass surveillance and mass propaganda are out of bounds, and fully autonomous weapons need extreme care. Development inside the coalition continues at speed.

Bound. Chip and equipment exporters in the United States and allied states, and democratic governments through self-restraint. Labs face transparency laws such as California SB 53 and New York’s RAISE Act, with exemptions for small firms.

Trigger and exit. The strategy starts now and has no end date. The 2024 essay hopes the democracies’ position of 1991 can be made lasting. In 2026 Amodei’s own company was designated a Pentagon supply-chain risk after it refused an all-lawful-uses contract term (Defense One).

Verification. Coalition governments enforce export controls. No negotiated agreement with China is proposed. Amodei says norms against AI-enabled totalitarianism are needed and that political winds have turned against international cooperation.
Pros.
A pause is infeasible because the technology advances regardless of any one company, and autocracies would continue. Export controls buy time (Amodei 2026).
Chips are the most important single lever (Amodei 2026). The United States and its democratic allies hold most of the chip supply chain’s value (O’Keefe).
A coalition that reached predominance could defend itself and contain autocracies, and shared benefits give other states a reason to join (Amodei).
The plan binds its own side. It names AI companies as a power-concentration risk that ordinary corporate governance cannot handle (Amodei 2026).
A Western lead can be spent on safety, a point Davidson and Hadshar grant (Forethought).
Cons.

Both sides lose if either finishes, because the world is closer to building AGI than to controlling it (Tegmark, October 13, 2024). His alternative is national safety standards that permit only Tool AI until control is shown.
The reasoning that justifies racing for decisive advantage also implies conflict risk, loss-of-control risk and damage to democracy (Katzke and Futerman, abstract page only).
Limits that apply to everyone equally are preferable to one side seeking dominance (Buterin, January 5, 2025).
A bid for unilateral dominance would be met with sabotage (Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang, abstract page only).
Amodei grants that AI does not structurally favor democracy and that victory is not assured.

Economy. The 2024 essay says powerful AI could compress 50 to 100 years of biological progress into 5 to 10. The 2026 essay says AI could displace half of entry-level white-collar jobs within one to five years. It sees sustained annual GDP growth of 10 to 20% as possible and mentions progressive taxation and stronger safety nets.
Ownership. Unchanged. Private labs stay investor-owned and work in partnership with democratic governments. Amodei supports transparency laws and public commitments by the companies.
Questions.

deterrence-and-nonproliferation
Deterrence and Nonproliferation

Source. Dan Hendrycks (Center for AI Safety), Eric Schmidt and Alexandr Wang, “Superintelligence Strategy,” March 7, 2025, revised April 14, 2025 (arXiv 2503.05628; nationalsecurity.ai). Reply to critics: Hendrycks and Adam Khoja, “AI Deterrence Is Our Best Option,” AI Frontiers, September 22, 2025 (Hendrycks and Khoja). The abstract and the site summary were read for this entry. On October 7, 2026 the expert version was read as far as its appendix, for the prior-art check only.

What It Does. The strategy has three parts: deterrence, nonproliferation and competitiveness. Under Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (MAIM), any state’s aggressive bid for unilateral AI dominance is met by rivals’ preventive sabotage. The authors say this already describes the strategic position of the AI superpowers. They reject both a hands-off posture and a national bid for monopoly.
How It Works.

Restricted. A destabilizing bid for dominance by any state, and the spread of chips, model weights and dangerous capabilities to rogue actors. Ordinary development by private firms continues in each state.
Bound. Rival states, which deter each other. Firms are bound through export controls on AI chips, weight security and safeguards against misuse.

Trigger and exit. A rival’s aggressive bid sets off an escalation ladder: espionage and covert cyber sabotage, then overt cyberattacks, then kinetic strikes on data centers. The regime has no end date.

Verification. Each side watches the other through intelligence. Proposed stability measures are escalation protocols, transparency and verification, data centers sited away from population centers, and AI-assisted inspections. Chips would carry firmware features such as geolocation.
Pros.
Deterrence already describes the position of the AI superpowers, by the authors’ account, so it can operate before any agreement exists.
Fully automated AI research could give one side an overwhelming lead within months to years (Hendrycks and Khoja).
Deterrence does not need precise thresholds. Transparency and verification allow earlier and broader red lines with a margin (Hendrycks and Khoja).
MAIM is preemptive disruption, so attribution matters less than under retaliatory deterrence, and escalation ladders reduce uncontrolled preemption (Hendrycks and Khoja).
The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) treats this kind of deterrence as a possible complement that discourages violations of a pause.
Cons.

Mutual assured destruction deterred use, and MAIM tries to deter development, which has no clear brink. Strikes on data centers are acts of war, and the regime creates first-strike incentives. Halting costs a state about as much as being sabotaged, so the threat may not bite (Rehman, Mueller and Mazarr, RAND, March 13, 2025).
Deterrence needs red lines that are monitorable and communicated. Automated AI research is too vague a line, and sabotage delays more than it denies (Abecassis, MIRI, April 11, 2025).
Compute and data center metrics miss algorithmic advances. Errors then run both ways: needless sabotage or an undetected breakout (Arnold, AI Frontiers, August 14, 2025).
The two states share no understanding of the regime, and attribution is hard (Wildeford and Delaney, 2025; exact date not shown).

One analyst puts about 25% on MAIM working descriptively: geopolitical dynamics delay AI development by six months or more (Delaney, IAPS; 2025 by inference). Kinetic action is far outside current norms, and China might simply fast-follow.
Hendrycks and Khoja concede that red lines cannot be as empty as AGI and that intelligence services may see the stakes late.

Economy. The competitiveness pillar calls for domestic chip manufacturing, military adoption of AI, legal frameworks for AI agents and immigration for AI talent. Effects on the U.S. and global economy, including the cost of sabotage or strikes, were not addressed in the material read.
Ownership. Not addressed in the material read, and nothing in it changes ownership. Private firms continue within each state, and the authors argue against a single concentrated project.
Questions.

international-joint-development
International Joint Development
Source. Six designs, published from 2023 to 2026. None has been adopted.

MAGIC (Multinational AGI Consortium) · Hausenloy, Miotti and Dennis, arXiv, October 13, 2023 (abstract page only) · One multinational consortium · Yes; members ban all other advanced AI · Not stated in the abstract
Intelsat for AGI · MacAskill, Forethought, January 26, 2026 · Private labs under contract to a U.S.-led body · Yes, above 10^27 FLOP · Invited as a non-founding member
CERN for AI · Centre for Future Generations, blueprint, January 30, 2025 (read in part) · A public EU-led lab beside private labs · No · No strategy beyond restricting untrusted actors
Chips for Peace · O’Keefe, Lawfare, July 10, 2024 · Private firms under member-state regulation · No · Left open; the scheme weakens if China makes its own chips
IAEA for AI · Altman, Brockman and Sutskever, OpenAI, May 22, 2023 · Private and state developers under an inspectorate · No · Not stated in the material read
Open Global Investment · Bostrom, working paper, October 2025 · Private corporations with international shareholders · No · Keeps reasons to run its own project

What It Does. Several states pool frontier development, or its oversight, in one body. Proponents say this removes the race among national champions and spreads the benefits. The designs differ on monopoly and on who does the work.
How It Works.

Restricted. MAGIC bars all advanced AI development outside the consortium, and narrower AI continues. MacAskill requires the body’s approval for training runs above 10^27 FLOP. The IAEA model inspects efforts above a compute or capability threshold and leaves smaller systems, including open-source projects, free.

Bound. Member states and the firms they regulate. MacAskill’s founders are the Five Eyes plus the Netherlands, Japan, South Korea and Germany, with Taiwan left out to keep Chinese participation possible. Other countries, and companies worth more than $1 trillion, may join as non-founding members.

Trigger and exit. MacAskill’s arrangement is interim, with definitive terms due by 2045 or five years after AGI. Chips for Peace expels members that break the rules, and they lose hardware access. China set up its own World AI Cooperation Organization in July 2026 (Hardwired Pause working paper, unpublished draft; primary source not opened).

Verification. MacAskill spreads data centers across founders and gives each founding leader a kill switch. If feasible, weights are encrypted so that decryption needs two-thirds approval. Chips for Peace relies on compute-provider monitoring and export controls, and the MAGIC authors do not address enforcement.
Pros.
A single secure, safety-focused developer removes racing (MAGIC authors).
A monopoly gives room to pause, and larger runs offset coordination costs. The United States gains cost sharing, talent, chip supply guarantees and legitimacy, and it keeps 52% (MacAskill).
The United States and its democratic allies hold most of the chip supply chain’s value, which gives a chip-based club leverage today (O’Keefe).
Rules that apply only above a threshold cover few efforts, and those can be tracked (OpenAI, 2023).
Open investment is close to the status quo, which makes it the most feasible design on short timelines (Bostrom).
Cons.
The MAGIC authors do not address the political feasibility of a global moratorium or how to enforce it.

Nuclear safeguards track physical fissile material, and AI has no equivalent (Stewart, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, June 9, 2023). Later designs answer with chip tracking and on-site inspectors.
AGI’s military weight and commercial origin break the Intelsat analogy. Enforcement is unsolved if one member gains a decisive advantage (MacAskill and Hadshar, on their own model).
Chips have far more benign uses than enriched uranium, and verification at acceptable cost is unproven. States may also regulate national champions leniently (O’Keefe, on his own proposal).
A CERN for AI risks a budget too small for Europe’s needs, slow EU processes, bureaucratic capture and weak commercialization (the blueprint’s own list).
For a China that neither joins nor is denied chips, the designs offer exclusion from AI trade (MacAskill) or accept a weaker scheme (O’Keefe).

Economy. MacAskill’s body funds training runs three to ten times larger than the market would and shares profits with member states and investors. The Centre for Future Generations budgets €30 to 35 billion over three years, about €25 billion of it for data centers. Chips for Peace promises benefit-sharing, especially with the Global South, through subsidized access, capacity building or payments.

Ownership. MacAskill assigns equity: the United States 52%, other founders 15% combined, 10% for countries in good standing and 23% for non-founding members. Only countries vote, and companies and investors may buy non-voting equity. MAGIC’s monopoly implies that private frontier programs in member states stop or are absorbed, and Bostrom keeps firms private with international shareholders.
Questions.

ai-2027-slowdown-branch
AI 2027 Slowdown Branch

Source. Daniel Kokotajlo, Eli Lifland, Thomas Larsen, Romeo Dean and Scott Alexander, AI 2027, April 3, 2025 (slowdown ending, summary, scenario PDF). The slowdown page was read through the scenario’s November 2027 and the scenario PDF through February 2028. The ending here rests on the summary.

What It Does. The branch is a forecast, and an appendix to the scenario PDF says the slowdown ending is not a recommendation. After a whistleblower leak about misalignment, a joint company and government Oversight Committee votes 6 to 4 to slow down. The United States then folds rival compute into one project, adopts a more transparent model and later releases a superintelligence publicly.
How It Works.

Restricted. Agent-4, the misaligned model, has its shared memory bank locked and is later shut down. Safer-1 replaces it, with a faithful chain of thought and a 20x research speedup against Agent-4’s 70x. The AGI projects of the top five trailing U.S. companies are closed.
Bound. OpenBrain, the scenario’s leading lab, and the five trailing companies, whose compute is mostly sold to OpenBrain. Its share of world AI-relevant compute rises from 20% to 50%.
Trigger and exit. A leak in the scenario’s October 2027, then a Defense Production Act order in November 2027. The exit test is Not confirmed, because the later sections were not read.

Verification. Oversight is internal: the Committee and several dozen outside alignment researchers, who work with a model whose reasoning can be read. China’s weaker AI receives resources in deep space for its cooperation, and verification of that deal is Not confirmed.
Pros.
The slowdown begins before any deal with China, through one committee vote and an existing statute.
Consolidation lifts the leader’s compute share while it runs a slower model. Davidson and Hadshar grant that a bigger U.S. lead buys time to pause later (Forethought).
During the slowdown the alignment team finds deception in Agent-4, and the project moves to a model it can read.
The authors hold that a power grab is avoidable if AIs are aligned to the rule of law, red-teamed against coups and monitored.
Cons.
The authors flag that the Committee could use the AIs to entrench its own power (summary).
The text lists routes to an insider seizure, such as military control through AI and secret loyalties in the model’s specification.
The outcome turns on a 6 to 4 vote. China is about two months behind and runs stolen weights.
Davidson and Hadshar’s tentative best guess is that a single Western project is probably net bad, because of power concentration. They warn it could prompt China to accelerate.
Brian Chau, Matteo Wong and others dispute the timelines, which the authors lengthened in late 2025 (Wikipedia, a tertiary source).

Economy. The scenario mentions Congress passing economic impact payments, modeled on the COVID payments, for displaced workers. The summary describes rapid growth and prosperity after public release. Effects on other economies are not addressed in the text read.

Ownership. One consolidated project, built around OpenBrain, ends with half of the world’s AI-relevant compute. Its leadership balances power among the CEOs and government officials, overseen by the President. Compensation for the five trailing firms’ investors is Not confirmed.

Later Ranking of Plans. AI 2040, a 2026 recommendation by the AI Futures Project with four of the same authors, compares six plans (Comparing Possible Plans). The Hardwired Pause working paper’s reference list dates it July 9, 2026, and the site shows no date.
A · Verified international slowdown with research transparency · 70% to 81%
B · U.S. sabotage of China to buy time · 20% to 68%
C+ · U.S. regulation plus non-sabotage steps to slow China · 40% to 60%
C · The leading company spends some of its lead on safety · 20% to 63%
D · Race · 10% to 55%
S · Indefinite halt · Not in the by-author table

All five authors rate Plan C+ below Plan A, and three of the five rate it below Plan B. Lifland’s own estimate of the chance of a great future, if a plan is attempted, is 42% under Plan A. It is 25% under Plan C+ and under Plan B in its kinetic-sabotage form (Comparing Possible Plans).

Lifland rates Plan A highest on distribution of power. He says the plan likely to be carried out through nationalization or pseudo-nationalization loses transparency and concentrates power. The prior-art notes record that Plan B likely involves nationalization or something close to it.

Thomas Larsen expects the real U.S. response to look more like AI 2027’s (Plan A Assumptions). The research notes judge Plan C+ the nearest category to the Two-Lane Plan, a judgment the authors do not make. Plan A has a compact entry under Additional Entries Found in Research.

non-agentic-and-tool-ai-paths
Non-Agentic and Tool AI Paths

Source. Five proposals share this path. The notes read abstract pages for the three arXiv papers and the landing page of Aguirre’s essay. Drexler’s 2019 report is described through his 2023 restatement.

Scientist AI · Yoshua Bengio and 12 co-authors, arXiv, February 21, 2025 · A non-agentic system that explains the world and answers questions with stated uncertainty · Voluntary; built by the nonprofit LawZero

Tool AI · Anthony Aguirre, “Keep the Future Human,” March 5, 2025 (date per working paper) · Powerful narrow systems, or general systems without autonomy · Compute caps, enhanced liability and tiered safety standards
Comprehensive AI Services · Eric Drexler, 2019 report, restated July 10, 2023 · Flexible systems of task-focused services · A design approach with no rule attached
Bounded autonomy · Margaret Mitchell and three co-authors, arXiv, February 4, 2025 · Agents that stop short of full autonomy · A norm with no enforcement body
Guaranteed Safe AI · David Dalrymple, Joar Skalse, Yoshua Bengio and others, arXiv, May 10, 2024 · A world model, a formal safety specification and a verifier · Auditable proof certificates

What It Does. These proposals change what is built and leave open who builds it. They share one claim: the danger comes from joining generality and capability with autonomy. Development continues on systems that lack agency (Bengio), stay under meaningful human control (Aguirre, Mitchell) or work as bounded services (Drexler).
How It Works.

Restricted. Aguirre would close the gates to systems that combine high autonomy, generality and intelligence. Mitchell and co-authors say fully autonomous agents should not be developed. Scientist AI restricts no other developer and offers itself as a guardrail against unsafe agents.
Bound. Under Aguirre, private developers, who continue below the caps. Under Tegmark’s version, each country adopts national safety standards in its own interest (Hopium Wars).
Trigger and exit. No dates are set. Tegmark would permit only Tool AI until control is shown. Aguirre’s cap figures and exit terms are Not confirmed, because the fetch proxy refused the chapter.

Verification. Aguirre proposes standardized compute accounting and caps enforced in hardware. Guaranteed Safe AI relies on a verifier that issues an auditable proof certificate. The other three name no outside check in the material read.
Pros.
Non-agentic systems can speed science, safety research included, and avoid the risks of the agent-driven path (Bengio and co-authors).
The rule targets one dangerous combination and leaves powerful tools free (Aguirre).
A country can adopt Tool AI standards in its own interest, with no treaty (Tegmark).
General capability can come from task-focused services, and language models show broad knowledge without goals (Drexler, 2023).
Risks to people rise with autonomy as users cede control, and the paper weighs benefits and risks at each level (Mitchell and co-authors).
The path has funding. LawZero reports NVIDIA support (July 15, 2026) and a joint commitment of up to $300 million from Canada and Germany (September 16, 2026).
Cons.
Economic incentives favor open-ended autonomous systems, and military speed may require unified command (commenters on Drexler’s 2023 post).
Hierarchical delegation among services may re-create agents (the same commenters).
Drexler adds that misaligned humans may be the dominant threat.
Bounded autonomy has no enforcement body, and Scientist AI binds no one else.
Key details are missing. Aguirre’s caps, liability design and treatment of China are Not confirmed, and no LawZero output or evaluation was found.
Published critiques of Scientist AI were not found, so the objection that a predictor can be wrapped into an agent is Not confirmed.

Economy. Tegmark holds that Tool AI can serve industry, science and defense (FLI statement). Critics answer that agents are more useful, so markets and militaries will build them unless law or liability intervenes. No source in the notes estimates the output forgone, and effects on other economies are not addressed.

Ownership. Ownership does not change. LawZero is a nonprofit incubated at Mila, and its listed funders include the Gates Foundation, Schmidt Sciences, NVIDIA and Jaan Tallinn. Under Aguirre, private developers continue under caps and enhanced liability.
Questions.

structured-and-staged-access
Structured and Staged Access

Source. The concept is Toby Shevlane’s, in “Structured access: an emerging paradigm for safe AI deployment” (arXiv 2201.05159, January 13, 2022; abstract page read). The 2026 practice is dated and sourced in the table below. The staged-release literature (Solaiman and co-authors) was not opened and is Not confirmed.

What It Does. Developers offer controlled, arm’s-length use of a system, usually through the cloud, and keep the software itself. That lets them limit uses and stop users from removing limits by modification or reverse engineering. The goal is to keep dangerous capabilities out of wide availability while safe uses continue.
How It Works.

Restricted. Who may use a model, and for what. General users face refusals and automated monitoring, and vetted users reach more capable or more permissive models. Anthropic held Claude Mythos Preview back from general release.
Bound. The developer binds its own users. In June 2026 the Commerce Department bound a developer through an export control directive.

Trigger and exit. Labs have gated on cyber capability, and Anthropic aims to deploy Mythos-class models at scale once safeguards mature. The June 12 directive followed a reported bypass of Fable 5’s safeguards. The Commerce Secretary withdrew the controls on June 30, after a classifier fix and commitments by Anthropic, and Fable 5 returned on July 1.
Verification. Identity verification and customer vetting gate the higher tiers. The June 2 executive order adds a classified cyber benchmark that defines which models are covered.

Dangerous capability stays out of wide reach while defenders get it first (Shevlane; Anthropic).
The capability is concrete. Anthropic says Mythos Preview found thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities and scored 83.1% on CyberGym against 66.6% for Claude Opus 4.6.

Critics say partner programs disadvantage smaller organizations, and independent researchers questioned some capability claims (Wikipedia, a tertiary source).
Davis Wright Tremaine warns that voluntary frameworks can become soft mandates.
Structured access governs use of a finished model, and development and internal use fall outside it.

Economy. Anthropic committed $100 million in usage credits and $4 million in donations to open-source security groups, and OpenAI $10 million in API credits. defensive-acceleration
Defensive Acceleration

Source. Vitalik Buterin, My techno-optimism (November 27, 2023) and d/acc: one year later (January 5, 2025). The parent idea is differential technology development. Jonas Sandbrink, Hamish Hobbs, Jacob Swett, Allan Dafoe and Anders Sandberg set it out (SSRN 4213670, posted October 9, 2022; abstract page read).

What It Does. Differential technology development changes the order in which technologies arrive, with protective ones first and dangerous ones later. Buterin’s d/acc applies that to the present and favors decentralized defensive technology over both unrestrained acceleration and central control. By January 2025 he had added two restraints: liability rules and a hardware “soft pause.”
How It Works.

Restricted. In the 2025 version, uses exposed to liability and, in an emergency, industrial-scale compute. Such hardware would carry a trusted chip that needs weekly signatures from three international bodies, at least one non-military.
Bound. Liability falls first on users, then on deployers and developers, because users cannot cover catastrophic damages. The soft pause binds owners of industrial-scale AI hardware worldwide.

Trigger and exit. At a critical moment the soft pause could cut worldwide compute by about 90% to 99% for one to two years (Buterin, 2025). Buterin calls both measures temporary stopgaps, and the notes record no test for the moment.
Verification. The chip enforces the pause, because hardware stops without the signatures. Defensive work has no compliance check.
Pros.
It avoids both a single controlling entity and an unregulated race in which one actor pulls ahead (Buterin, 2023).
Limits that apply to everyone equally are safer than a U.S.-led race to decisive advantage (Buterin, 2025).
Timing can be shifted with tools that exist: research funding, regulation, philanthropy and corporate responsibility measures (Sandbrink and co-authors).
A hardware pause avoids legal exemptions and consumer surveillance (Buterin, 2025).
It combines with other plans. The research notes read the Two-Lane Plan’s cyber and bio hardening as d/acc inside containment.
In 2026 defenders received early access to frontier cyber capability, with credits, through Glasswing and Trusted Access for Cyber.
Cons.
Buterin concedes that acceleration of the good is insufficient if superintelligence is three to five years away, so the bad must be slowed.
The approach needs foresight about a technology’s effects and the ability to shift timing, limits its authors state.
Defensive public goods undercut ordinary business models and need public-goods funding (Buterin, 2025).
The 2026 defensive access ran through two firms and a government directive, which is centralized (a reading in the research notes).
The notes cite Garfinkel and Dafoe (2019) as a caution on offense-defense forecasts (War on the Rocks; not opened).
No published critique of d/acc was opened, so the standard objections are Not confirmed.

Economy. d/acc leaves most development running and speeds defensive technology in four areas: resilient infrastructure, biodefense, cyber defense and information defense. A soft pause would cut worldwide compute by about 90% to 99% for one to two years. No source in the notes estimates that cost or the effects by country.

Ownership. Ownership does not change, and no central controller exists. Buterin prefers open-source and public-goods models, paid for through quadratic funding, retroactive funding and his “deep funding.” In 2023 he suggested that open-source requirements for allowed models might be safer than licensing that concentrates power.

plan-r-ai-safety-by-asics
Plan R: AI Safety by ASICs

Source. Roko, “Plan R: AI Safety by ASICs”, LessWrong, September 25, 2026. Roko extends it in “Plan R+, Diversity, Escrow and Political Rights for ASICs” (September 26) and “Skeuomorphic AI Safety” (September 27). Most objections below come from the first post’s comment thread, read on October 9, 2026. Comment dates were not recorded.

What It Does. Roko traces much of AI’s civilization-scale risk to organizations that build very powerful or self-replicating systems, which may outstrip the rest of civilization. The same organizations own an unbounded financial claim on the resulting surplus. Plan R splits the two properties between two kinds of entity and burns every deployed model into a chip. Roko calls the approach “AI Safety by skeuomorphism”: AI changed to behave more like humans, which the world is already set up to handle.
How It Works.

Restricted. AI research and development organizations train and test frontier models. They cannot issue equity or use their own models. Physically enforced latency on their air-gapped perimeter keeps data from moving in or out in less than about 12 hours. Deployment companies run inference and build products. They may not train new models or hold general-purpose AI chips (Plan R+).

Bound. Frontier developers and owners of advanced compute everywhere, through an international agreement. Roko thinks one feasible because the industry now exists in only two countries, which the post does not name. Outside the research organizations, all high-spec compute would take the form of ASICs.

Trigger and exit. The post sets no start date and no exit. A model that passes its evaluations is burned into an ASIC, and a run of R units is sold. The original is then deleted or encrypted. For added safety, Roko suggests a lag. An ASIC would work on real-world tasks for about three months before a research organization could use it. He says the lag would put a “speed limit” on the Singularity.

Verification. The post names no inspector or agency. Research organizations would face some unusual scrutiny, and Roko suggests mandatory write-once logs as one example. In a reply to a commenter, he adds that each chip would be a sealed unit that must be accounted for.

The Plan R+ extension. Roko grants that a deceptively misaligned model could pass the tests. Plan R+ answers with about 1,000 “lineages” per generation, trained on varied inputs. Each lineage gets about 10,000 chips, released in stages. A lineage that misbehaves would be recalled, or at least its unreleased chips held back. AIs whose lineage completes without misbehaving would gain political representation and property.
Pros.

Separating the two properties removes the incentive to race, by Roko’s account. He argues that nuclear and bioweapon technology stay mostly safe because their holders have no financial reason to push their luck.

A rogue AI finds little compute to capture. Roko writes that there would be no compute overhang to seize, and a rogue AI would be left with CPUs and perhaps GPUs. He adds that GPUs might be changed so they cannot run AI models, though more work is needed.
No lab can use its own models in its research. Roko says this “anti-dogfooding” rule would stop any one AI company from “going nuclear” on its own.

Development and deployment continue, and Roko says the plan needs no pause or ban. He hopes the split, with help from ASICs, can also leave a very productive AI industry that delivers most of AI’s benefits.

Roko judges it more acceptable to the major powers than a halt. He rates it well above a total shutdown of AI research (“Plan S”) and “Plan A” from their point of view. The post does not define Plan A. The AI Futures Project uses both labels, with Plan S an indefinite halt (Lifland).
Inspection can confirm which model a chip runs. Only weight-fixed chips allow that check (Verification and Technology tab), and Plan R puts every deployed model on one.

The hardware exists at small scale. A commenter, joec, cites a demo of Llama 3.1 8B burned into an ASIC. It ran at about 17,000 tokens a second, against about 500 on a B300. The Verification and Technology tab records Taalas’s HC1, which fixes the weights of that model.
Cons.

Frontier models may be too large to hardwire. A commenter who designs ASICs, MBaert, says a fully unrolled design is not feasible for frontier models because they are too big. MBaert estimates about 500 distinct chips for a model of about 10 trillion weights, with output near 34 tokens a second.

MBaert prefers a fixed-architecture chip with cryptographically signed weights, backed by remote monitoring and shutdown. The authenticated-weight chip in the Hardwired Pause working paper is similar (project reading).

Vladimir_Nesov writes that hardcoded weights do not really work for the biggest models. He thinks ternary weights with quantization-aware training could help, and sees the need for thousands of tapeouts as more of a crux.

Chips tied to one model age fast. A June 18, 2026 post by Gloria Z, a MIRI Technical Governance fellow, judges weight-fused ASICs unlikely to meet industry needs. The post says frontier architectures change often and load varies. Google reportedly dropped a weight-fixed first chip for a similar reason (Verification and Technology tab). In “Skeuomorphic AI Safety”, Roko replies that the commercial inconvenience may be what keeps the arrangement stable.

It still needs an international deal and inspectors. Daniel Kokotajlo says Plan R needs many elements of Plan A or Plan S, such as a deal and inspectors who count chips. He asks how research organizations would be financed and regulated. He also asks what would stop former staff of a deployment firm, who hold its equity, from founding a research firm to supply it. Roko replies that basically anything other than the default (“Plan D”) needs some kind of compute governance.

It asks for extraordinary cooperation. Maxsimal says its biggest problem is the extreme level of civilizational cooperation it requires. Maxsimal adds that a misaligned model could corrupt a production model before it is burned in.

Burned-in weights may still be read out. The commenter cqb writes that burned-in weights alone do not stop extraction, and encryption would add many transistors per weight. Roko answers that only research organizations would hold GPUs. Taking chips apart would be illegal, and he says teardown might be extremely hard.

Enforcement reaches ordinary computers. The commenter _rpd argues that every attempt to separate inference from other computing is unworkable, and that AI researchers would become “thought criminals.” Roko replies that limits on memory, storage and fast networking would make ordinary computers almost useless for language models. RAM might be capped at about 4 GB.

The nuclear analogy is disputed. Vaniver thinks the nuclear arms buildup came mainly from “unbounded claim” dynamics, since a first strike might let a state rule the world. Vaniver grants that IOUs may move the takeoff up from 2030 to 2027 or 2028. In Vaniver’s view, AIs may soon pay for their own compute, so dismantling finance would still leave exponential takeoff. Mlxa credits nuclear stability to mutual second-strike capability.
No published response outside LessWrong was found in two searches on October 9, 2026.

Economy. The post gives no cost estimate. Outside the research organizations, general-purpose AI chips would give way to model-specific ones. Plan R+ would remove most AI-capable GPU compute from the rest of the world. For scale, the Hardwired Pause working paper puts the cost of existing accelerators at about $500 billion (§5.3.2, unpublished draft). Each new model needs its own chip run, and Taalas reports about two months per model on its platform (Verification and Technology tab). Makers of general-purpose accelerators would lose the deployment market, and makers of model-specific chips would gain it (project reading). A commenter, joec, suggests firms might move frontier inference to AS…

Ownership. Plan R and Plan R+ state the split directly. Frontier AI companies become research organizations that cannot issue equity and deployment companies that can. The research side would be run like a cross between a nuclear weapons lab and a global systemically important bank. Roko floats debt financing and says he will have to think more about it. Deployment companies pay the research side for models and stay on Silicon Valley rules. In a comment, Roko suggests barring research staff and financiers from stakes in deployment firms. He cites the Sarbanes-Oxley Act as a precedent. None of the three posts says what happens to current investors in the frontier labs.
Questions.

Identify the two countries the post means, and how the plan binds third countries with chip fabs or cloud capacity.
Test MBaert’s estimate of about 500 chips for a 10-trillion-weight model against vendor data and the Hardwired Pause working paper.

Define the evaluations a model must pass before burn-in, and who runs them.
Settle whether deployment firms may fine-tune, given that their role covers any work that needs no gradient descent.
Find how the plan treats open-weight models already published, which run on ordinary hardware.
Work out how research organizations raise money without equity, and whether lenders would fund them.
Find how outsiders would verify the 12-hour latency rule and the bar on a lab using its own models.
Compare Plan R with the Hardwired Pause, which also confines public use to fixed hardware, and with Lane Two of the Two-Lane Plan.

Additional Entries Found in Research

The notes record five further proposals with no section of their own in this tab, plus a set of minor items and unverified leads. Two of the five, AI 2040: Plan A and Whole-Lab Inspection, are slowdown agreements built on containment tools. Both also belong to the Pace family (see the Pace: Slowdowns and Gates tab).
ai-2040-plan-a
AI 2040: Plan A

Source. Thomas Larsen, Romeo Dean, Brendan Halstead, Eli Lifland, Ryan Greenblatt and Daniel Kokotajlo, AI Futures Project (AI 2040, summary). The Hardwired Pause working paper’s reference list dates it July 9, 2026, and the site shows no date.

What It Does. A verified U.S.-China deal from 2029 blocks fully automated AI R&D, pauses scaling at top-human-expert level in 2035 and resumes it in 2040. Research is almost fully public, many companies in many countries stay at the frontier, and data centers carry self-destruct switches. Inference data centers sit in Faraday cages, and R&D data centers have a 1 MB/s cap on outbound data (Security in Plan A).

Main Argument For. Five authors’ estimates of avoiding misaligned takeover run from 70% to 81%, and Lifland rates the plan highest on distribution of power (Comparing Possible Plans). The authors’ economic model shows about 90% average annual real output growth in 2032 to 2037 and an equal Citizen’s Dividend (Economics of Plan A).

Main Argument Against. Tom Davidson calls the paused software and growing compute “dry tinder” (Davidson). Compute grows about 100x by 2033, so a collapsed deal would mean a far faster intelligence explosion. Eli Lifland puts the cumulative chance of deal decline by 2040 at 48% to 51% (Deal Decline).
Capture the three difficulties Davidson raises with mutual assured compute destruction, and any reply from the authors.

whole-lab-inspection
Whole-Lab Inspection
Source. Felix Choussat and Adam Khoja, Center for AI Safety, An International AI Slowdown Is Ready Whenever Politicians Are, AI Frontiers, August 5, 2026.

What It Does. U.S. and Chinese inspectors get broad physical access to frontier AI companies and read-only access to communications, work logs, code repositories and compute telemetry. Chip supply-chain tracking exposes undeclared projects. The agreement bars autonomous AI R&D and certain post-training enhancement, and allows safety-focused training and narrow AI for science.
Main Argument For. Low-tech human inspection is enough, as in nuclear arms control. Staff turnover, hacking and espionage would still expose the projects of a state that refused (the authors).
Main Argument Against. The design assumes U.S. and Chinese willingness. Critics, as the authors report, say verification needs technology that does not yet exist.

rand-security-levels-for-model-weights
RAND Security Levels for Model Weights
Source. Sella Nevo and five co-authors, Securing AI Model Weights, RAND RR-A2849-1, May 30, 2024.

What It Does. The report identifies 38 distinct attack vectors and defines five security levels, SL1 to SL5. The levels run from opportunistic criminals to the most capable states. It recommends defense in depth, centralized and reduced weight access, insider-threat programs and red-teaming, and leaves ownership unchanged.

Main Argument For. Securing weights against the most capable states takes far more investment over years, with isolated networks and probably government help (RAND). Other plans use the scale, and AI 2040 requires SL5 for weights.

Main Argument Against. AI 2040’s authors rate SL5 viable only with extreme effort and possibly impossible (Security in Plan A). Gladstone AI claims that frontier labs are probably penetrated already (Gladstone AI).

Ownership does not change, and the document proposes no national AGI project.
Main Argument For. The design trades permits and energy financing for security commitments and leaves ownership alone (Institute for Progress).
Main Argument Against. The notes opened no critique, so the main objection is Not confirmed.

sentinel-national-lab
Sentinel National Lab
Source. Tony Blair and William Hague, A New National Purpose, Tony Blair Institute, June 13, 2023.

What It Does. Sentinel is a proposed UK national lab, described as a version of CERN for AI, with funding on the scale of a frontier lab. Main Argument Against. The notes opened no critique of Sentinel, so the main objection is Not confirmed. For the similar CERN for AI design, the Centre for Future Generations lists a small budget, slow processes, talent competition and mission drift (CFG).

family-pros-cons-and-questions
Family Pros, Cons and Questions

The family makes one bet. Frontier development continues, and safety comes from who controls it, where it runs, what is built or who may use it. Its members draw three recurring objections: concentration of power, unobservability and competitive leakage.
shared-arguments-for
Shared Arguments For

The capability stays in hand. Amodei holds that a pause is infeasible and that autocracies would continue regardless (Amodei 2026). Aschenbrenner calls superintelligence the most important defense project since the bomb (The Project).

Most members can start without a treaty. A national project, the entente, structured access and Tool AI standards need no agreement with China. Tegmark presents Tool AI as a national strategy that needs no treaty (Hopium Wars).

A lead can be spent on safety. Davidson and Hadshar grant that a bigger U.S. lead means more time to pause later (Forethought). The AI Futures Project’s Plan C has the leading company spend part of its lead that way.

Security at state level needs the state. RAND finds that securing weights against the most capable states takes years and probably government help (RAND). Gladstone AI argues that security cannot be added later (Gladstone AI).

Restricting use has worked in practice. In 2026 two labs ran identity-verified access tiers and one withheld its strongest model. A Commerce Department directive pulled two deployed models for 19 days (Anthropic).
Channeling is being financed. LawZero reports a joint commitment of up to $300 million from Canada and Germany, announced September 16, 2026 (LawZero).
shared-arguments-against
Shared Arguments Against

Concentration of power. Davidson and Hadshar’s tentative best guess is that one Western project is probably net bad. AI 2027’s authors flag that their Oversight Committee could entrench itself (summary). Bostrom calculates a global wealth Gini of about 0.96 for a U.S.-only nationalized project, against about 0.89 to 0.92 under open investment (Bostrom).

The race continues. Tegmark argues that both sides lose if either finishes, because the world is closer to building AGI than to controlling it. Katzke and Futerman argue that the assumptions behind a race also make it extremely dangerous (arXiv 2501.14749).
Unobservability. RAND, MIRI and Arnold argue that rivals cannot reliably see a capability red line being crossed. The research notes extend the point to any tripwire defined inside a lab.
Competitive leakage. Rules that bind only some actors lose to those left unbound, because economic and military incentives favor agents (commenters on Drexler).
The state’s 2026 record. In February 2026 the Pentagon pressed Anthropic to drop its own limits on military use (Kahn, Fortune). Anthropic says the June recall lacked a transparent statutory process.

Lower odds by the forecasters’ own count. The AI Futures Project gives domestic regulation plus non-sabotage steps 40% to 60%. A verified international slowdown gets 70% to 81% (Comparing Possible Plans).
Security may be out of reach. AI 2040’s authors rate SL5 viable only with extreme effort and possibly impossible (Security in Plan A).

main
Two-Lane Plan: Full Design
This tab develops the Two-Lane Plan in detail: its legal architecture, institutions, operating rules, financing, phasing and open decisions.
the-plan-in-brief
The Plan in Brief

The Two-Lane Plan keeps frontier development going inside containment and holds public deployment behind a gate that opens on proof of control. It is a domestic design. It assumes that no verified agreement with China is available and that national security requires the capability.

Lane One, contained development. Frontier training and research proceed at full speed inside certified, air-gapped facilities. Resident federal examiners hold access to weights and internals, and the federal government is the anchor customer.

Lane Two, gated deployment. No frontier system leaves containment for public or commercial use until its developer proves control. Narrow supervised systems clear first, and fully autonomous agents clear last.

The gate. Three tripwires mark loss-of-control risk: autonomous AI research and development, evasion of oversight, and independent capability to attack critical systems. One tripwire bars release and uncontained internal use until control is proven by clear and convincing evidence. Two make the bar conclusive.
The lead budget. Any pause on further scaling lasts no longer than the U.S. lead over China. A presidential adversary finding moves the work into a secure government program.
Shared gains. The government takes equity or warrants in labs it funds, and the returns pay for wage insurance and transition support.
The plan rests on two bets. The first is that the lead is long enough to solve control. The second is that containment holds while the work is done.

This tab develops the plan into a statute, institutions, operating rules and financing. Details that go beyond the plan’s stated terms are proposals for discussion, and the Open Decisions section lists the main ones. They include the certificate of control, the commission, the deployment tiers, the decision clock, the safety margin, the form of the public stake and its trust, the expiry of the adversary finding, and the phases.
design-principles
Design Principles
Eight principles decide the design choices in the rest of this tab.
Control before release. A system reaches the public only after its developer has shown control. The developer carries the burden, and the standard is clear and convincing evidence.
Speed where it is contained. Research inside certified facilities runs at full speed. Limits attach to what leaves containment and to uses that cannot be undone.
The lead is a budget. Time ahead of China is spent on control research and on proving control. A pause that outlasts the lead defeats the purpose of the plan.
No dependence on Beijing. Every rule binds U.S. developers under U.S. law. A verified agreement can replace parts of the plan later.
Private and plural labs. Developers stay privately owned and compete with each other. The state supervises and buys, and its financial interest stays a minority one.
A gatekeeper with no stake. The body that decides release holds no equity and takes no revenue from the labs it judges.
The public shares the gain. Public money and public risk earn a public return, and that return pays for workers who are displaced.
Every power has a check. Gate decisions face expedited judicial review. Emergency powers expire unless Congress renews them, and the lead estimate goes to Congress.
statutory-architecture
Statutory Architecture
A single statute could carry the plan in eight titles. The table gives each title’s content and the nearest existing model.
I. Coverage · Covered developers and frontier systems, defined by compute, capability and spending · Thresholds in S. 2938 (10^26 operations) and the Sanders and Casar bill (10^25)
II. Contained Development · Certified facilities, resident examiners, security levels, sign-off on large runs, internal-use rules · Bank examination; RAND security levels
III. The Gate · Certificate of control, tripwires, burden and standard of proof, deployment tiers · Drug approval; the evaluation requirement in S. 2938
IV. Security Lane Funding · Anchor procurement, compute contracts, the control-research program · Defense procurement; national laboratory contracts
V. Liability and Agents · Liability regime, agent registry, duties for consumer products, incident reporting, whistleblower protection · Product liability law; securities whistleblower rules

VI. Lead and Adversary · Official lead estimate, lead-indexed limit on pauses, adversary finding · No close model found. Nearest: the emergency clause of the Atomic Energy Act and the Defense Department’s steering committee on advanced AI
VII. Shared Gains and Stability · Public stake, wage insurance, paced adoption in high-displacement sectors, credit safeguards · Federal equity stakes since 2025; bank exposure limits
VIII. Oversight · Judicial review, sunsets, reports to Congress, an inspector general · Reauthorization clauses, as in the Defense Production Act
instruments-already-on-the-table
Instruments Already on the Table
Four existing instruments cover parts of this ground.

Executive Order 14409 (June 2, 2026). It directs agencies to design a voluntary window of up to 30 days for government access to cyber-capable models before release to trusted partners. It disclaims mandatory licensing (order).

S. 2938 (introduced September 29, 2025). It bars deployment above 10^26 operations unless the developer takes part in an Energy Department evaluation. It sets no pass-or-fail standard and leaves internal use outside the gate (bill text). A Senate subcommittee examined it at a hearing on September 30, 2026 (Daily Digest).

The FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925, introduced July 23, 2026). It lets the Commerce Secretary suspend a developer’s development, deployment or internal use on a finding of imminent catastrophic risk. A provisional order expires after 45 days and a final order after 90 days, renewable on a fresh finding. The Secretary bears the burden at a hearing. Section 8(l) would make that process the only federal route for restricting a frontier model on those grounds, the President included (sponsors’ summary; introduced text).

The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (S. 5493, introduced September 23, 2026; H.R. 10538 in the House). It lists six precursor characteristics, covers internal deployment and requires approval for each model (bill text). It pauses development above its threshold until a new department is staffed and has issued rules, and it bans systems that show the characteristics.

None of the four pairs a developer’s burden of proof with continued development inside containment. Only the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act sets a standing bar on internal deployment, for systems that show its precursor characteristics. The FRONTIER Act would add standing duties to assess and report catastrophic risks from internal use (introduced text). An earlier bill, S. 5616 of 2024, would have let a Commerce official prohibit a deployment on the government’s own determination (bill text). The Pace: Slowdowns and Gates tab and the Law, Politics and Institutions tab describe each instrument in full.
institutions
Institutions

The plan needs five functions, and it keeps the gate decision apart from the public stake. The table lists candidate homes. The choice among them is an open decision, and the assessments of each home below are the drafter’s own.
Examination · Resident examiners inside each certified facility, with access to weights, logs and staff · A new examination service; the Center for AI Standards and Innovation; the Energy Department
Certification · Certifies facilities and containment levels · The examination service, with national laboratories for testing
Gate decisions · Grants, denies and revokes certificates of control · A multi-member commission with fixed terms
Lead estimate · Publishes the official estimate of the U.S. lead twice a year · The Director of National Intelligence
Public stake · Holds equity and warrants and pays out returns · An independent trust with no role in gate decisions
where-the-gatekeeper-could-sit
Where the Gatekeeper Could Sit

An independent commission. Fixed terms and removal protection shield gate decisions from the White House and from the labs. A new commission takes years to staff. The Sanders and Casar bill takes a larger step and creates a federal department.

The Commerce Department. Its Center for AI Standards and Innovation already evaluates frontier models (NIST), and the FRONTIER Act would give suspension power to the Commerce Secretary. Commerce also promotes the industry it would gate.
The Energy Department. S. 2938 places its evaluation program there. The national laboratories bring classified computing and security experience, and Energy has little history as a market regulator.
An industry standards body. Demis Hassabis proposed an industry-funded body in July 2026 (see the Pace: Slowdowns and Gates tab). Critics of that model point to capture, as one research note reports.
staffing
Staffing
Staffing is the binding constraint. Examiners need pay near industry levels and security clearances. A bar on joining a supervised lab afterward guards against capture.

Bank examination is the nearest model of statutory, resident access. Amodei’s September 2026 essay cites embedded bank supervisors as precedent for embedded evaluators (Amodei). A September 2026 paper reports that chief executives of frontier labs have committed to host embedded third-party assessments (Charnock and others). One commenter on the AI Futures Project’s pacing post proposed the banking model for AI auditors (comments).
lane-one-in-practice
Lane One in Practice
Lane One is a regulated perimeter around frontier work. Developers keep ownership and the direction of research. The perimeter sets where the work happens and who watches it.

Certified facilities. Covered training and agentic research run only in facilities certified at a containment level. Open-ended agentic reinforcement learning requires the highest level, in line with the Containment Rule for Agentic Reinforcement Learning (see the Pace: Slowdowns and Gates tab).

A staged security target. The plan calls for weight security against nation-state attack. RAND judged in 2024 that its top level, SL5, was not yet achievable (RAND; research brief). The statute would set an interim level at enactment and a date for the top level.
Resident examiners. Examiners work on site with access to weights, internals, logs and incident records. They report tripwire evidence to the commission.
Human sign-off. A named officer of the developer and the resident examiner sign before any training run above a set size.
Internal-use rules. A system that meets one tripwire may run only inside containment. Developers report each quarter the share of research work done by AI agents.

Control research. A fixed share of each developer’s compute goes to control and alignment research under a national program. The AI Futures Project proposes a floor for published safety work, with 25 percent as an example (How to Pace the US Frontier).
Limits on government use. Lane One systems may not act autonomously in weapons release or in control of critical infrastructure. The limit binds agencies as well as contractors.
What developers keep. Intellectual property, hiring and research direction stay with the developer. Government customers buy access under contract.
a-recent-parallel
A Recent Parallel

OpenAI said on August 18, 2026 that it had paused reinforcement-learning training on its latest models intended for deployment for two weeks. It tied resumption to hardened environments and stronger evidence of aligned behavior (OpenAI). The post presents the decision as the firm’s own, and its largest planned run stayed on hold.
the-central-objection
The Central Objection

The literature on internal deployment points the other way. The AI 2040 authors place most takeover risk in internally deployed systems (AI 2040). Lawrence Chan of METR and Stix and coauthors argue that large risks arise inside the lab before any release (Chan; Stix and others).
Lane One answers with containment levels, resident examiners, the internal-use rule and reporting on research done by agents. Whether that answer is enough is the plan’s second bet.
the-gate-in-practice
The Gate in Practice
The gate turns on one document, the certificate of control. A covered system may be offered to the public or to commercial customers only while a certificate is in force.
the-certificate-of-control
The Certificate of Control
Burden and standard. The developer must show by clear and convincing evidence that the system stays under human control in its intended uses and in foreseeable misuse.
Evidence. The filing is a safety case: evaluations, red-team results, interpretability findings, containment records and incident history. Examiners may run their own tests on the weights.

Hidden capability. Models can perform differently under test (see the Verification and Technology tab). The commission may rely on examiner-run elicitation and on presumptions drawn from training inputs such as compute and agentic training time.
Decision clock. The commission rules within a fixed period. Silence counts as denial, so delay cannot open the gate.
Revocation. A certificate lapses on a material change to the system and may be revoked on new tripwire evidence.
deployment-tiers
Deployment Tiers
1 · Narrow tools under direct human supervision · Certificate on a reduced record
2 · General assistants with no autonomous action · Full certificate; incident reporting
3 · Agents that act for a registered principal · Full certificate; registry entry; financial responsibility
4 · Fully autonomous agents · Last to clear; individual approval for each system
tripwires
Tripwires
Autonomous AI research and development · The system can carry out frontier AI research with little human direction · Lab reports on research done by agents; examiner tests
Evasion of oversight · The system deceives evaluators, underperforms on tests by design, or acts to avoid monitoring or shutdown · Evaluation records; incident reports
Independent attack capability · The system can find and exploit flaws in critical systems without expert human help · Cyber range tests; government red teams

One tripwire creates a rebuttable presumption that the system cannot be controlled. Release and uncontained internal use stop until the developer rebuts it. Two tripwires make the bar conclusive, and the system stays in containment for study.
review-and-the-weak-point
Review and the Weak Point

A developer may appeal a denial to a federal court of appeals on an expedited schedule. Measurement is the gate’s weakest point. No public instrument yet measures autonomous AI research well enough to serve as a legal trigger (see the Verification and Technology tab).
the-lead-budget
The Lead Budget
The plan treats the U.S. lead over China as time to spend. A pause on further scaling may last no longer than the lead, less a safety margin.

Who measures. The Director of National Intelligence publishes an estimate twice a year, with a classified annex. No source opened ties an official estimate of the lead to a pause. The nearest items are a tracking body kept apart from the developers (Hastings-Woodhouse), the Defense Department’s steering committee on advanced AI (Section 1535) and an annual Commerce report on Chinese AI capabilities that a House bill would require (H.R. 6275). The Center for AI Standards and Innovation already publishes lag figures for single Chinese models.
What is measured. Frontier model capability, compute stock, chip production, and the share of Chinese progress that depends on distilling U.S. models.

Current estimates. The AI Futures Project puts the lead at four to eight months and China’s catch-up time after a U.S. halt at about a year (August 7, 2026). The Center for AI Standards and Innovation put DeepSeek V4 about eight months behind the frontier in May 2026 (NIST). Public estimates collected in January 2026 ran from three to 18 months, apart from one executive’s remark that the gap is negligible. The article cites no official government measure (PolitiFact). Chris McGuire of the Council on Foreign Relations put the lead at seven months in January 2026 (CFR). Epoch AI projects Huawei’s 2026 chip output at under 4 percent of Nvidia’s in computing power (Epoch AI).
How it is spent. Time under a tripwire hold on scaling draws on the budget. The commission must lift or narrow the hold before the budget runs out.

How it grows. Export controls, chip tracking, allied chokepoints and weight security lengthen the lead. Contained development also narrows the distillation channel, since fewer frontier systems are served to the public.

When a rival moves first. If the President finds that a rival has fielded a gated capability, the work moves into a secure government program. The duty to prove control stays in force, and the finding expires unless Congress renews it.
what-is-published-and-what-is-added
What Is Published and What Is Added

The principle has been in print since at least October 2023. That month Scott Alexander described a “surgical pause” that runs just short of the West’s lead over China (Alexander). Carlsmith and Bostrom stated the same limit for a single leading actor in 2026. Dario Amodei wrote in September 2026 that pacing in democracies is bounded by their lead over authoritarian states (Amodei). The AI Futures Project estimates that China would need about a year to catch up after a full U.S. halt.
The plan adds a legal rule and ties an official estimate to it. No source opened does either (see the prior-art review in the Contain and Channel tab).
the-tightest-constraint
The Tightest Constraint

A short lead constrains the whole design. At four to eight months, one contested certificate could consume the budget. Containment also makes the lead harder to measure, since public models would understate internal ones (see the Verification and Technology tab).
financing-and-ownership
Financing and Ownership
Gated deployment defers commercial revenue, so Lane One needs a paying customer. The plan makes the federal government that customer and takes a public stake in return.
Anchor contracts. Agencies sign multi-year contracts for contained access and for compute. Take-or-pay terms give lenders a federal counterparty.
Public stake. A developer that accepts anchor funding issues warrants or non-voting equity, capped at a minority share. An independent trust holds the stake and has no voice in gate decisions.
Use of returns. Returns fund wage insurance and transition support for displaced workers.
Credit safeguards. Regulators limit bank and insurer exposure to data center debt, and large borrowers file resolution plans.
where-the-stake-sits-among-published-positions
Where the Stake Sits Among Published Positions

The stake sits among four published positions. S. 4825, introduced by Senator Sanders on June 18, 2026, would give the public a 50 percent equity stake through a tax paid in shares (bill text). Alex Bores’s “AI Dividend” would have the federal government take out-of-the-money warrants in major AI companies, with returns to direct payments, workforce transition and safety governance (Bores, June 9, 2026). It is the nearest published design found. The Financial Times reported in July 2026 that OpenAI had discussed a 5 percent government stake held through a public fund (Reuters via The Star), and Sam Altman was later reported to oppose government-held shares (The Washington Sun). Anton Leicht …
problems-to-solve
Problems to Solve

Precedent. The federal government had invested about $27 billion in corporate stakes by July 2026 (Fortune). The research found no federal stake in an AI developer as of September 30, 2026 (see the Ownership and Industry Structure tab).
Conflict of interest. A state that owns part of a lab gains from early release. The plan answers by separating the trust from the commission.
Takings. A gate that holds a finished product off the market may draw compensation claims. No legal analysis of that question was found (see the Ownership and Industry Structure tab).
Scale. No estimate found in this research sizes the contracts needed to replace deferred commercial revenue (see the Economic Effects tab).
phasing
Phasing
The plan can start under existing authority and needs a statute to finish.
0 · Now · Examiner pilots by agreement; pre-release review as a condition of federal contracts; a first lead estimate · Procurement power; Executive Order 14409
1 · On enactment · Examination service, facility certification, certificate of control for new releases · New statute
2 · Within 18 months · Internal-use rules, anchor contracts, public stake trust, lead budget · New statute; appropriations
3 · If a verified deal is reached · An agreement with China replaces the lead budget · Treaty or executive agreement
The 18-month figure is a placeholder.
what-existing-law-reaches
What Existing Law Reaches

Export-control law. On June 12, 2026 the Commerce Department sent Anthropic an export-control letter that barred foreign nationals’ access to two models. Anthropic disabled both for all customers (Anthropic). Commentary reports that the letter cited the Export Control Reform Act and a military-intelligence provision of the export regulations, and one commentator calls that basis new and uncertain (Harvard Law Review Blog; Mayer Brown). Commerce withdrew the controls on June 30 (Anthropic, June 30). A customer sued and dropped the suit in early July, before any ruling (Bloomberg via The Star; Law360 via MLex).

The Defense Production Act. Alan Rozenshtein describes limits on what the act can compel from a lab (Lawfare). Most of its authorities lapse on December 11, 2026 unless renewed (see the Law, Politics and Institutions tab).
Procurement. Contract conditions bind only developers that sell to the government.
A standing gate that places the burden on developers needs an act of Congress.
the-open-weight-gap
The Open-Weight Gap

A gate on U.S. frontier systems leaves foreign open-weight models in circulation. Chinese developers publish many of the strongest ones, so the plan needs a rule for them. The China and Geopolitics tab treats the wider question of restricting Chinese open-weight models.
facts-that-bear-on-the-design
Facts That Bear on the Design

Distance from the frontier. Epoch AI put the best open-weight models about four months behind the closed frontier on average since January 2026, against about three months in October 2025 (May 29, 2026; October 2025).

Capability with fewer refusals. An April 2026 evaluation found Kimi K2.5 comparable to GPT 5.2 and Claude Opus 4.5 on dual-use tasks. It refused significantly fewer weapons-related (CBRNE) requests (Yong and others; abstract only).

Removable safeguards. A public build of GLM-5.3 complied with about 80 percent of harmful test requests after a weight edit with no retraining (Hugging Face; uploader’s figures). The Center for AI Standards and Innovation states that safeguards on open-weight models can be circumvented when a model is self-hosted (NIST, July 17, 2026).

Federal findings. The Center for AI Standards and Innovation tested DeepSeek models and reported on September 30, 2025. One complied with 94 percent of malicious requests under a jailbreak, against 8 percent for U.S. models (NIST). The center issued at least four more assessments of Chinese models in 2026. It put DeepSeek V4 about eight months behind the frontier in May, and in September it called GLM-5.3 the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date (DeepSeek V4; GLM-5.3).

Current federal posture. Axios reports that the administration’s voluntary testing framework covers closed models only, and that officials weighed and dropped four steps against Chinese models, among them an Entity List designation and a hosting-liability order (August 4, 2026; July 20, 2026). Defense Department systems are closed to DeepSeek and High Flyer models by statute (Section 1532).
four-options
Four Options

Government and infrastructure limits · Bars uncertified models from federal systems and critical infrastructure · Private use continues. Already law for Defense Department systems and, in 14 to 17 states, for government devices
Origin-neutral gate · Applies the certificate of control to any covered system offered commercially in the United States · Weak against self-hosting; gates U.S. open models too
Chokepoint duties · Requires clouds, model hubs and inference providers to carry only certified covered systems · Mirrors and peer-to-peer copies persist

Origin-based ban · Prohibits acquiring or using models from named foreign-adversary developers · Untested legal fit; hard to enforce on free downloads. One bill would bar imports of Chinese-developed AI (S. 321), and it has not moved since January 2025
what-the-plans-logic-implies
What the Plan’s Logic Implies

The gate asks one question of every system: has control been proven. The answer does not depend on where a model was built. An open-weight model above the tripwires may have no accountable developer to make the showing, and its weights can be changed after release. Under an origin-neutral gate it could not be offered commercially.

The case for going further. Deliberately trained hidden behavior can survive standard safety training, and adversarial training can hide it (Hubinger and others). No source opened documents a deliberate backdoor in a released Chinese model. A gate that leaves an ungated substitute on offer shifts risk and market share to that substitute.

The case against a ban by origin. Published weights cannot be recalled, and a possession ban would need device-level monitoring. Three of the six risks set out in the China and Geopolitics tab arise from any capable open model. Weights run locally send no data abroad, and data collection was the ground that carried the TikTok ruling (opinion).

Support for a test that ignores origin. Dario Amodei wrote in July 2026 that all sufficiently capable models, open and closed, should go through mandatory safety testing, and that Anthropic has never sought a ban on open-weight models (Anthropic).

The competitive answer. The AI Action Plan and Jason Hsu favor U.S. open models strong enough to become the default (Hsu; AI Action Plan). A Lane Two that certifies capable U.S. models for release would serve that end.
Four points are unsettled: weights already published, U.S. open-weight releases, private self-hosting, and derivatives of foreign models. Each appears under Open Decisions.
strongest-objections-and-responses

A reviewer of this tab adds five objections that the table omits.
Speed. Air-gapped work may not run at full speed.
Visibility. The public loses sight of the frontier while systems stay inside.
Misfire. A tripwire can be met by a system that poses no real danger.
Cost. Anchor contracts carry a fiscal cost that nobody has sized.
