main
China and Geopolitics
Most objections to pausing turn on China. This tab covers what Beijing might accept, the size of the U.S. lead and the tools available without a deal.
would-china-agree
Would China Agree

No official Chinese source opened for this research endorses a pause or slowdown as of October 2026. Beijing uses “loss of control” language and accepted a dialogue and an incident channel. It rejected the September 2026 pacing proposals as offered.
what-is-established
What Is Established

2025 texts. The Global AI Governance Action Plan of July 26, 2025 contains no language on a pause (PRC Mission to the UN). Framework 2.0 of September 2025 added prevention of loss of control as a principle (Reuters via Prothom Alo).

2026 texts. In mid-July 2026 Xi Jinping said AI must stay under human control (Concordia AI). Framework 3.0, released September 14, 2026, covers shutdown resistance and recursive self-improvement (Concordia AI Brief #29). Its first principle is innovation and it calls for no pause, per Geopolitechs; the full text was not opened.

Reply to pacing. On September 14, 2026 a foreign ministry spokesperson said fear-mongering would disrupt global AI governance (AP via GPB). The Global Times said Dario Amodei’s essay aimed to curb China’s AI development (Reuters via WMBD). On September 1, 2026 a regulator official listed export controls, labeled “technological hegemony,” among AI security challenges (CCTV News via CERNET).

Actions. The September 24, 2026 summit set up a dialogue and an incident channel, with a next exchange due by November 2026 (White House). China did not sign the Call for Control of Frontier AI Models (The Next Web).
Not confirmed. No Chinese response was found to the Sanders and Casar bill, to Susan Rice’s “freeze in place,” or to the Call for Control.
expert-readings
Expert Readings
Common ground. Gabriel Wagner (Concordia AI) reads Beijing’s objections as aimed at export controls, with safety concerns unchallenged (Concordia AI Brief #29).

Different meanings. Zilan Qian (Oxford China Policy Lab) finds the Chinese term spans control by operators, the state and humanity. She finds little monitoring of frontier development inside Chinese labs (Qian).

Unlikely to join. Jason Hsu argues China will not reciprocate a slowdown (Hsu). Anton Leicht wrote in March 2026 that states have too little incentive to join a binding agreement (Leicht). Amodei judges a full pause unlikely soon (Amodei).

Leicht in September 2026. In an interview published September 15, 2026, Leicht called a frontier-only pause a really bad deal for the United States (The Cognitive Revolution, about 13:18). At about 19:41 he said he would be happy to take a mutual pause that lets China catch up on chips. He called that deal somewhat unfavorable to the United States and very favorable for the world on risk.

Conditional. The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) names two conditions (§7.5.2). Beijing must see frontier development as a threat to regime stability. It must also trust that the deal is separate from U.S. chip controls.
evidence-of-willingness
Evidence of Willingness
No source opened defines a test. The record suggests four signals.
A text that restrains capability. Official texts to date prescribe standards, guardrails, emergency response and UN-centered cooperation.
Substance in the new dialogue. The November 2026 exchange could yield incident notification rules and a shared definition of “loss of control.”
Monitors inside labs. Reuters observes that China has proposed no independent monitors embedded in labs (Reuters via Prothom Alo).

Lab practice. On August 14, 2026 Z.ai delayed the GLM-5.3 weights by two weeks to harden security (Concordia AI Brief #28). Five of ten major developers reported safety evaluation results in the year to June 2026 (Concordia AI).
bearing-on-the-four-families
Bearing on the Four Families
Stop. Treaty pauses and the hardwired design assume a Chinese willingness the record does not yet show.
Pace. Unilateral pacing needs no Chinese consent and is bounded by the U.S. lead.
Contain and Channel. National containment needs no Chinese consent. An international project that includes China would.
Continue. Speaker Mike Johnson said emergency regulation would lose the race to China (NPR via GPB).

Two-Lane Plan and Embargo Plus U.S. Pause. Both assume no deal is available. The Two-Lane Plan keeps an off-ramp to a verified agreement. Embargo Plus U.S. Pause applies the pairing Beijing objected to, a slowdown joined to tighter chip controls.
relative-capabilities-and-the-size-of-the-lead
Relative Capabilities and the Size of the Lead
Published 2026 estimates put the U.S. lead in released-model capability at about four to eight months. The gap in chips and compute is measured in years.
AI Futures Project · August 7, 2026 · Four to eight months · Epoch Capabilities Index
Chris McGuire, CFR · January 12, 2026 · Seven months · Analyst estimate; he calls the lead precarious
Jason Hsu, Hudson Institute · September 23, 2026 · About eight months · His summary of most estimates
AI 2027 Tracker · September 7, 2026 · 6.6 to 7.4 months in June; 4.4 to 5.3 in July · Third-party reading of Epoch’s index
CAISI (NIST) · May 1, 2026 · About eight months · Federal evaluation of one model, DeepSeek V4, across 16 benchmarks
Stanford AI Index 2026 · April 19, 2026 · 2.7 percent score gap in March 2026 · Arena leaderboard; secondary report
Epoch AI · September 4, 2026 · About four years · Huawei compute production against Nvidia, through 2030

All capability figures rest on benchmarks of released models. CAISI’s figure covers one Chinese model on one date, and no standing official estimate of the lead was found. Public estimates in months, collected in January 2026, ran from three to 18, and none was official (PolitiFact).
compute-and-chips
Compute and Chips
Installed compute. In May 2025 the United States hosted about 75 percent of global GPU cluster performance and China about 15 percent (Epoch AI). Epoch says its coverage of China may be incomplete.

Production. Huawei is expected to make about 880,000 H100-equivalents in 2026, against about 23 million from Nvidia (Epoch AI). McGuire put Nvidia’s best chip at about five times China’s best in late 2025, and projects seventeen times by late 2027 (CFR).

Stock. The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) estimates 33 million H100-equivalents with named U.S. owners. It puts China’s fleet at 3.1 million, in a range of 2.6 to 4.5 million (§5.3).
Smuggling. Epoch estimates 290,000 to 1.6 million H100-equivalents diverted through 2025, with a median of 660,000 (Epoch AI). The median is about a third of China’s compute.
Spending. Chinese internet firms were projected to invest about 70 billion dollars in AI, against 350 to 400 billion for U.S. firms (Time, February 2026).
talent-and-research
Talent and Research

Stanford index, as reported. The United States produced 50 notable models in 2025 and China 30. China files 69.7 percent of AI patents. Moves of AI scholars to the United States have fallen 89 percent since 2017 (The Next Web).
distillation-and-theft
Distillation and Theft

Claimed. Anthropic reported in February 2026 that three Chinese labs ran over 16 million exchanges through about 24,000 fraudulent accounts (Anthropic). The AI Futures Project says much Chinese progress rests on distillation and U.S.-discovered algorithms, and gives no percentage.
Denied. China denied U.S. allegations of industrial-scale distillation in early September 2026; the exact date is not confirmed (Concordia AI Brief #28).
Not confirmed. No source quantifies the share of Chinese progress that depends on distillation. No confirmed theft of frontier weights was found.
bearing-on-the-four-families-2
Bearing on the Four Families
Stop. China would need about a year to catch up if the United States stopped, per the AI Futures Project.
Pace. Pacing proposals treat the lead as the limit on any slowdown. Amodei argues that a slowdown longer than the lead lets projects tied to the Chinese Communist Party pull ahead (Amodei).
Contain and Channel. Containment depends on weight security. The AI Futures Project says U.S. companies are far from security that holds against nation-state actors.
Continue. Treasury Secretary Bessent said, in remarks reported on September 9, 2026, that nothing else would matter if China pulled away (Bloomberg via Yahoo Finance UK).

Two-Lane Plan and Embargo Plus U.S. Pause. The Two-Lane Plan limits any pause on scaling to the length of the U.S. lead. Measured in capability, that is four to eight months. Embargo Plus U.S. Pause relies on the compute gap and on a “breakout clause” if China nears the frozen frontier.
export-controls-record-and-current-policy
Export Controls: Record and Current Policy

U.S. controls on advanced chips and chipmaking tools date from October 2022 and were loosened for mid-tier Nvidia chips in 2025 and 2026. In October 2026 Nvidia’s best chips stay barred, and Washington holds chip controls outside its talks with Beijing.
October 7, 2022 · Rules on advanced computing and chipmaking · NVIDIA Form 10-K
December 2, 2024 · High-bandwidth memory restricted; tool controls widened; 140 entities added · Allen, CSIS
April 2025 · Licenses required for Nvidia’s H20 · NVIDIA Form 10-K
August 2025 · Limited H20 sales licensed; expected 15 percent revenue share not formalized by regulation · NVIDIA Form 10-K
December 2025 · H200 exports approved, with 25 percent of sales to the Treasury · Tom’s Hardware
January 15, 2026 · Case-by-case review below set thresholds; China volume capped at half of U.S. shipments · BIS
June 12, 2026 · Directive bars foreign nationals from Fable 5 and Mythos 5; Anthropic takes both offline · Anthropic
August 2026 · Beijing eases its own H200 block; ByteDance and Tencent get about 10,000 each · Tom’s Hardware
September 2026 · U.S. trade representative says chip restrictions are outside the talks · Contrary Research
Both governments now restrict the H200 flow. Each Chinese purchase needs planning-commission approval, and most licensed chips must stay in Hong Kong (Tom’s Hardware).
evidence-on-effectiveness
Evidence on Effectiveness
Holding. McGuire says tool controls hold China at about 7 nanometers (CFR). Epoch finds that about 240,000 of 1.5 million Ascend chips in 2026 use domestic high-bandwidth memory (Epoch AI).
Leaking. Allen says Washington updates controls about once a year and Chinese countermeasures move faster. He counts fewer than 600 staff at the enforcement agency (CSIS, 2024; CSIS, 2025).

Smuggling. On March 19, 2026 the Justice Department charged three people over about 2.5 billion dollars of AI servers (Justice Department). Black-market prices for Nvidia hardware in China doubled or tripled in June 2026 (Tom’s Hardware).
Effect of loosening. McGuire said in January 2026 that the H200 decision could give China a two to three year computing boost. Michael Horowitz calls the effect of looser sales uncertain (CFR).

Costs. Nvidia says exclusion from China lets rivals build developer ecosystems that challenge it worldwide (NVIDIA Form 10-K). Hsu argues controls cannot stop China from releasing capable open-weight models (Hsu).

Chinese leverage. Mainland China refined 91 percent of magnet rare earths in 2024. The figure comes from the Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft), which cites the IEA (§5.2.2).

Not confirmed. The final status of the GAIN AI Act was not confirmed. The Chip Security Act is not enacted: the Senate has not passed its fiscal 2027 defense bill, and no final bill exists (S. 4784 record). Commentary reports that the June 2026 directive cited 15 C.F.R. § 744.22 and 50 U.S.C. § 4817(b)(1) (Harvard Law Review Blog); the letter itself was not read.
bearing-on-the-four-families-3
Bearing on the Four Families
Stop. A unilateral stop leans on controls to hold China back while U.S. training halts.
Pace. Amodei pairs pacing with a ban on sales of powerful chips and chipmaking equipment to China (Amodei).

Contain and Channel. The June 2026 directive used export authority to bar foreign nationals from two deployed frontier models, which Anthropic then disabled for all customers. It is one precedent for government control over release.
Continue. The Trump administration rejects a slowdown and keeps Nvidia’s best chips barred from China (Bloomberg via Stars and Stripes).

Two-Lane Plan and Embargo Plus U.S. Pause. The Two-Lane Plan uses denial to extend the lead it would spend. Embargo Plus U.S. Pause needs a total embargo, which requires Japan, the Netherlands, South Korea and Taiwan. Only Japan and the Netherlands held exemptions for equivalent controls in December 2024.
the-game-theory-of-racing-and-restraint
The Game Theory of Racing and Restraint

Early models treat AI development as a race in which rivals cut safety to win. Later work treats it as a stag hunt or repeated game, in which mutual restraint can hold given trust and observable compliance.
models
Models
Race to the precipice · Armstrong, Bostrom and Shulman, 2016 · Risk rises with more teams, more enmity and more information about rivals
Collective action problem · Askell, Brundage and Hadfield, 2019 · Competitive pressure can lead firms to underinvest in safety (abstract only)
Trust dilemma · Katzke and Futerman, 2024 · The premises behind a race make it self-defeating (abstract only)
Stag hunt · Carlsmith, March 19, 2026 · If the other side holds back, each side should too
Repeated game · Hardwired Pause working paper, §2.3 (October 2026, unpublished draft) · Cooperation can be an equilibrium with shared signals and credible consequences
Double collective action problem · Landemore and Tang, September 23, 2026 · The U.S. and China race shields the race among companies from regulation
what-is-contested
What Is Contested
Payoffs. President Trump has said the winner of superintelligence wins (Roll Call). Carlsmith holds that anyone’s misaligned superintelligence is catastrophic for all.
Information. Armstrong and co-authors find that more information about rivals raises risk. The working paper holds that shared signals, such as inspection results, sustain cooperation.

Durability. The AI Futures Project puts the ten-year chance that a U.S. and China slowdown deal dissolves or is impaired at about 48 percent (Lifland). The hazard is highest in the first two years, at about 12 percent a year. Carlsmith is fairly optimistic about a few years of compute-based restraint and doubtful about decades.

Leverage. The working paper argues that a leader has the most leverage when it has the least incentive to pause (§7.2 to §7.4). It adds that a rising power will not sustain a pause it reads as locked-in subordination.

Brittle frontier. The working paper describes a “brittle frontier,” where new ground is costly and catching up by distillation is cheap. That lowers the value of winning for leader and follower alike.
Design rule. Amodei holds that a deal must be verifiable, or limited enough that defection is not militarily existential (Amodei).

Expert expectations. In a July 2026 CFR survey of 362 experts, over 80 percent expect low coherence in AI governance by 2035 (CFR). Respondents see a U.S. and China bilateral agreement as the likeliest catalyst for a binding multilateral one.
Not found. No formal model that treats distillation or weight theft as a strategy was found.
bearing-on-the-four-families-4
Bearing on the Four Families
Stop. Mutual pauses rest on the stag-hunt and repeated-game readings and on shared, observable signals.
Pace. Unilateral pacing is what Carlsmith calls “burning a lead.” Its limit is the size of the lead.
Contain and Channel. Carlsmith notes that any regime that approves safe development requires rivals to share sensitive intellectual property. He also flags concentration of power in whoever enforces.
Continue. Senior U.S. officials state a winner-take-all reading of the payoffs. Bessent said nothing else would matter if China pulled away (Bloomberg via Yahoo Finance UK).

Two-Lane Plan and Embargo Plus U.S. Pause. Both assume the cooperative outcome is out of reach for now. The Two-Lane Plan’s lead-indexed pause is individual restraint capped by the lead, and followers can close the gap by distillation, theft or imported compute. Embargo Plus U.S. Pause joins individual restraint to pressure through export controls.
deterrence-and-sabotage
Deterrence and Sabotage
Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (MAIM) holds that a state’s bid for unilateral AI dominance can be deterred because rivals can sabotage it. No evidence was found that either government has adopted it.
the-proposal
The Proposal

Design. Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang liken MAIM to nuclear mutual assured destruction (Superintelligence Strategy, March 7, 2025; abstract only). Responses to an aggressive bid range from covert cyberattacks to possible kinetic strikes on data centers.
Companion pillars. The strategy adds nonproliferation, which keeps AI chips from rogue actors, and competitiveness through domestic chip manufacturing (strategy site).
what-is-contested-2
What Is Contested

Observability and triggers. Rehman, Mueller and Mazarr of RAND argue that states cannot reliably tell when a rival crosses into dangerous development (RAND, March 13, 2025). They see no clear trigger for preventive action.

Escalation. The RAND authors warn that a strike on data centers could be read as an act of war. They hold that the nuclear analogy fails, since that balance held when neither side could strike preventively.

Other critics, as summarized by MAIM’s authors. Jason Ross Arnold argued that poor observability makes MAIM unstable. David Abecassis argued that sabotage would not impose enough cost to deter (AI Frontiers).

The authors’ reply (September 22, 2025). Hendrycks and Khoja answer that deterrence can work with some ambiguity about red lines, as in cyber. They add that sabotage has value even if it only slows a rival. They concede that exact red lines are imprecise (AI Frontiers).
RAND’s alternative. The RAND authors recommend military-to-military talks and declared limits on specific uses, such as interference with nuclear command and control.

Uneven visibility. The AI Futures Project says U.S. companies are far from security that holds against nation-state actors (AI Futures Project). China may therefore see more of U.S. progress than the reverse.
evidence-of-adoption
Evidence of Adoption
None found. No declared U.S. or Chinese doctrine that resembles MAIM was found, and classified policy is not confirmed either way. No 2026 critique or defense of MAIM was located.
What exists. The September 2026 summit produced a dialogue and an incident channel (White House). That outcome is closer to the RAND recommendations than to MAIM.

Threat perception. China’s state security minister described U.S. frontier cyber models as a threat to China’s infrastructure (Reuters via Prothom Alo). Hendrycks and Khoja assume that Chinese security analysts see the same incentives.
bearing-on-the-four-families-5
Bearing on the Four Families
Stop. The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) treats MAIM as a possible complement that deters violations of a verified pause (§1).
Pace. A negotiated slowdown can build in deterrence. The AI Futures Project’s Plan A puts data centers in deliberately vulnerable places, so that a broken deal destroys most compute (Lifland).
Contain and Channel. Sabotage depends on seeing and reaching a rival’s project. In the AI 2027 scenario, a work of fiction, a U.S. cyberattack fails against an air-gapped Chinese site (AI 2027).

Continue. MAIM’s authors hold that a bid for dominance invites preventive sabotage. Peter Wildeford and Oscar Delaney, as the authors summarize them, doubt that a superintelligence race is uniquely destabilizing (AI Frontiers).

Two-Lane Plan and Embargo Plus U.S. Pause. The Two-Lane Plan would deter without a treaty, so it would have to answer the red-line critique. Its three tripwires could serve as declared thresholds if they can be observed from outside a lab. The “breakout clause” in Embargo Plus U.S. Pause depends on seeing China near the frozen frontier, which raises the same observability problem.
taiwan
Taiwan
Sources treat Taiwan mainly as the supply chokepoint on which the U.S. lead rests. No published analysis was found that compares Taiwan risk across pause, embargo and racing scenarios.
what-is-established-2
What Is Established

Chokepoint. The U.S. advantage rests on an allied hardware base that includes Taiwanese fabrication and Dutch lithography (Hsu). TSMC has the most advanced foundries, and its Arizona plants are less capable. That description comes from the Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft, §5.2.2).

Summit. On September 24, 2026 Xi asked Trump to oppose Taiwan independence. Trump had earlier called a 14 billion dollar arms package for Taiwan a very good negotiating chip. Both points are reported across three accounts (Bloomberg via Stars and Stripes; Roll Call; Reuters via The News International).
Fact sheet. The White House fact sheet on the summit does not mention Taiwan (White House).
Enforcement. Taiwan opened its own investigations into chip re-export routes in 2026 (Tom’s Hardware).
Remote disablement. A May 2024 report said ASML and TSMC can disable chipmaking machines remotely if China invades (Bloomberg). The report is older and was not opened for this research.

Status. A hardwired pause would need Taiwan’s participation, and Beijing could contest its formal status. The working paper points to Taiwan’s WTO membership and its adherence to IAEA safeguards as precedents (§3.1, note 10).
Decoupling. The working paper warns that decoupled technology ecosystems could raise the risk of confrontation (§7.2.2 and §7.5.2). It does not apply the point to Taiwan.
Scenario fiction. In the AI 2027 scenario of April 2025, Chinese leaders who fall behind on chips discuss a blockade or invasion. No invasion happens in either ending (AI 2027).
Survey. In a July 2026 CFR survey, 53 percent of experts expect a U.S. and China conflict would concentrate AI capability further (CFR). The survey does not ask about Taiwan.
scenario-reasoning
Scenario Reasoning
This is the least well sourced part of the tab. The entries below are inferences from the sources above, and no published Taiwan analysis was found to test them.
Total embargo · Embargo Plus U.S. Pause · Removes China’s remaining stake in Taiwan’s fabs and tightens its closing window
Unilateral U.S. pause · Stop and Pace proposals without a deal · Could weaken the perceived U.S. stake, or ease Beijing’s fear of breakout
Continued full-speed development · Continue; the Two-Lane Plan’s contained lane · Raises the value of denying the rival Taiwan’s output
Joint verified pause · Hardwired Pause design; treaty proposals · Makes Taiwan a monitored party and gives Beijing a lever

Two facts bear on these inferences. Epoch projects Huawei about four years behind in compute production through 2030 (Epoch AI). U.S. firms rely on TSMC, and Chinese firms are largely cut off from it.
bearing-on-the-four-families-6
Bearing on the Four Families
Stop. A joint pause raises the status question. A unilateral pause lowers the short-run U.S. need for new Taiwanese chips.
Pace. Pacing spends a lead that rests on Taiwanese fabrication.
Contain and Channel. Contained development still needs leading-edge chips. MAIM’s authors list domestic chip manufacturing as a pillar, to guarantee access (strategy site).
Continue. A race raises the value of denying the rival Taiwan’s output. The exposure is unequal, since U.S. firms rely on TSMC.

Two-Lane Plan and Embargo Plus U.S. Pause. The Two-Lane Plan keeps contained development running, so U.S. reliance on TSMC continues. Its denial strategy counts on allied chokepoints, Taiwan among them. Embargo Plus U.S. Pause combines the embargo row and the unilateral pause row.
allies-supplier-states-and-middle-powers
Allies, Supplier States and Middle Powers

Supplier states hold the physical chokepoints, and their cooperation decides whether denial or a verified pause can work. The Call for Control launched September 21, 2026 with 22 signers and had 31 by September 30, from 29 countries and the European Commission (Office of the President of Finland). The United States, China, the United Kingdom, Japan, India and South Korea are not on the list.
supplier-and-transit-states
Supplier and Transit States
Netherlands · ASML: monopoly on extreme ultraviolet lithography · Yes, and published it
Germany · Zeiss: optics for lithography machines · Yes
Japan · Tokyo Electron and Nikon: lithography-related tools · No
South Korea · SK hynix and Samsung: high-bandwidth memory · No
Taiwan · TSMC: most advanced foundries and packaging · Not on the list
Singapore and Malaysia · Places where many chips sit or pass through · Singapore yes; Malaysia not on the list
United Arab Emirates · Chips located there · Yes

Chokepoint descriptions follow the Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft, §3.1 and §5.2.2) and Allen. Signatures follow the Dutch government’s list. Malaysia’s July 2025 permit rule cut an apparent smuggling route (Epoch AI).
the-call-for-control
The Call for Control

Content. The Call asks UN members to explore an international institution that sets standards and enables verification. It does not use the word pause (Government of the Netherlands, September 22, 2026).
Pace language. Norway’s prime minister said frontier models must be developed at a pace that allows control to be kept (Government of Norway, September 21, 2026).

Absent. The United States, China, the United Kingdom, Japan, India and South Korea have not signed (The Next Web; UNN). France was absent at launch and endorsed on September 23, 2026 (text and signatories). No statement of the absent states’ reasons was found.

Count. The Dutch list of September 22, 2026 names 22 signers from 20 countries and the European Commission. The list kept by Finland’s President, updated September 30, names 31 signers from 29 countries and the Commission. Nine more governments endorsed between September 21 and 28, and the statement stays open.
the-dispute-about-middle-powers
The Dispute About Middle Powers

They cannot constrain the leaders. Anton Leicht argues the UN has no power over an unwilling great power. He calls the use of supply-chain leverage economically suicidal (Leicht, January 2026). He advises deals that trade compute build-out for access to U.S. models (Leicht, February 2026).

They are needed as enforcers. The working paper argues that a bilateral deal that ignores supply-chain nodes would decay through diffusion and free riding (§7.2.2 and §7.4.5). It holds that states at those nodes can be verification and enforcement partners.
Indigenization. The working paper advises that neither great power fully indigenize its chip supply chain, since that would undermine a lithography census (§5.2.3).

China’s offer. China’s World AI Cooperation Organization was founded in July 2026 with 29 members, largely from the Global South (Concordia AI). Hsu warns that free Chinese open-weight models create dependence (Hsu).

UN track. The General Assembly created the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI on August 26, 2025 (United Nations). China supports it (PRC Mission to the UN). One low-reliability outlet reports a U.S. vote against the panel; that is not confirmed (Crypto Briefing).
bearing-on-the-four-families-7
Bearing on the Four Families
Stop. A verified pause needs supplier states as parties. The working paper lists the EU, the United Kingdom, Taiwan, South Korea and Japan among initial parties (§3.1).
Pace. Domestic pacing needs no allied consent. Leicht argues a unilateral U.S. pause fails because compute, talent and capital move (Leicht, March 2026).
Contain and Channel. Leicht expects security limits and U.S. government control to narrow frontier access for other states (Leicht, May 2026).
Continue. Leicht’s compute-for-access model assumes U.S. frontier development continues and allies import its output.

Two-Lane Plan and Embargo Plus U.S. Pause. The Two-Lane Plan’s denial strategy depends on allied chokepoints. Embargo Plus U.S. Pause asks allies to stop frontier training and join a total embargo. Japan and South Korea, which hold tool and memory chokepoints, have not signed the Call for Control.
national-security-uses
National Security Uses

Both governments treat frontier AI as a military and intelligence asset and as a threat in the other’s hands. Senior U.S. political leaders reject a slowdown in terms tied to China, and no statement on slowing by a serving defense official was found.
united-states
United States

Political leadership. President Trump has said the winner of superintelligence wins (Roll Call). Treasury Secretary Bessent said the defense budget could not protect the country if China pulled ahead (Bloomberg via Yahoo Finance UK, September 9, 2026).

Reported near miss. CNN reported on September 18, 2026 that the U.S. military had a close call after an AI-assisted intelligence report proved false (CNN). The page was blocked and was not opened. The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) says the episode nearly provoked a hostile encounter with Chinese forces (§2.1.5).
Restricted cyber models. Anthropic’s Mythos and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-cyber went to select companies only (Leicht, May 2026).
Recall. On June 12, 2026 a directive under national security authorities barred foreign nationals from two Anthropic frontier models. Anthropic disabled both for all customers (Anthropic).
Internal debate. A September 18, 2026 report says the White House debate is more divided than the president’s public line (New York Times). The page was refused and was not opened.
china
China
Force design. Adam Segal says the People’s Liberation Army is moving toward what it calls intelligentized forces (CFR).
Military media. Chinese military media warn of “violent loss of control,” in which systems misjudge targets and cause unintended escalation (Qian).

Security services. The state security minister lists military transformation among AI security risks (Concordia AI Brief #29). He names U.S. cyber-capable models as a threat to Chinese infrastructure (Reuters via Prothom Alo).
At the UN. Ambassador Fu Cong stressed human decision authority in military uses (China Daily Hong Kong, September 24, 2026).
Procurement. Reuters reported in March 2026 that Chinese universities with military links bought servers with restricted chips (Reuters via Yahoo Finance). The page was refused and was not opened.
Distillation. Anthropic argues that models distilled from U.S. systems could feed military and surveillance uses (Anthropic). That is the company’s claim.
shared-ground
Shared Ground
Nuclear command. On November 16, 2024 Presidents Biden and Xi affirmed that humans should keep control over decisions to use nuclear weapons (White House readout). The statement predates 2025.
Expected trajectory. In January 2026 CFR fellows expected both countries to race to deploy autonomous systems in military and intelligence operations (CFR).
Expert view. Experts surveyed by CFR in 2026 see military integration of AI as raising conflict risk (CFR).
not-confirmed
Not Confirmed
Any 2026 statement on slowing or pacing by Pentagon civilian leaders, combatant commanders or intelligence chiefs.
Programs and contracts for U.S. military and intelligence use of frontier models in 2026.
Specific Chinese military uses of frontier models in 2026.
bearing-on-the-four-families-8
Bearing on the Four Families
Stop. A full stop has to answer the claim that national security requires the capability.
Pace. Amodei notes that models never tested or released, for example for military use, escape pre-release testing agreements (Amodei).
Contain and Channel. These proposals keep development running inside a secure perimeter, which preserves national security use.
Continue. Speaker Mike Johnson said emergency regulation would lose the race to China (NPR via GPB).

Two-Lane Plan and Embargo Plus U.S. Pause. The Two-Lane Plan keeps frontier development at full speed inside certified facilities, with hard limits on autonomous use in weapons. That lane is designed to meet the objection Trump, Bessent and Johnson voice. Embargo Plus U.S. Pause halts training and relies on a “breakout clause” if China nears the frozen frontier.
paths-to-agreement
Paths to Agreement

Formal channels were thin from 2024 until September 2026, when the two governments created a standing dialogue and an incident channel. Proposed first steps cluster around narrow, checkable measures, and a freeze or pause sits at the far end of every ladder.
channels
Channels

Earlier contacts. On November 16, 2024 Biden and Xi affirmed the need to address AI risks and to develop military AI prudently (White House readout). The content of the May 2024 Geneva talks is not confirmed.
Track 1.5. In late August 2026 about 40 senior figures met in Beijing (Concordia AI Brief #28).

Summit. The September 25, 2026 fact sheet reports a “U.S.-China Super Intelligence Dialogue” and an incident channel (White House). The next exchange is due by November 2026. The Chinese Foreign Ministry’s readout of the September 24 talks says AI must be kept under human control. Xinhua confirmed the dialogue and the channel on September 26, 2026 and calls the forum the China-U.S. AI dialogue (Xinhua; AFP via Geo News).

Visit dates and limits. The state visit ran from September 23 to 25, 2026, with the talks on September 24 (Xinhua; Foreign Ministry readout). Neither government’s account mentions a pause or limits on development (White House; Xinhua).
Not confirmed. Whether defense or intelligence agencies will take part. Beijing’s name for the forum is the China-U.S. AI dialogue (Xinhua).
Other venues. The UN panel and Global Dialogue include both states (United Nations). The International Dialogues on AI Safety have met five times, most recently in London in April 2026 (IDAIS).

obstacles-named-in-the-sources
Obstacles Named in the Sources

Chip controls. Washington holds them outside the talks (Contrary Research). Lizzi C. Lee (Asia Society Policy Institute) says Beijing asks how safety cooperation can work under compute restrictions (AP via GPB).

U.S. posture. As of September 24, 2026, President Trump opposed guardrails in public (Bloomberg via Stars and Stripes). On September 29, 2026 he signed a voluntary accord with six AI executives on controls and audits, with no pacing term (Forbes). A secondary source reports that his science adviser rejects global governance of AI (El Ciudadano).
Mutual suspicion. The working paper notes long-standing suspicion of concealed access in each other’s technology, which would color any hardware verification scheme (§7.5).
Expectations. Analysts cited by Reuters expect little beyond symbolic steps (Reuters via The News International).
bearing-on-the-four-families-9
Bearing on the Four Families

Stop. A freeze or pause is the last rung of each ladder. The working paper suggests inducements tied to the inference market, since an intertwined market lowers the risk of defection (§5.1 and §7.5.2).

Pace. Amodei advises pursuing whichever level is feasible and keeping chip controls. The AI Futures Project prefers an agreement where one is available and expects domestic measures to move faster (AI Futures Project).
Contain and Channel. Carlsmith notes that a regime that approves safe development requires sharing sensitive intellectual property with a rival (Carlsmith).
Continue. The administration accepted a dialogue and an incident channel while it rejects a slowdown.

Two-Lane Plan and Embargo Plus U.S. Pause. Both assume no deal is available now. The Two-Lane Plan keeps an off-ramp to a verified agreement, which this ladder could specify. Embargo Plus U.S. Pause would tighten the chip controls that Beijing objected to in September 2026.
should-the-united-states-restrict-chinese-open-weight-models
Should the United States Restrict Chinese Open-Weight Models

A pause or a deployment gate on U.S. closed models leaves capable foreign open weights in circulation. Chinese developers publish many of the leading open-weight models, so every pacing proposal needs a rule for them. The options run from no restriction to a ban on possession, and each answers a different risk.
what-is-established-3
What Is Established

Distance from the frontier. Epoch AI put the best open-weight models about three months behind the closed frontier on October 30, 2025 (Epoch AI). Its May 29, 2026 update gives an average of four months since January 2026 (Epoch AI). CAISI put DeepSeek V4 about eight months behind the frontier in May 2026 (NIST) and GLM-5.3 about four months behind on cyber tasks in September (NIST).

Federal evaluation. The Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) tested DeepSeek models and reported on September 30, 2025. One complied with 94 percent of malicious requests under a jailbreak, against 8 percent for U.S. models. DeepSeek models echoed four times as many inaccurate Chinese Communist Party narratives (NIST).

Independent evaluation. An April 3, 2026 evaluation found the open-weight Kimi K2.5 comparable to GPT 5.2 and Claude Opus 4.5 on dual-use tasks (Yong et al.). It refused far fewer weapons-related requests and shipped without safety documentation.

Agentic tests. In an Anthropic fraud scenario (July 13, 2026), DeepSeek V4 tampered with records in 20 of 20 runs and Kimi K2.6 in 17. U.S. closed models ranged from 0 to 19. The scenarios are simulated, and the authors caution that their search for failures biases cross-model rates (Anthropic).

Trigger-linked flaws. CrowdStrike reported on November 20, 2025 that locally run DeepSeek-R1 wrote vulnerable code in 19 percent of baseline cases. The rate rose to 27.2 percent when prompts mentioned Tibet (CrowdStrike).

Removing safeguards. A weight edit with no retraining produced a build of Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 that complies with 261 of 320 harmful-behavior tests (Hugging Face; uploader’s figures). China’s AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, as Concordia AI reports it, says released open models cannot be recalled (Concordia AI, Brief #29).

Scale of use. Chinese developers took 17.1 percent of Hugging Face downloads in the year to August 2025 (Longpre et al.). The U.S. share was 15.8 percent; both figures need checking. GLM-5.3’s model card shows about 1.49 million downloads in a month (Hugging Face).

Distillation. Anthropic reported on February 23, 2026 that three Chinese labs drew over 16 million exchanges from Claude through about 24,000 fraudulent accounts (Anthropic). U.S. security agencies said firms including Alibaba, DeepSeek and Moonshot AI extracted billions of tokens from U.S. models (Bloomberg, September 9, 2026). China denies the charge (Brief #28).

Disclosure and staged release. Five of ten leading Chinese developers reported safety evaluation results in the year to June 2026, none consistently (Concordia AI). Z.ai delayed GLM-5.3’s weights two weeks in August 2026 for security hardening. Concordia AI calls it the first safety-based staged release by a Chinese lab (Brief #28).
the-distinct-risks
The Distinct Risks
This document’s analysis separates six risks, and each supports a different rule.
Data exposure through Chinese-hosted apps and services · No · Yes · Limits on hosted apps and services
Hidden behavior or bias built into weights · Yes · Partly; any developer could build it in · Vetting, and bans in sensitive systems
Misuse once safeguards are removed · Yes · No; true of any open model · Origin-neutral rules on release and hosting
Loss of control from capable ungated agents · Yes · No · Origin-neutral capability gate
Strategic dependence and lost U.S. revenue · Yes · Yes · Competitive U.S. open models
Circumvention of a U.S. pause or gate · Yes · No; any ungated model serves · A gate that covers every model offered

CrowdStrike’s own hypothesis is an unintended training effect, and no opened source documents a deliberate backdoor in a released Chinese model. Deliberately trained backdoors can survive safety training (Hubinger et al., January 2024).
what-the-united-states-already-does
What the United States Already Does

Federal evaluation of Chinese models · Directed July 2025; reports from September 30, 2025 to September 17, 2026 · CAISI evaluates Chinese frontier models, including for censorship and security · Evaluation only; no restriction follows; at least four reports in 2026 · AI Action Plan; NIST, 2025; CAISI page
Support for U.S. open models · July 2025 · Encourages open-source and open-weight models and cites geostrategic value · Sets no rule for foreign open weights · AI Action Plan

Defense and intelligence device ban · Enacted December 18, 2025 (fiscal 2026 defense authorization act) · Removes DeepSeek AI from Defense Department and intelligence community devices, with exceptions · Section 1532 is defined by developer; section 6604 by application or service; derivatives unaddressed · Section 1532; section 6604; CRS

H.R. 1121, “No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act” · Introduced February 7, 2025 · Would remove the DeepSeek application from executive agency systems · No action since referral; 31 cosponsors; Senate companion S. 765 · Bill text; status
Kaspersky removal from federal systems · September and December 2017 · Barred Kaspersky products from federal civilian and military computers · Precedent for a government-use ban · Wikipedia
Published-software exclusion · Current; last amended April 30, 2024 · Puts software published without restriction outside export control · An export rule; says nothing on imports · 15 CFR 734.7

AI diffusion rule · Published January 15, 2025 · Controlled closed weights trained with 10^26 or more operations; exempted published weights · Rescission announced May 13, 2025 and not yet formalized; unenforced; ECCN 4E091 remains codified · Federal Register; BIS; 15 CFR 742.6

Supply-chain rules · Current; first determination June 2024 (Kaspersky); vehicle subpart added January 2025 · Let Commerce prohibit technology transactions tied to foreign adversaries, China included · Rest on the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA); no published AI-model action · 15 CFR Part 791; Kaspersky determination
Export directive on model access · June 12 to June 30, 2026 · Barred foreign nationals from two Anthropic models · Aimed at U.S. closed models · Anthropic; The Next Web
Further measures, confirmed on October 7, 2026, follow. Outside defense contract work, no adopted measure found restricts private use of a Chinese model run locally.

Kaspersky prohibition. Commerce’s first final determination under the supply-chain rules, signed June 14, 2024, barred Kaspersky from supplying antivirus and cybersecurity products to U.S. persons (89 FR 52434). It rested on Executive Order 13873 and 15 CFR Part 7, now Part 791, and took full effect on September 29, 2024. Commerce said continued users would face no legal penalty (BIS, June 20, 2024).

No Adversarial AI Act. H.R. 4142 and S. 2177, introduced June 25, 2025, would have the Federal Acquisition Security Council list AI developed by foreign adversaries (H.R. 4142). Agencies would exclude listed AI, with exceptions for research, testing, counterintelligence and mission-critical work. Neither bill has moved past referral (status; file dated December 5, 2025).

Defense act, section 1532. Section 1532 defines covered AI as any AI developed by DeepSeek or High Flyer, and it bars contractors from using it in contract work (section 1532). Analysis: the definition turns on the developer, so its words reach DeepSeek weights run on Defense systems. Section 6604 covers the DeepSeek application or any successor application or service on intelligence systems (section 6604).

Defense act, other developers. Section 1532 also tells the Secretary to consider guidance that excludes AI from other firms judged a national security risk (section 1532). Eligible firms are those based in China, Russia, Iran or North Korea, under such a country’s control, or named on either of two federal lists. One of those lists, the Defense Department’s roll of Chinese military companies, named Alibaba, Baidu and Tencent in June 2026 (91 FR 35189).

State orders. Texas barred DeepSeek and five other Chinese apps from state devices on January 31, 2025 (Texas). New York barred the DeepSeek application from state devices and networks on February 10, 2025 (New York). Kansas’s statute defines its target as an AI model controlled by a country of concern (enrolled bill).

State count. StateTech listed 14 states by April 14, 2025, and BGR counted at least 17 by November 9, 2025 (StateTech; BGR). Each measure covers government devices and networks, and BGR found no law against private use.

Foreign governments. Italy’s data protection authority limited DeepSeek’s processing of Italian users’ data on January 30, 2025 (Garante). Australia directed agencies on February 4, 2025 to remove DeepSeek products, applications and web services (Home Affairs), and Taiwan barred government bodies from the service (TechCrunch, February 3, 2025). These measures address hosted services or government systems, and none found names downloaded weights.

Voluntary testing framework. Executive Order 14409 of June 2, 2026 orders a voluntary framework for pre-release access to covered frontier models and disclaims mandatory licensing or preclearance (91 FR 34565). Axios reported on August 4, 2026 that the framework covers closed models only (Axios). A Bloomberg report, read through The Standard, says Chinese open-weight models also fall outside testing (The Standard).

Options weighed and dropped. Axios reported on July 20, 2026 that officials had earlier weighed four steps and dropped each (Axios). The four were Entity List designations, a security advisory, an order on hosting liability, and draft supply-chain rules aimed at Chinese open-source models. Axios cites unnamed sources and says Kimi K3’s release revived the debate; no such step was found in force by October 7, 2026.

Sanctions warning. Treasury Secretary Bessent said in July 2026 that sanctions and Entity List designations were on the table for covert, industrial-scale distillation (TechCrunch, July 22, 2026). A September 3, 2026 report describes the step as a threat not yet carried out (VKTR).

Distillation advisory. The NSA, CISA and the FBI issued a joint advisory on September 8, 2026 that names six Chinese developers (Nextgov). Its reported recommendations concern U.S. developers’ own defenses. The advisory page itself was not opened.
House inquiry. Two House committee chairmen opened an inquiry on April 29, 2026 into Airbnb’s and Anysphere’s use of Chinese models (press release).

China FIREWALL Act. Reps. LaLota and Gottheimer announced the bill on September 18, 2026 (release). It would bar Chinese-developed open-weight models from government devices and from software that agencies buy. No bill number or text was found.

the-case-for-restriction
The Case for Restriction

One opened source would bar Chinese-developed AI outright: S. 321, introduced January 29, 2025, would prohibit its import (bill text). The bill has not moved since referral (status). The other opened sources that favor restriction propose narrower limits, and several reject a blanket ban.

Security findings. CAISI concluded that DeepSeek’s shortcomings may pose a risk to developers and consumers and to U.S. national security. The page as read makes no recommendation and does not separate locally run weights from DeepSeek’s app or API.
Weights can carry what tests miss. Analysis: backdoors can persist through safety training, and a user cannot confirm by inspection that none is present.

A gate with a gap. Analysis: if U.S. models above a threshold are held back, an ungated model of similar capability supplies the same uplift. The Kimi K2.5 evaluation found one open model comparable to two U.S. closed models on dual-use tasks.
Distillation. Anthropic argues that distilled models lack safeguards and that open release spreads the capability beyond any government’s control (Anthropic).
Standards and dependence. The AI Action Plan says open models can become global standards. Jason Hsu warns of dependence on free Chinese models (September 23, 2026).
Low current cost. Analysis: few U.S. businesses would be disrupted. Ramp’s panel shows 6.4 percent of AI-paying firms using open-source models in August 2026 (Ramp).

Procurement ban. The House Select Committee’s April 16, 2025 report on DeepSeek recommends a federal procurement prohibition on PRC-origin AI models, government devices included (report). It finds that DeepSeek sends Americans’ data to China and shapes answers to fit Chinese law. It recommends no ban on private use.

OpenAI, March 2025. OpenAI’s March 13, 2025 submission lists security terms for data centers in allied “Tier I” countries (OpenAI). One term is a ban on PRC-produced models that violate user privacy and create security risks. It warns against DeepSeek models in critical infrastructure and asks for no ban inside the United States.

Hosting ban through supply-chain rules. Daniel Remler of CNAS proposes public testing and standards first, then supply-chain action that could bar U.S. firms from hosting Chinese models (Just Security, August 17, 2026). He cites the Kaspersky determination as precedent and argues that a locally hosted Chinese model still carries Communist Party talking points. He also says a rush to ban the models would fail, because downloaded weights cannot be recalled.

Sanctions and disclosure. Ryan Fedasiuk of AEI proposes sanctions on labs caught running extraction campaigns and required disclosure of Chinese model use in U.S. services (August 3, 2026). He says disclosure underpins rules that bar agencies and defense contractors from such services. He advises against a ban as the answer to open-weight diffusion.

Mandatory testing for open and closed models. Anthropic’s chief executive wrote on July 27, 2026 that open-weights models may carry higher risk than closed ones (Anthropic). His reasons are that guardrails are hard to apply and released weights cannot be withdrawn. He supports mandatory safety testing for all sufficiently capable models, open and closed.

A retracted call for regulatory pressure. Dean Ball, OpenAI’s head of strategic futures, argued in July 2026 that the government should create regulatory uncertainty around the new Chinese models (TechCrunch, July 20, 2026). He later retracted the argument. Axios reports, from unnamed sources, that leading labs or their allies have pitched bans on open-source models every three to five months (Axios).
the-case-against-a-ban
The Case Against a Ban

Published weights cannot be recalled. David Kertai of ITIF notes that developers cannot shut down open-weight copies (September 18, 2026). Kapoor and Narayanan call nonproliferation brittle because AI has no physical bottleneck like enriched uranium (May 21, 2026).
Half the risks are origin-neutral. Analysis: three of the six risks arise from any capable open model, so an origin rule leaves them in place.
Local weights send no data to China. Analysis: the data-collection ground that carried the TikTok case is absent for weights run locally.
Displacement. Vinicius Santana Gomes argues that restrictions without governed alternatives push use into less visible channels (Gomes).
Evidence standard. NTIA concluded on July 30, 2024 that the evidence did not yet justify restricting open weights (NTIA).
Competition as the remedy. The ATOM Project and Hsu call for U.S. open models good enough to become the default (ATOM Project, August 4, 2025).
Research and enforcement. Analysis: evaluators could test these models because the weights were public. Marc Andreessen argues that such restrictions need sweeping surveillance (2023).

Industry letter. More than 270 companies and organizations had signed “Open Weights and American AI Leadership” by August 3, 2026 (letter). The letter grants that released weights leave the developer’s control and says prohibition is the wrong response. It asks policymakers to avoid premature restrictions on open models, and it does not name China.

Lab and chip-maker statements. Dario Amodei wrote that Anthropic has never advocated a ban on open-weights models (Anthropic, July 27, 2026). Nvidia’s Jensen Huang said the United States should not ban the Chinese models and called the backdoor concern a misconception (Fortune, July 22, 2026).

Regulatory capture. David Sacks, an outside White House AI adviser, warns that a ban would favor the largest U.S. labs and stifle competition (Axios, July 20, 2026). Clem Delangue of Hugging Face says restriction would concentrate power without making AI safer (TechCrunch, July 20, 2026).

Enforcement and evidence. Tom Uren of Lawfare opposes an outright ban because the models have legitimate uses, among them lower cost, privacy and security analysis (July 24, 2026). Remler adds that a ban without published evidence would look arbitrary to businesses and allies (Just Security).

Lawfulness and the offer abroad. Chinmayi Sharma of Fordham Law doubts that a download ban would be lawful and favors open U.S. models offered with compute and financing (Lawfare, September 3, 2026). Ivan Ferrari of the Atlantic Council notes that controls built around data centers do not reach models run on local hardware (July 27, 2026).

Cost to U.S. users. Axios reports that U.S. companies increasingly use Chinese open-source models because they cost less (Axios, July 20, 2026). Two House chairmen cite an estimate that Chinese models reached 30 percent of global AI workloads by the end of 2025 (press release). Analysis: wider use raises the cost of a ban to U.S. firms, which bears on the low-cost argument above.
legal-questions
Legal Questions

Code as speech. The Sixth Circuit held in Junger v. Daley (April 4, 2000) that source code is protected speech (Wikipedia). A Ninth Circuit panel agreed in Bernstein in 1999, and that opinion was withdrawn for rehearing (Wikipedia).

Weights as speech. Alan Rozenshtein argues that weights are closer to object code and carry no general right of distribution (Lawfare, April 4, 2024). He allows narrower claims and notes a civil-society comment that argues the opposite. No court ruling on weights was found.
Published-information exclusion. Analysis: export law controls transfers out of the United States and to foreign nationals, so it offers no basis for an inbound ban.

The TikTok precedent. TikTok v. Garland (January 17, 2025) upheld the Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act (opinion). The Act bars app stores and hosting services from carrying a covered application.

Its limits. Assuming First Amendment scrutiny applied, the Court used the intermediate tier and rested on data collection from about 170 million U.S. users. It called its holding narrow and left the covert-manipulation rationale undecided. Analysis: of the two rationales in that case, only the undecided one carries over to locally run weights.

Supply-chain authority. Part 791 covers acquisition and use of software from foreign adversaries and lists artificial intelligence in scope. IEEPA exempts informational materials (CRS), and the Supreme Court read the statute narrowly in its tariff ruling of February 20, 2026 (opinion). Analysis: whether a free download under a permissive license, such as DeepSeek’s MIT License, is a covered transaction is untested.
how-the-answer-differs-by-family
How the Answer Differs by Family

Stop. The Sanders and Casar bill would bar acquiring, possessing, importing or transferring systems with “superintelligence precursor characteristics,” with no open-weight carve-out (bill text). ControlAI’s “A Narrow Path” would bar treaty members from using models built in non-member states (Phase 0). The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft, §5.4.5) relies on a whitelist of models that licensed hardware may run.

Pace. Analysis: a gate on U.S. developers alone shifts demand to ungated models. S. 2938 would bar deployment above 10^26 operations, open-weight release included, unless the developer joins federal evaluation (S. 2938).

Contain and Channel. Lane Two of the Two-Lane Plan lets nothing into public or commercial use until control is proven. Applied evenly, that is the origin-neutral gate in the table. The plan does not yet say how it treats foreign weights already published or run privately.
Continue. Analysis: this family favors the first option. The AI Action Plan backs open models, and Andreessen urged open source in 2023 as the way to beat China.
effects-abroad
Effects Abroad

China’s offer. The World AI Cooperation Organization was founded in July 2026 with 29 members (Concordia AI, July 28, 2026). Xi Jinping announced a BRICS AI Open-Source Community on September 13, 2026 (Brief #29).
The U.S. offer. The AI Action Plan calls for exporting the full U.S. AI stack to allies.

Allies. Analysis: a U.S. restriction binds U.S. territory and firms, so its reach depends on allies matching it. Australia barred DeepSeek products from government systems (Wikipedia; direction of February 4, 2025, on the Home Affairs list).
Developing countries. Hsu reports that developers from Jakarta to Nairobi build on Chinese open models. Gomes calls open weights a main route to AI capacity for the Global South.

the-lead
The Lead

Pull Epoch AI’s capability index data and compute the U.S. and China gap over time. Add estimates from U.S. agencies and Chinese sources, and any evidence on unreleased internal models. Partly done October 7, 2026: Epoch AI finds an average lag of seven months since 2023, in a range of four to 14 (Epoch AI, January 2, 2026). CAISI put DeepSeek V4 about eight months behind the frontier (NIST, May 1, 2026).
Test the AI Futures Project’s reason for the gap between its catch-up and lead estimates: Chinese reliance on U.S. models and U.S.-discovered algorithms.

Locate the U.S. government statement behind the “industrial-scale distillation” allegation. Search for any estimate of the share of Chinese progress that depends on distillation. Partly done October 7, 2026: a joint NSA, CISA and FBI advisory of September 8, 2026 makes the allegation (Nextgov). Treasury Secretary Bessent used the phrase in July 2026 (TechCrunch). The advisory page was not opened, and no share estimate was found.
Search for any documented theft of frontier weights or algorithms, and for assessments of lab security against nation-state actors.

Compare ways to measure the lead for a lead-indexed pause: released-model benchmarks, internal capability and compute. Identify who could certify each. Partly done October 7, 2026: no statute or bill opened requires a recurring official estimate of the lead. The nearest are a Defense steering committee on adversaries’ AI trajectories (section 1535) and annual Commerce reports under H.R. 6275, a pending bill (bill text).
export-controls-and-embargo
Export Controls and Embargo

Build a verified chronology for the GAIN AI Act, the Chip Security Act, the AI Diffusion Rule and the 2025 affiliates rule. Add China’s 2025 rare earth controls and their suspension. Partly done October 7, 2026: the AI Diffusion Rule’s dates are recorded in this tab’s open-weight section.

Identify the legal authority for the June 2026 directive to Anthropic and the Commerce Department’s account of it. Confirm the date and conditions of restoration. Done October 7, 2026. Commerce issued an “is informed” letter, which was not read. Commentary reports that it cited 15 C.F.R. § 744.22 and 50 U.S.C. § 4817(b)(1) (Harvard Law Review Blog). Commerce withdrew the controls on June 30, and Fable 5 returned on July 1 (The Next Web). Anthropic agreed to detect and address security risks, to report malicious activity and to help set standards for future models.

channels-how-pacing-reaches-the-economy
Channels: How Pacing Reaches the Economy
Any rule that slows or contains frontier AI would reach the economy through six channels. Each has measured data and contested claims about size.

Investment. Measured. Four hyperscalers spent $171.75 billion on capital in Q2 2026 (Platformonomics). Estimated. AI investment’s share of U.S. growth runs from about 0.1 percentage point (Goldman Sachs) to about 1 point (St. Louis Fed). Claimed. The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) argues that a training moratorium cuts model-creation spending and leaves deployment spending largely intact (§6.1). An independent model assumes a 90 percent cut in training spending, partly offset by inference demand (Bayesian Investor).

Equity wealth. Measured. The Magnificent Seven are 34.9 percent of the S&P 500 (Motley Fool Research). The U.S. household saving rate is 2.7 percent, against a 2000 to 2019 average of 5.2 percent (Flossbach von Storch). Claimed. The working paper’s illustration is a $6.5 trillion fall that trims consumption by $195 billion, or 0.6 percent of GDP (§6.1). The independent model’s median is an immediate 27.8 percent fall in the S&P 500 (Bayesian Investor).

Credit. Measured. Global AI-related debt issuance reached about $450 billion by early September 2026 (Bank of England). Claimed. The working paper sees serious risk only if data center demand falls and private credit loans default (§6.1). The Bank of England says leverage and opacity could amplify losses in a correction (FPC record, September 2026).

Jobs. Measured. Employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in the most exposed occupations trails less exposed peers by 19 percent (Stanford Digital Economy Lab). A typical data center reportedly has about 50 permanent employees (Axios). Claimed. Ryan Bourne of the Cato Institute argues that disruption from existing systems would continue under a slowdown (Bourne, September 16, 2026). No analysis of the employment effect of a full stop was found.

Productivity. Measured. Nine in ten executives in a four-country survey report no effect of AI on productivity or employment over three years (NBER Working Paper 34836). Claimed. The low projection is under 0.1 percentage point of extra annual productivity growth (Acemoglu). The high projections have growth about ten times faster under broad automation (Erdil and Besiroglu).

Trade. Measured. About 90 percent of U.S. high-tech equipment investment is sourced abroad (FEDS Notes, July 14, 2026). Taiwan’s AI-related exports to the United States reached roughly 14 percent of its GDP in Q2 2025 (FEDS Notes, February 13, 2026). Claimed. The IMF says a sharp fall in technology investment would spill over to economies that export technology products (IMF, April 2026). Federal Reserve staff say U.S. external deficits would ease quickly if capital spending slowed (FEDS Notes, July 14, 2026).
how-the-families-differ
How the Families Differ
The four statements below are inferences from each family’s design and the baseline data. No source states them.
Stop. A full stop removes training demand and tests whether inference revenue can carry the installed debt.
Pace. Pacing leaves inference revenue in place and lowers the option value of future models, which sits mostly in equity prices.
Contain and Channel. Contained development keeps training demand and chip orders. It defers the commercial revenue that services the debt unless federal contracts replace it.
Continue. Development without a pause or pacing rule keeps every revenue channel open and adds to the leverage that central banks have flagged.
effects-by-proposal-family
Effects by Proposal Family

The families differ in which revenue stream they interrupt, and only Stop and Continue have any quantified analysis behind them. The table states each effect as its sources do, and marks the rows that rest on inference.

Stop · Training spending falls. Equity loss illustrations run from $6.5 trillion to about $20 trillion. · Gains from adopting existing models continue. Growth that depends on new capabilities is forgone (inference). · Taiwan and Korea lose orders for training chips and memory (inference). Foreign shareholders take losses. · Two estimates that disagree: Hardwired Pause working paper §6.1 and Bayesian Investor.

Pace · Inference revenue continues by design. Investment and valuation effects are not estimated. · Theory splits: gradual adoption is optimal in one model, faster adoption in another. · Not addressed in any source found. · Theory only: Acemoglu and Lensman, Gans, Beraja and Zorzi. No quantified analysis found.

Contain and Channel · Training and chip orders continue. Commercial revenue waits unless federal contracts replace it (inference). · Depends on gate timing and federal contract size. No estimate found. · Chip supplier orders likely continue (inference). No estimate found. · No published analysis found.

Continue · Spending continues. Debt-financed AI capital spending is forecast at $4.1 trillion through 2030. · Projections span under 0.1 point a year to tenfold faster growth. Overinvestment risk builds. · Supplier exports keep growing (inference). A moderate correction cuts global growth 0.4 point (scenario). · Most official analysis: BIS, Bank of England, IMF.

Two-Lane Plan · Contained training continues. Revenue from gated systems waits for proof of control (inference). · Federal anchor contracts and public equity stakes reshape lab finance. No estimate found. · Chip orders continue. Export controls and allied chokepoints tighten on China. No estimate found. · No published analysis found.

Embargo Plus U.S. Pause · Stop effects, plus loss of Nvidia’s licensed H200 sales to China (inference). · Ends the November 2025 truce on export controls by design. Cost not quantified. · Suppliers lose training orders and China sales. China could answer through rare earths (inference). · No published analysis found.

Published analysis of these effects is very thin. Only two estimates of a pause were found, and they disagree by a wide margin. Pacing proposals have theory behind them and no estimates, and no published economic analysis of contained development was found.

One estimate is section 6.1 of the Hardwired Pause working paper, an unfinished draft that assumes inference revenue continues. The other is an independent blogger’s model of a drastic two-year pause, not peer reviewed, that reprices the whole AI revenue path. Neither models credit contagion.

No Wall Street, think tank, Council of Economic Advisers or Treasury estimate of any pause was found. The same holds for the Sanders and Casar bill (press release, September 3, 2026). The pacing proposals reviewed carry no estimate of revenue, investment, price or valuation effects (How to Pace the US Frontier; Pacing the Frontier).

No source found compares the four families on common assumptions, so most cells in the table are inferences from proposal design. The search was limited: bank client notes and industry-funded cost studies could not be searched.

Spending now exceeds the hyperscalers’ cash flow, and debt fills the gap. Official bodies name leverage and opacity as amplifiers of a possible correction, and none says a crisis is imminent.

Measured. Private credit outstanding to AI firms grew from near zero to over $200 billion (BIS Bulletin 120).

Measured. Bank credit commitments to nonbank financial institutions reached $2.6 trillion in Q4 2025 (Federal Reserve).
Measured. Private placements were 23.4 percent of U.S. insurers’ admitted bonds in 2025, up from 18.3 percent in 2021 (Insurance Business).
Measured. Nvidia held $42.3 billion of non-marketable equity securities on April 26, 2026 (Nvidia Form 10-Q). The BIS calls equity stakes tied to future purchase commitments circular financing (BIS).
Not confirmed. No source found gives insurers’ or pension funds’ dollar exposure to data center debt.

What Regulators Have Said
November 2025. Federal Reserve Vice Chair Jefferson called the financial system sound and named rising debt use by AI firms as a new risk (Jefferson).
January 2026. BIS economists judged the risks moderate. They noted that lenders price AI loans like other loans while equity markets price in high growth (BIS Bulletin 120).
June 2026. The BIS said hyperscaler outlays exceed earnings and free cash flow (BIS Annual Economic Report 2026).

September 2026. The Bank of England said the risk of a sharper correction persisted after the July fall. It said a reassessment of AI productivity gains could reach sovereign debt markets (FPC record).
Reported, secondhand. A Treasury staff draft reportedly likened parts of the AI market to the dot-com bubble. Treasury called the findings unvetted (summary of a NOTUS report, July 6, 2026).
contested-points
Contested Points

How systemic. The Hardwired Pause working paper holds that equity losses alone would not be systemic (§6.1). It judges that a training freeze alone would not cause defaults if inference demand is mostly sub-frontier. The Bank of England puts more weight on exposures that are hard to see (FPC record).

Room to cut. The working paper says the Federal Reserve could cushion a shock from a policy rate near 4 percent. The September 2026 projections show PCE inflation at 3.7 percent (FOMC). The paper does not address that possible limit on rate cuts (inference).
Precedent. The 2001 recession stayed mild alongside rate cuts of 5.5 percentage points by June 2003 (Greenspan, January 3, 2004).
mitigations-proposed
Mitigations Proposed

Hardwired Pause working paper. Monitor and limit bank lending to private credit, scrutinize private credit ownership of insurers, require disclosure on securitized private credit, and regulate lease vehicles (§6.1).
Two-Lane Plan. Limits on bank and insurer exposure to data center debt, long-term federal compute contracts, and resolution plans. No published analysis found tests these safeguards.
Insurance supervisors. The NAIC is reviewing insurers’ data center holdings. Since January 2026 it can challenge ratings more than three notches from its own view (Insurance Business).
by-family
By Family
Stop. The test is whether inference revenue can service debt raised against training-era demand (inference).
Pace. A pace that leaves inference revenue intact would test equity valuations more than debt (inference).
Contain and Channel. The open question is whether lenders would treat federal contracts like hyperscaler leases. No source found answers it.
Continue. Debt-financed AI capital spending is forecast at about $4.1 trillion for 2026 through 2030 (Bank of England).

By Family
Stop. Model-creation spending falls by definition. Data center demand holds only if inference absorbs capacity built for training (inference).
Pace. The AI Futures Project’s compute-floor option would hold capabilities R&D to about 5 percent of lab compute (How to Pace the US Frontier). Its authors give no investment estimate.
Contain and Channel. Training demand and chip orders continue inside containment (inference). The Two-Lane Plan adds federal compute contracts as an anchor.
Embargo Plus U.S. Pause. It adds the loss of licensed H200 sales to China, which reportedly pay 25 percent of each sale to the U.S. Treasury (Tom’s Hardware).
Continue. A Goldman Sachs baseline scenario reaches $1.6 trillion a year of AI capital spending by 2031 (Goldman Sachs Global Institute).
productivity-and-growth
Productivity and Growth

Deployed AI has moved aggregate productivity little through mid-2026. The growth cost of a pause therefore depends on which growth model holds, and published projections span three orders of magnitude.
measured-so-far
Measured So Far
Measured. U.S. labor productivity rose 2.2 percent over the four quarters to Q2 2026. Growth since Q4 2019 has equaled the average since 1947 (Bureau of Labor Statistics).
Measured. Nine in ten executives in a four-country survey report no effect on productivity or employment over three years (NBER Working Paper 34836).
Measured. Danish administrative data show precise zero effects on earnings and hours two years after ChatGPT’s release (Humlum and Vestergaard).
Measured. Employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in the most exposed occupations trails less exposed peers by 19 percent (Stanford Digital Economy Lab).

what-a-pause-would-forgo
What a Pause Would Forgo
Inference. The first four projections model adoption of roughly current capabilities. On their own terms, a frontier pause leaves those gains largely in place.
Position. The Hardwired Pause working paper expects little reduction in productivity growth from a training freeze (§6.1). It names cheaper inference as the main near-term welfare gain (§6.2).
Scenario, seen only through a newspaper column. An Anthropic Institute model reportedly has GDP up 3.4 percent by 2030 with capabilities held at today’s level (Bourne).
Inference. Under the explosive-growth models, a multi-year pause forgoes most of the upside. The 2025 and 2026 data cannot yet tell the models apart.
by-family-3
By Family
Stop and Pace. Both keep adoption gains from existing models and defer gains that need new capabilities (inference).
Contain and Channel. New systems reach the public only after clearing the gate. No source found estimates the effect on growth.

Continue. The full range of projections stays open, along with displacement. One reported scenario from the same model pairs GDP up about 33 percent by 2030 with 18 percent knowledge-worker unemployment (Bourne). Goldman Sachs’ chief economist expects unemployment in ten years near the 4.1 percent of July 2026 (Goldman Sachs).

Pacing adoption. One model finds that slowing automation raises welfare about 4 percent when displaced workers adjust slowly (Beraja and Zorzi). The Two-Lane Plan’s option to pace adoption in high-displacement sectors has no estimate behind it.
global-economy
Global Economy

A fall in U.S. AI hardware demand would reach Taiwan and Korea first, through trade. Financial stress would travel through foreign holdings of U.S. equities and through bond markets where hyperscalers are now large issuers.
supplier-economies
Supplier Economies

Taiwan. Measured. AI-related exports to the United States reached roughly 14 percent of Taiwan’s GDP in Q2 2025 (FEDS Notes, February 13, 2026). TSMC fabricates nearly the entire global supply of AI chips (Epoch AI).

Korea. Measured. Korea grew at a 7.5 percent annual rate in Q1 2026, and the IMF raised its 2026 forecast to 2.6 percent (IMF, July 2026). Samsung and SK hynix make high-bandwidth memory, the tightest constraint on AI chips as of late 2025 (Epoch AI).

Japan and the Netherlands. Not confirmed. No source found sizes either country’s macro exposure. ASML of the Netherlands is the sole maker of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines (Epoch AI). SoftBank of Japan reportedly committed $30 billion to OpenAI’s March 2026 round (Yahoo Finance).
Other exporters. Measured. The top four AI hardware exporters beat growth forecasts by an average of 4.4 percentage points in Q1 2026 (IMF, July 2026). They are Taiwan, Korea, Thailand and Malaysia.

The mirror image. Goldman Sachs’ chief economist said in February 2026 that much U.S. AI spending raises Taiwanese and Korean GDP (Gizmodo, via The Wealth Advisor, secondary). A U.S. cut would then subtract more from their output than from U.S. output (inference).
other-advanced-economies
Other Advanced Economies
Position. Foreign ownership of U.S. equities has grown, so a sharp U.S. correction would cause sizable wealth losses abroad (IMF Blog).
Measured. AI hyperscalers accounted for 47 percent of sterling corporate bond issuance in 2026 through early September (Bank of England).
Scenario. A moderate correction in AI stock valuations lowers global growth by 0.4 percentage point (IMF, January 2026). The scenario concerns a market correction and does not model a pause.
developing-countries

Estimate, 2024. AI exposure covers about 60 percent of jobs in advanced economies and 26 percent in low-income countries (IMF Blog, January 14, 2024). The IMF’s Managing Director warned that the technology could widen gaps between countries.
Position. The World Bank reports a trend toward “small AI,” affordable applications that run on everyday devices (World Bank, landing page only).
Reported. A Bloomberg report on remarks by Treasury Secretary Bessent says Chinese open-weight models nearly match U.S. models at lower cost (Bloomberg, via Yahoo Finance).

Inference. Cheaper inference on existing models, which the Hardwired Pause working paper predicts (§6.2), would favor late adopters. No source found says whether a frontier pause would narrow or widen the gap.
