the-economics-of-delay-growth-against-risk
The Economics of Delay: Growth Against Risk
Formal economics on trading growth against catastrophic risk is thin and recent. Its answers turn on risk aversion and on whether AI extends life, and no paper found prices a pause of defined length.
Jones (2024) · AI yields 10 percent growth with 1 percent annual existential risk · Log utility: run AI about 40 years. Risk aversion of 2: about 4.5 years.
Jones (2024), mortality case · AI also halves mortality; risk aversion of 2 · Acceptable existential risk rises from 2.2 percent to 26.7 percent.
Jones (2025) · 1 percent catastrophic risk over ten years, half removable; $10 million life value · Optimal mitigation spending of 15.8 percent of GDP; 8.1 percent on average across draws.
Acemoglu and Lensman (2023) · Harms are uncertain and society learns over time · Gradual adoption is optimal.
Gans (2024) · Harms are learned through use; adoption is reversible · Faster adoption can be optimal.
Beraja and Zorzi (2022) · Displaced workers move slowly and cannot borrow freely · Slowing automation raises welfare about 4 percent.
Bostrom (2026) · Counts people alive now; lifespan 40 years without, about 1,400 with · Development pays unless catastrophe odds exceed about 97 percent.
Carlsmith (2026) · Background mortality 0.75 percent a year; other existential risk 0.1 percent · Multi-year pause pays only if it cuts alignment risk 0.1 to 1 percent yearly.
what-each-side-draws-from-the-models
What Each Side Draws From the Models

For a pause. Under standard risk aversion, the 2024 Jones model accepts about 4 percent total existential risk for consumption gains (Jones 2024). His 2025 paper finds mitigation spending of at least 1 percent of GDP justified in most scenarios examined.

Against a pause. If AI halves mortality, the risk Jones’s model tolerates rises about tenfold. Bostrom counts about 170,000 deaths a day without the technology (Bostrom). Carlsmith lists costs of restraint that include deaths during delay and ground ceded to authoritarian states.
A benchmark. The United States gave up about 4 percent of GDP in the pandemic to address a mortality risk near 0.3 percent (Jones 2025).

The value of health gains. Murphy and Topel valued a 1 percent cut in cancer mortality at nearly $500 billion in 2005 dollars (NBER Working Paper 11405). No source found estimates AI’s effect on the pace of medical progress.
bearing-on-the-families
Bearing on the Families
Stop. Jones’s 2025 paper concerns mitigation budgets and does not model a pause. A pause spends through forgone output, so the pandemic figure serves only as a benchmark (inference).

Pace. Acemoglu and Lensman support gradual adoption, and Gans supports faster adoption where use reveals harms. Beraja and Zorzi give the nearest formal support for pacing adoption in high-displacement sectors (inference).

Contain and Channel. If harms are learned in contained testing, as the Two-Lane Plan assumes, the Gans objection weakens (inference). Neither paper models contained development. Bostrom’s advice has the same shape: move fast to capability, then pause briefly before full deployment.
Continue. The mortality result and Bostrom’s lifespan arithmetic are formal support this family can cite (inference).
open-questions
Open Questions

No published work found estimates the economic effect of pacing or of contained development, and neither named plan has been modeled. The tasks start with that modeling and end with checks on secondhand figures.
modeling-not-found-in-published-work

Determine how lenders and rating agencies would treat long-term federal compute contracts against hyperscaler leases. Use defense procurement and advance purchase commitments as precedents.
Compare Stop, Pace, Contain and Channel, and Continue on one set of assumptions for investment, valuations, credit and jobs.
Add credit contagion to a pause model. Neither the Hardwired Pause working paper nor the Bayesian Investor model includes it.
Estimate what share of non-frontier compute and data center orders is bought in expectation of future frontier models.
Estimate how much leading-edge chip and memory capacity serves training, and whether inference demand could absorb it.
Estimate revenue, investment, price and valuation effects for each of the AI Futures Project’s four pacing options (How to Pace the US Frontier).
Estimate federal budget sensitivity under each family: capital gains and corporate receipts, payroll taxes under displacement, support for insurers or banks, and anchor contracts.
Test whether the Federal Reserve could offset a pause-induced demand shock with PCE inflation projected at 3.7 percent for 2026 (FOMC).
Price a pause of defined length against a defined cut in risk with the Jones framework and current adoption data (Jones 2024).
Estimate AI’s marginal effect on the pace of medical progress. Apply Murphy and Topel’s longevity values to price delay (NBER Working Paper 11405).
Build on Beraja and Zorzi to estimate the employment and welfare effects of pacing adoption in high-displacement sectors (NBER Working Paper 30154).
Model spillovers from a policy-induced U.S. slowdown to Taiwan, Korea, Japan and the Netherlands.
Estimate the cost of Embargo Plus U.S. Pause beyond a stop. Count Chinese retaliation through rare earths and lost China sales for chip and equipment makers.
Analyze how a frontier pause and cheaper inference would affect late-adopting countries while Chinese open-weight models stay available.

Economic Redesign
This tab asks what would have to change in the U.S. economy under each family of proposals, from the tax base to the safety net.
the-question
The Question

The U.S. economy taxes work and insures people through their jobs. Its stock index funds are concentrated in AI-linked firms. Advanced AI strains each arrangement, and the order of the strains depends on what happens to the frontier.

Seven systems are in play: labor markets, the tax base, income support, public stakes, competition rules, capital markets and the power grid. Forecasts run from a productivity gain under 1 percent over ten years (Acemoglu, 2024) to wage collapse under full automation (Korinek and Suh, 2024). That spread is the planning problem every proposal in this tab tries to handle.
why-the-answer-differs-by-family-inference
Why the Answer Differs by Family (Inference)
Stop. Frontier training halts while released models stay in use. Displacement from those models continues, and the financial risk peaks when a halt is announced.
Pace. The same tools are needed, and the state partly sets the schedule. Time becomes available to build them in steps.
Contain and Channel. The state becomes both funder and anchor customer of the frontier labs. Capability built in containment reaches the public economy in steps, at each release decision.
Continue. The same tools are needed in the least time. Triggers written into law in advance carry the most weight, because new legislation would lag events.
Contained development raises the concern in The Intelligence Curse most directly. A state with frontier capability inside a perimeter depends less on its citizens’ labor and taxes.
what-the-evidence-supports
What the Evidence Supports

No published analysis compares redesign needs across the four families. The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) covers a stop, and the AI 2040 economics supplement covers a paced path. Nothing comparable exists for contained development with gated deployment.
Two unpublished plans by Brad Carson have their own rows in the family table: the Two-Lane Plan and Embargo Plus U.S. Pause. No outside economic assessment of either exists.

The cross-family comparisons in this tab are therefore inference from the research notes and should be labeled as original analysis. The sources were read through a tool that condenses pages, so each figure needs checking against its original before publication.
labor-markets-and-displacement
Labor Markets and Displacement

The measured effect through mid-2026 is a hiring shortfall for workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations. Occupation-level government data show no aggregate displacement, and forecasts cover almost the full range of outcomes.
what-is-established
What Is Established

Entry-level hiring. Stanford researchers used ADP payroll records through June 2026 in a paper revised August 12, 2026. Employment of 22-to-25-year-olds in the most exposed occupations fell about 11 percent from November 2022. In the least exposed it grew about 10 percent, and the authors put the gap at 19 percent.
Mechanism. The gap comes from reduced hiring, and separations did not rise. The authors call the facts descriptive and make no causal estimate.
Whole occupations. The Budget Lab at Yale (May 7, 2026) found the effect on exposed occupations close to zero through March 2026.

Young workers’ unemployment. St. Louis Fed economists (June 30, 2026) studied April 2023 to December 2025. Demand for AI-related skills explained roughly one third of the rise among 18-to-24-year-olds. The broad decline in job openings was the larger factor.
The research notes read these findings as compatible. A small entry cohort can lose hiring while whole occupations show almost no effect.

the-tax-base-and-the-federal-budget
The Tax Base and the Federal Budget

Federal revenue rests on labor income, so a falling labor share weakens the budget even when output grows. Most analysts in the notes prefer broad capital, profit or consumption taxes, while members of Congress have introduced AI-specific levies.
what-is-established-2
What Is Established

Revenue mix. CBO (February 2026) projects fiscal 2026 revenue of $5,596 billion. Individual income taxes supply $2,751 billion and payroll taxes $1,826 billion, about 82 percent together by the research notes’ calculation.
Labor’s share of revenue. RAND (August 31, 2026) puts it near two thirds. Korinek and Lockwood (January 8, 2026) put it near three quarters.
Trust funds. Payroll taxes supplied 91.3 percent of Social Security’s revenue in 2025 (CRS, June 25, 2026). The 2026 Trustees project depletion of the retirement fund in late 2032.

Growth and revenue. The Budget Lab at Yale (July 20, 2026) finds rapid adoption adds up to $216 billion of revenue in 2030. The gain would roughly double if labor and capital shares held at 2026 levels. Capital income is taxed more lightly: top federal rates are 37 percent on labor income and 23.8 percent on capital gains.
what-is-contested
What Is Contested
Which threat is larger. Patel and Gordon (Brookings, August 7, 2026) say the larger fiscal threat is debt already on the books. They cite CBO debt of 101 percent of GDP now and 175 percent by 2056.
General revenue and trust funds (inference). Higher output could lift general receipts modestly while the payroll-funded trust funds weaken.

safety-net-and-income-support
Safety Net and Income Support
Proposals in 2026 have moved from universal cash toward support that switches on at measured thresholds. Their shared precondition is delivery capacity in the state unemployment systems.
what-is-established-3
What Is Established

Cash experiment. The OpenResearch study paid 1,000 adults $1,000 a month for three years (NBER w32719, revised August 2026). Income apart from the transfer fell about $1,900 a year, and labor market participation fell 4.2 points. The authors found no effect on job quality (figures confirmed on the NBER page, October 7, 2026).
Delivery capacity. Anthropic (June 2026) notes that many state unemployment systems buckled under pandemic claim volumes. NELP (September 2026) calls those systems threadbare.
Federal warning. Fed Governor Barr (February 17, 2026) said a rapid “jobless boom” would require a restructured safety net.
what-is-contested-2
What Is Contested

What the cash result means. Critics read less work with no better jobs as a case against universal income today. Supporters can answer that a market with jobs says little about one where work is scarce (the notes’ inference). OpenResearch’s own summary stresses greater agency in job decisions and more interest in entrepreneurship.
New programs or repaired ones. Gimbel argues for stronger unemployment insurance over elaborate new programs. Anthropic, OpenAI and investor Alap Shah propose new layers that activate at thresholds.
Universal income. Anthropic lists it only for its most severe tier. Leicht and Ball say polling shows citizens are uninterested in it.

sharing-the-gains-public-stakes-funds-and-dividends
Sharing the Gains: Public Stakes, Funds and Dividends

Proposals for a public claim on AI returns take three forms: a tax paid in equity, negotiated or purchased equity, and a voluntary pledge. They differ in who bears the dilution and in whether the state gains control or only cash flow.
what-is-established-4
What Is Established

The Intel stake. On August 22, 2025 the government bought 9.9 percent of Intel for $8.9 billion. The stake is passive, with no board seat, and came with conditional five-year warrants for a further 5 percent.
Dividend scale. Alaska paid $1,000 per recipient in 2025, about $620 million across 618,863 approved applications.

June 2026 exchange. Altman met Sanders and endorsed public equity in principle (Fortune, June 6, 2026); Sanders’s office said Altman committed to none of the senator’s requests. President Trump spoke that week of a possible partnership that benefits Americans (Associated Press). Whether White House meetings followed is Not confirmed.

July to September 2026. The Financial Times reported on July 2 that OpenAI had discussed a 5 percent stake for the government, as relayed by Reuters. In that account, leading U.S. AI firms would each place 5 percent of equity in a vehicle like the Alaska Permanent Fund. At an $852 billion valuation, a 5 percent share of OpenAI would be worth about $42.6 billion (CNN). Euronews reported that Sanders considered the offer far too small. The Washington Sun later reported that Altman privately opposed the government holding OpenAI shares (September 9, 2026). The paper added that he backed some version of redistributing company shares to the public.
Fund plan. A February 3, 2025 executive order required a sovereign wealth fund plan within 90 days (later status Not confirmed).

what-is-contested-3
What Is Contested

Whether the state should hold stakes. Leicht and Ball (June 4, 2026) say government stakes in frontier labs bet on one trajectory for where value lands. Their essay also rejects narrow token taxes, job guarantees and universal income.

How large, and who controls. Sanders pressed for 50 percent so the public would hold decision power, and Altman declined that figure. Under S. 4825, a seven-member Independent Commission for Democratic AI would govern the fund and vote its shares. The Intel terms sit at the passive end.
the-two-lane-plan-beside-the-published-proposals
The Two-Lane Plan Beside the Published Proposals
Model. It is negotiated equity, like the Intel stake, taken as a condition of federal funding.
Use of returns. Returns go to wage insurance and transition support. The Sanders bill authorizes direct payments to the public, and OpenAI says its fund’s returns could go directly to citizens.

Closest published relative. New York Assemblyman Alex Bores proposed an “AI Dividend” (Searchlight, June 9, 2026). The federal government would take out-of-the-money warrants in major AI companies. Returns would go to direct payments, workforce transition and public infrastructure for governing AI safely. It has no procurement element and names no wage insurance (see the prior-art review in the Contain and Channel tab).
Timing (inference). Bargaining power over equity or warrants is highest before the state commits funding.
Strongest objection (inference). Leicht and Ball’s argument applies: a stake bets that value lands at the labs.
how-it-differs-by-family-inference-4
How It Differs by Family (Inference)
Stop. Windfall mechanisms have less to capture. An approved-model list creates regulatory rents, which supports license fees or a stake set when the list is granted.
Pace. Windfall capture stays relevant, and permit auctions become a natural revenue source.
Contain and Channel. The claim is strongest, because public money and public risk-bearing support equity as a condition of funding.
Continue. The claim must be legislated against industry resistance.
what-is-unknown-4
What Is Unknown

No total market value for federal corporate stakes was found. Fortune (July 26, 2026) counts about $26.7 billion invested across 30 equity or quasi-equity deals, led by the Intel stake. The Ownership and Industry Structure tab covers the individual stakes.
No legal or market analysis of S. 4825’s equity levy was opened.
competition-and-industrial-policy
Competition and Industrial Policy

The notes infer that each family changes what competition policy is for. A frozen list of approved models would turn today’s leaders into licensed incumbents. A contained lane would make entry depend on certification and contracts.
what-is-established-5
What Is Established

Partnership ties. An FTC staff report (January 17, 2025) covered the Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet partnerships with OpenAI and Anthropic. Cloud providers hold equity and revenue-sharing rights, and developers committed much of the investment to the partner’s cloud.
Price pressure. Ramp (September 9, 2026) reports token prices down 41 percent since March 2026.
State-backed channel. Executive Order 14363 (November 24, 2025) launched the Genesis Mission. It joins national laboratory supercomputers with private partners for AI-driven research.

Antimonopoly rules · Narechania and Sitaraman, January 2024 · Utility-style regulation and public options, ahead of after-the-fact antitrust
Public AI · Sitaraman and Pascal, 2024 · Public data centers and models; structural separation across chips, cloud and models
Right to AI · OpenAI, April 2026 · Baseline model access through free or low-cost channels
Separation of AI operations · S. 4825, June 18, 2026 · Covered firms separate AI operations from other business lines within 90 days
Regulated approved-model list · Hardwired Pause working paper, §3.3.2 and §6.4 · Model owners barred from inference licenses; licensing to independent providers at regulated rates

what-is-contested-4
What Is Contested

Private plurality or public structure. Leicht (March 31, 2026) counts development by several private companies in democracies as a favorable feature of the present. Sitaraman and Pascal argue that utility regulation is compatible with innovation and cite Bell Labs.
Restraint and centralization. Carlsmith (March 19, 2026) worries that international restraint regimes push toward centralized development and concentrated government power.

Entrenchment under a freeze. The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) says a whitelist could entrench the leading developers, perhaps permanently. It adds that the whitelisting body would be open to capture.
how-it-differs-by-family-inference-5
How It Differs by Family (Inference)

Stop. Competition policy becomes franchise regulation: rate regulation, mandatory licensing, separation of model owners from inference providers, and a transparent approval body. The working paper expects rivalry to move to cost and speed, with lower token prices once inference-only chips arrive (§6.2, §3.4.1). Makers of training hardware lose, and owners of approved models gain a protected position.
Pace. Compliance costs for compute floors and safety cases favor large labs.

Contain and Channel. Certification and anchor procurement decide who can be a frontier developer. The lane would resemble defense procurement or a regulated utility, and public-option arguments move to the center of the design.
Continue. Conventional antitrust on partnerships and vertical integration remains the main tool.
what-is-unknown-5
What Is Unknown
No published analysis covers competition among labs under a contained lane with gated release. The Two-Lane Plan is unpublished, so none is expected yet.
Antitrust enforcement actions on AI in 2026 were not searched.
The working paper cites a SemiAnalysis estimate that two labs devote 62 percent of compute to research and training (§6.2). That source was not opened.
capital-markets-pensions-and-savings
Capital Markets, Pensions and Savings

Savers are exposed to AI through two channels: index concentration and private credit, where pensions and insurers are major funders. No published dollar estimate of pension, 401(k) or insurer exposure to AI-linked assets was found.
what-is-established-6
What Is Established

Index concentration. The Magnificent Seven are 34.9 percent of S&P 500 market value (Motley Fool Research, updated October 5, 2026). A saver in an S&P 500 index fund therefore holds about a third of that money in seven firms.
Return concentration. Cembalest (J.P. Morgan, January 1, 2026) counts 42 AI-related companies behind 65 to 75 percent of S&P 500 returns since November 2022.
Build-out. Goldman Sachs (May 1, 2026) puts 2026 AI capital spending at $765 billion. Its 2026 to 2031 total is near $7.6 trillion.

Private credit. The Federal Reserve (May 2026) sizes private credit at about $1.4 trillion, or 10 percent of nonfinancial corporate debt. About half of the 20 market contacts it surveyed in March and April 2026 cited AI as a stability risk.
Who funds it. A 2024 Fed note put pension funds at 31 percent of private credit capital and insurers at 9 percent. Those shares date from late 2021.
what-is-contested-5
What Is Contested

Equity losses from a pause. The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) models a Magnificent Seven fall to early-2025 values, about $6.5 trillion. It estimates spending would drop about $195 billion, or 0.6 percent of GDP, and calls that an upper bound (§6.1). The scenario is a thought experiment.

Where the danger sits. The same paper locates it in debt markets. It lists data center loans from private credit funds, bank credit lines to those funds, and securitized tranches with unknown holders.
Whether a pause is the only trigger. Fed Governor Barr (February 17, 2026) describes a stall in which overinvestment fails to earn its return. No pause is involved.

Revenue under a freeze. The working paper argues data center revenue may hold, because most enterprise demand is for inference below the frontier. Ramp (September 9, 2026) shows the shift to cheaper models and also revenue pressure from price cuts.

Who Has Proposed What
Limits on lending to private credit · Hardwired Pause working paper, §6.1 · Bank regulators monitor and limit loans to private credit funds
Insurer scrutiny · Hardwired Pause working paper, §6.1 · Insurance regulators review private credit firms’ purchases of insurers
Disclosure · Hardwired Pause working paper, §6.1 · More disclosure by securitizers; stronger rules for AI firms’ special-purpose vehicles
Credit safeguards · Two-Lane Plan (Brad Carson, unpublished, October 2026) · Limits on bank and insurer exposure to data center debt; resolution plans
Federal compute contracts · Two-Lane Plan · Long-term federal contracts for compute
how-it-differs-by-family-inference-6
How It Differs by Family (Inference)
Stop. The need is most urgent on day one: a valuation reset and stress in private credit, insurers and securitized data center debt.
Pace. Repricing is gradual as expected training demand falls.
Contain and Channel. Federal compute contracts steady cash flows and concentrate counterparty risk on the government.
Continue. The build-out and leverage are largest, so the loss is largest if returns disappoint.
A stall in capabilities, a token price war or a failed financing could also trigger repricing. The notes infer that credit safeguards are useful under every family.
what-is-unknown-6
What Is Unknown
Dollar exposure. No source quantified pension, 401(k) or insurer holdings of AI-linked equities or data center debt.
Fall 2025 survey. The Fed report says more contacts cited AI in spring 2026 than in fall 2025. The fall share is unsettled: machine readings of its charts gave zero and about 35 percent.
energy-and-infrastructure
Energy and Infrastructure

Data centers used 4.4 percent of U.S. electricity in 2023, and forecasts for 2030 approach 12 percent. Grid plans assume that growth continues, so a stop or strict pace would raise the question of who pays for stranded capacity (inference).
what-is-established-7
What Is Established
Demand. The 4.4 percent and 12 percent figures come from Axios (August 25, 2026). The reading did not name Axios’s source, and the 2030 figure is not reconciled with the Lawrence Berkeley report.
Global share. The IEA (2025) puts global data center use at 415 terawatt-hours in 2024, with 45 percent in the United States. It projects about 945 terawatt-hours by 2030.
Frontier sites. Epoch AI (updated October 5, 2026) tracks 93 frontier AI sites with 17.9 gigawatts of total facility power.

Prices. EIA (October 6, 2026) expects residential prices of 18.2 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2026, against 17.3 cents in 2025. Axios reports that capacity prices in PJM, the largest grid operator, rose elevenfold in recent years.

Local opposition. Axios counts at least 75 projects worth about $130 billion delayed in the first quarter of 2026. Data Center Watch counted $64 billion blocked or delayed from May 2024 to March 2025. A typical large project brings about 50 permanent jobs.
Share of GDP. Computing infrastructure investment reached about 1.5 percent of GDP in the first quarter of 2026 (Epoch AI, June 5, 2026).
what-is-contested-6
What Is Contested

Who pays. Senator Hawley wants data center development halted until companies pay for their own power, grids and water (Associated Press, June 2026). The AI Action Plan (July 2025) takes the opposite emphasis and calls for faster permitting.
The forecasts. The IEA says about 20 percent of planned projects could be delayed by grid constraints. Its 2035 range runs from 700 to 1,700 terawatt-hours.
Obsolescence. Goldman Sachs (May 1, 2026) flags the risk that equipment becomes obsolete before it is depreciated.
Energy under a freeze. The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) expects inference-only chips to lower energy cost per token (§6.2).

redesign-needs-by-proposal-family
Redesign Needs by Proposal Family

Measurement, delivery systems and pre-legislated triggers come first under every family. What differs is the time left for the rest and where the first shock lands. This summary and the table are inference from the research notes, extended to the two named plans from their descriptions.

Stop · Credit-exposure safeguards; rules and pricing for the approved-model list; baseline labor data · New tax bases; dividend design; universal income floors · Who holds data center debt, and how large the losses would be

Pace · Lab and employer reporting; pre-legislated safety-net triggers; stepwise shift toward capital and consumption taxes · Universal income floors; direct taxes on autonomous systems; permit auctions · Economic effects of the pacing options; their proposers give almost no analysis

Contain and Channel · Public financial terms before funding; certification and procurement rules; transition programs before each clearance · Dividend and capital-account design, until a fund holds assets · Size of the release shock at each gate clearance; no published analysis

Continue · Automatic triggers; modernized unemployment systems; tax parity for labor and capital; labor data · Same items as Pace, with less time before they are needed · How fast and how far labor’s share of income falls

Two-Lane Plan · Equity or warrant terms; federal compute contracts; credit-exposure limits; funded wage insurance before clearances · New tax bases; dividend and capital-account design · Lab revenue under gated deployment; fiscal cost of anchor procurement

Embargo Plus U.S. Pause · Stop-row measures, in place before announcement; a decision on compute already contracted · New tax bases; dividend design; universal income floors · Embargo cost to chip and equipment makers; cost of holding restart capacity

No published source compares redesign needs across the families, and no outside assessment covers the two named plans. The notes infer that displacement from released models continues under a stop, so job protection there needs a separate deployment policy. The notes judge the financial case for preparing before a stop stronger than the labor case.

Several leading proposals carry no economic transition measures. The announcement of the Sanders and Casar pause bill (September 3, 2026) contains no worker, tax or ownership provisions. The bill was introduced as S. 5493 on September 23, 2026 and as H.R. 10538 on September 24. The AI Futures Project’s four pacing options carry almost no economic analysis, and the July 2026 Pacing the Frontier letter is silent on jobs.

Ownership and Industry Structure
This tab covers who owns and controls frontier AI today and what each family of proposals would require to change.
the-question
The Question

Most proposals to pause, pace or contain frontier AI leave the companies in private hands and change who controls specific decisions. The proposals that change ownership come from two other debates. One concerns sharing AI’s gains, and the other concerns a lab that fails commercially.

Ownership and control are already separate. The OpenAI Foundation appoints every director of OpenAI Group PBC and held about 26% of its equity in October 2025 (OpenAI). Elon Musk holds about 85.1% of the voting power at SpaceX, which owns xAI (TechCrunch). Mark Zuckerberg holds 61.2% of Meta’s votes on 13.68% of its equity, per Wikipedia.
Three things can change hands. A proposal can move the economic return, the votes, or a veto over named decisions. Each can move without the others, so a stake proposal has to say which it wants.

Control has moved without ownership. In June 2026 the Commerce Secretary reportedly warned OpenAI not to release GPT-5.6 without approval. Export controls suspended access to two Anthropic models on June 12, 2026 and ended June 30; Fable 5 returned July 1 (Tom’s Hardware; Anthropic). The government held no share of either developer.

The two largest independent labs rent most of their hardware. OpenAI and Anthropic mostly rent compute from Microsoft, Oracle, Amazon and Google (Epoch AI). Rules that work through chips or data centers fall on those owners and their lenders.

Where ownership does change. Senator Sanders’s S. 4825 would place 50% of each covered company’s equity with the Treasury (bill text). Bruce Schneier and Nathan Sanders would nationalize OpenAI and Anthropic if markets reject them (schneier.com repost).

Across the four families. Most Stop and Pace proposals keep the labs private and add licenses and auditors. Contain and Channel proposals run from private labs in certified facilities to a single national or international project. Continue positions impose no change, though the federal government already holds equity in chipmakers and other suppliers (Council on Foreign Relations).
The family comparison in this tab is largely inference from the research notes. No source found compares the families on ownership.
who-owns-the-frontier-today
Who Owns the Frontier Today

The leading U.S. developers fall into three ownership types as of early October 2026. Two are mission-controlled private companies that are reported to have filed confidentially to go public. One is a founder-controlled listed company, and the others are divisions of listed parents.

OpenAI · Public benefit corporation controlled by a nonprofit foundation · Foundation about 26%, Microsoft about 27%, employees and investors 47% (October 2025, OpenAI) · $840 billion to $852 billion, 2026 round (press: Reuters, CNN) · Foundation appoints and can replace all directors

Anthropic · Delaware public benefit corporation (Anthropic) · Amazon, Google and other investors; percentages Not confirmed · $965 billion post-money, May 2026 (aggregator Trending Topics; Wikipedia) · Long-Term Benefit Trust elects directors through Class T stock

xAI (SpaceX) · Owned by listed SpaceX since February 2026 (Decrypt) · Musk about 85.1% of SpaceX votes (TechCrunch); public shareholders since June 2026 · $1.77 trillion (Wikipedia) to $2.7 trillion (TechCrunch), June 2026; Not confirmed · Dual-class shares; Class B carries ten votes

Google DeepMind · Unit of Alphabet · Alphabet shareholders; founders and insiders control the voting majority (per Wikipedia, December 2023) · No separate valuation · 2023 merger ended DeepMind’s bid for autonomy (per Wikipedia)

Meta Superintelligence Labs · Division of Meta, formed June 30, 2025 (per Wikipedia) · Zuckerberg 13.68% of equity, 61.2% of votes (per Wikipedia) · No separate valuation · Dual-class founder control at the parent

Microsoft AI · Division of Microsoft, created March 19, 2024 (per Wikipedia) · Microsoft shareholders; not researched · No separate valuation · Contract permits Microsoft to pursue AGI independently (OpenAI)

OpenAI’s percentages are stale. The 26% and 27% figures date from October 2025, before the 2026 funding round. An unofficial April 2026 cap table shows Microsoft 26.79%, the Foundation 25.80%, employees 15.88% and SoftBank 11.66% (Trending Topics, an aggregator). It is not an OpenAI disclosure, and current holdings are Not confirmed.

Regulated utility · Private monopoly or oligopoly; public in Schneier and Sanders · Regulator sets rates and conduct · Bell System, 1913 to 1984 (per Wikipedia); compute utility in Schneier and Sanders · No direct critic found in the notes

Government-owned, contractor-operated · Government owns the facility · Agency sets the mission; contractor runs operations · Atomic Energy Commission (DOE/OSTI); 16 of 17 national laboratories (per Wikipedia) · Precedents financed new plants; AI capacity is already privately built (notes’ inference)

International body · Treaty body or member states · Member-state council; votes weighted or equal · MAGIC; Intelsat model (Forethought); CERN · Enforcement (MAGIC, abstract only) and existing investors (Intelsat model) unaddressed by the authors

Models stack. The MP Materials deal alone combines preferred equity, warrants, a price floor, an offtake contract, a loan and governance vetoes (MP Materials 8-K). The research notes infer that a lab arrangement could combine a license, a resident examiner, a golden share and warrants.

Many small levers, on one account. Deric Cheng and Corin Katzke argue that government will assemble control from many levers and is unlikely to buy the firms (Convergence Analysis). They describe the levers and do not recommend them, and the paper dates from August 28, 2024.

A staged path, on another account. Paul Triolo forecasts that Washington would move in stages: visibility, then conditional permission, then classified development streams (Cairo Review, June 17, 2026). He sees hard nationalization as a live option only after those stages fall short or a crisis hits.

A halt right. Arbel, Goldstein and Salib propose a government right to order temporary halts to training or deployment of powerful systems (AI Nationalization, August 1, 2026). Halt orders could address only catastrophic risk and “hard” corporate power, and the right would be broadly discretionary. They find nationalization unwarranted for national security failures, monopoly power and inequality (abstract page only).

A legal line sits at board control. In Lebron (1995) the Supreme Court treated a corporation created by special law, with a permanently government-appointed board majority, as part of the government (Justia). A lab under such a board could face constitutional limits that a private lab does not. No source found applies the ruling to AI.

Private versions already exist. OpenAI’s foundation, Anthropic’s trust and the Microsoft and OpenAI expert panel on AGI are in place today. A public trustee or director could attach to those bodies. That step is an inference in the notes, and no source proposes it.
The Two-Lane Plan’s rung. The plan (Brad Carson, unpublished, October 2026) takes equity or warrants in labs the government funds. It leaves open who owns the certified facilities.

By family (an inference). Most Stop and Pace proposals sit on the first rung, with structural rules added; MAGIC pairs a moratorium with one international developer. Contain and Channel proposals span minority stakes, government-owned facilities, consortia and international bodies. Continue positions keep today’s private ownership and mission-control arrangements.

what-the-cases-suggest-for-ai-ownership
What the Cases Suggest for AI Ownership
The readings below are inferences in the research notes unless a source is linked.

Portfolio size. Trackers count $26.7 billion to $28.4 billion of investment across 30 to 42 deals since January 2025 (Council on Foreign Relations; Fortune). The totals are sums invested or announced, and Fortune valued the Intel stake alone at about $42 billion in July 2026. No deal is in an AI model developer as of September 30, 2026 (The National).

Cost. The wartime and atomic cases put the capital cost on the Treasury and kept title public. The 2008 and 2009 cases bought securities in failing firms. AI capacity is already built with private and foreign money, so either model would require the government to buy or allocate costly existing assets.

Control. Four designs recur. The 1946 commission gave full public control, and conservatorship gives board powers without share ownership. COMSAT gave a minority of public directors, and the Intel stake gives economics with almost no control.

Exit. Securities in recovering firms were sold within about four to six years. Operating entities lasted longer: Conrail took 11 years and the Reconstruction Finance Corporation 25. Amtrak and the Tennessee Valley Authority were never sold.

Shareholders. Owners and lenders of failing firms recovered little. The suit over AIG’s rescue won no damages, and Chrysler’s secured lenders received 29 cents on the dollar (per Wikipedia). A solvent lab valued near $1 trillion starts from a different position.

Seizure. The Supreme Court struck down the 1952 steel seizure for want of a statute (Youngstown). It held in 1951 that seizing and operating a coal mine was a taking and that the government owed the operating losses (Pewee Coal).

Statutes that permit operation. At least three statutes let the government operate private facilities, each with compensation. They are Atomic Energy Act §108 (licensed facilities), Communications Act §706 (stations) and Military Selective Service Act §18 (plants whose owners refuse mandatory orders). The first two require war or a declared emergency, and under the first Congress must declare it.

Oversight. TARP had a statutory inspector general, quarterly reports to Congress, an oversight panel and GAO audits. Fortune reports that the 2025 to 2026 portfolio has none of these and no consolidated public ledger.
Licensing. One study found that the 1956 Bell decree raised follow-on innovation only outside telecommunications, Bell’s own market (Watzinger et al., abstract only).
International laboratories. CERN gives each of its 25 member states one vote (CERN). ITER fixes cost shares by treaty, and Europe pays about 45.6% of construction (ITER).

Closest fit to containment. The contractor-operated laboratory model has been stable for 80 years, and it governs facilities the government built. Applied to AI, the government would own or lease data centers and contract labs to run them. That is close to the certified facilities in the Two-Lane Plan.

notes-on-the-rows
Notes on the Rows
The points below are inferences from the research notes unless a source is cited.

Stop. Revenue would shift from frontier progress to inference on a fixed set of models. The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) estimates that existing accelerators cost about $500 billion. It uses $1 trillion as an illustrative buyback budget (§5.3.2).
Pace. OpenAI and Anthropic rent their compute, so an allocation rule has to bind the cloud owner as well as the lab. The access required is closer to bank examination than to current AI oversight.

Contain and Channel, and the Two-Lane Plan. If nothing leaves containment until the gate is passed, government contracts become the main income. Warrants could be set to vest only when a lab’s systems clear the gate, as Intel’s warrants vest on a contingency.

Embargo Plus U.S. Pause. The research notes contain no ownership analysis of this proposal. Its breakout clause restarts contained development, so the Two-Lane Plan’s facility and stake questions would arise at that point (an inference).
National project. The leading labs rent their compute, so consolidation would fall mainly on Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Oracle, SpaceX, CoreWeave and Stargate’s partners.
Continue. Public ownership could still arrive through a rescue of heavily indebted infrastructure. AIG, GM and Conrail came into public hands that way.

shareholders-and-contract-holders
Shareholders and Contract Holders

A pause or gate takes no title. Shareholders bear the loss unless a court finds a regulatory taking. The notes’ reading is that pending IPOs strengthen the expectations argument and published safety rationales weaken it.

A release gate changes the business model. If nothing leaves containment until a gate is passed, commercial revenue from frontier systems stops. The notes infer that valuations would move toward those of defense contractors or regulated utilities. How those valuations compare is Not confirmed.

Directors have room to accept a pause (notes’ inference). Delaware law tells directors of a public benefit corporation to balance stockholders’ financial interests, affected parties and the stated public benefit (Delaware Code). Only holders of at least 2% of the shares can sue to enforce that balance. For listed companies the threshold is $2 million of stock if that is less.

Listing spreads the loss. SpaceX is already public. If OpenAI and Anthropic list, index funds and retirement savers would hold the equity. The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) expects a pause might delay those listings and thinks abandonment less plausible (§6.1).
Contract rights depend on continued development. Microsoft holds model intellectual property rights through 2032 and a $250 billion Azure purchase commitment from OpenAI (OpenAI).

Foreign investors are the hardest fit for containment (notes’ inference). SoftBank and MGX fund Stargate (OpenAI), and Singapore’s GIC and the Qatar Investment Authority hold Anthropic stakes (per Wikipedia). The MP Materials deal lets the Defense Department restrict foreign ownership above 14.9% (MP Materials 8-K). Investment-treaty protection for these holders is Not confirmed.

Employees

Exposure. An unofficial estimate puts OpenAI’s employee pool near 16% (Trending Topics, an aggregator). A $6.6 billion employee tender took place in 2026 (Private Market View, an aggregator). S. 4825 would tax later share issuances at 50%, and that covers conversions of employee compensation.

Under nationalization. Schneier and Sanders would move staff to civil-service pay (schneier.com repost). Cheng and Katzke note that U.S. labs pay largely in equity, which a takeover would disturb (Convergence Analysis).

Bargaining power. The project’s context brief reports that more than 1,000 frontier lab employees signed the “Pacing the Frontier” letter of July 28, 2026. The letter itself was not opened for this tab. Clearance or citizenship rules would collide with the labs’ international workforces (notes’ inference).

what-practice-shows
What Practice Shows
Stakes so far were negotiated. No case was found since 2025 in which the government took equity from an unwilling company. S. 4825 would be the first compulsory transfer (notes’ inference).

Legal footing is uneven. Fortune reports that only the Development Finance Corporation has clear authority to own equity. Defense Production Act §303, as read, does not mention equity (50 U.S.C. 4533). OpenAI’s reported plan may need an act of Congress (CNN), and S. 4825 is itself new legislation.
Two design poles exist. Intel’s terms give economics with passive voting, and U.S. Steel’s give hard vetoes with no economics. A lab stake could copy either.

S. 4825 reaches beyond the labs. It covers firms with over $200 million of gross receipts in AI data centers, computing infrastructure, AI services or advanced robotics (Sanders bill text). A seven-member commission would vote the shares and name board representatives. Covered firms must separate AI from other businesses within 90 days.

Who governs the fund. The Independent Commission for Democratic AI would sit in the Treasury, with seven members on five-year terms and at most four from one party (S. 4825). It must manage the fund to promote worker welfare, public safety, fair competition, environmental sustainability and financial solvency. Its board representatives must act to advance the same goals, and the commission must seat as many as the fund’s shares allow.
Payout rule. The bill authorizes yearly appropriations equal to 5% of the fund’s average market value, less administrative costs (S. 4825).
advocates
Advocates

Sam Altman. He has pitched the administration since 2025 on ceding OpenAI equity to a public wealth fund (Semafor). The Washington Sun reported that on July 29, 2026 he told conservative economists he opposed the government itself taking OpenAI shares (September 9, 2026). OpenAI told the paper it backs a government-administered public wealth fund and would not support a government ownership stake.

President Trump and his advisers. The President cited the Intel stake as precedent (CNN). Treasury Secretary Bessent favored seeding Trump Accounts, and Commerce Secretary Lutnick favored a sovereign-wealth-style fund (Semafor, June 17, 2026).
Senator Sanders and Steve Bannon. Sanders’s bill would take 50% and frames the transfer as a tax, with no compensation clause. Bannon said AI companies should be forced to surrender 50% (Fortune).
critics
Critics

Republican senators. Senator Cruz opposed federal equity stakes in private companies, and Senator Hawley objected to pairing bureaucrats with a Big Tech monopolist (Daily Signal). Senators Lummis and Kennedy voiced skepticism (Semafor).
Companies. Microsoft and Meta rejected the idea (Semafor). A source told Reuters that Anthropic and the administration had not discussed a stake (The Next Web).
Cato Institute. Tad DeHaven argues that government cannot be a neutral regulator of companies it owns (Thomson Reuters Checkpoint).
Transparency. Fortune reports no consolidated public ledger, and stakes in private companies produce no securities filings.

Payout doubts. Data Center Dynamics notes that the large AI companies are losing money, so near-term payments are unlikely. One report cites a $7 trillion estimate for the Sanders fund and does not name its source (The Next Web).

Leicht and Ball. They argue that government stakes in frontier labs bet on one view of where AI’s value will land (Leicht and Ball). This item comes from companion research notes and was not opened for this tab.

Contain and Channel. The Two-Lane Plan pairs equity or warrants with containment and a release gate.
Continue. No change is imposed, yet OpenAI has reportedly offered equity with no pause attached.

A tension. Senator Sanders’s stop bill and S. 4825 pull against each other financially, on the notes’ reading. A fund holding half of each AI company depends on value that a development ban would reduce.
concentration-of-power-and-safeguards
Concentration of Power and Safeguards

Writers who disagree on almost everything else agree that control of frontier AI by a single actor is a first-order danger. They hold that the danger exists whether the actor is a company or a government, and they split on the remedy.
positions
Positions
Avoid centralization unless other risks require it · Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar (Forethought, April 15, 2025) · Multi-party approval, audits for secret loyalties and shared frontier capabilities

One Western project is probably net bad, a tentative best guess · Davidson and Hadshar (Forethought, December 3, 2024) · If centralized: confine it to pre-training and safety testing; share models with private firms
A race to superintelligence is self-defeating · Katzke and Futerman (The Manhattan Trap, December 22, 2024) · International cooperation and verification
Private concentration is the present problem · Brennan, Kak and Myers West (AI Now, June 3, 2025) · Structural separation; limits on hyperscaler partnerships with AI startups
Democratic oversight is a better guardrail than shareholder pressure · Schneier and Sanders, August 2026 · National laboratories under congressional oversight
A government chain of command is the safer home · Aschenbrenner, “The Project”, 2024 · Congressional appropriations and Senate-confirmed officials
An owner-regulator is not neutral · Cato’s DeHaven (Checkpoint); Senators Hawley and Cruz (Daily Signal) · Opposition to federal equity stakes
Stopping the frontier removes the prize · Hardwired Pause working paper (§§6.4, 6.5) · Independent whitelisting; public-monopoly regulation of any resulting oligopoly
Deterrence, with no Manhattan Project for superintelligence · Hendrycks, Schmidt and Wang (Superintelligence Strategy) · Mutual threat of sabotage, chip nonproliferation and weight security
Only the landing page and executive summary of Superintelligence Strategy were read. Three of the items date from 2024: Aschenbrenner, Katzke and Futerman, and Davidson and Hadshar.
safeguards-sorted-by-what-they-divide
Safeguards Sorted by What They Divide
The Forethought paper on AI-enabled coups holds that company and government control need similar safeguards. The research notes sort its list into four groups, and ownership is only one of them.
Access to models · Multi-party approval; no single executive with unguarded access; audits for secret loyalties
Suppliers · Military AI bought from several independent suppliers
Oversight · Legislative committees, courts, allies and independent audits of contractors
Ownership · Several projects; a public-private form if one project is created

The 1946 benchmark. The atomic settlement used a five-member civilian commission, a nine-member scientific advisory committee, a military liaison committee and a joint committee of Congress (DOE/OSTI). The notes suggest measuring any national AI project against that list.

One-person vetoes. The President personally holds the U.S. Steel golden share while in office (AP via Spotlight PA). By the Forethought criteria, a veto held by a multi-member body would fit AI better (notes’ inference).
Committees can go either way. In AI 2027 a joint company and government committee votes 6 to 4 to slow down in one ending (AI 2027). It votes 6 to 4 to continue in the other (race ending).

Two routes to one federal control point. S. 4825 gives a commission half the votes in every covered company, and AI 2027 consolidates compute under one lab with a joint committee. The concentration critique applies to both (notes’ inference).

Political weight of the firms. The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) reports heavy political spending by frontier firms. It cites about $265 million pledged to political groups in the 2026 cycle (§§7.1, 7.4). That figure comes from a Wall Street Journal report that was not opened.
by-family
By Family
Stop. The Hardwired Pause authors say a pause keeps the prize from being created. They concede it could lock in incumbents’ market power and the values built into whitelisted models (§§6.4, 6.5).
Pace. The pacing options leave several private firms in place under embedded auditors. The company-side safeguards would then apply (an inference).

Contain and Channel. Critics hold that a single national project maximizes concentration and may speed China’s response (Forethought). The Two-Lane Plan’s adversary finding would need safeguards against misuse by a single official (notes’ inference).

Continue. Concentration proceeds by private means: a handful of labs, each tied to one or two hyperscalers (notes’ inference). AI Now argues that these firms are already structured to be too big to fail (AI Now).

domestic-legal-authority-to-pause-or-pace
Domestic Legal Authority to Pause or Pace
As of early October 2026 no federal statute pauses, licenses or gates frontier models. One existing authority, export control law, took two models off the market in June 2026.

Export Control Reform Act and its regulations · Control exports of dual-use items and “deemed exports” to foreign nationals · Used June 12, 2026 against two models; reaches foreign nationals only · Whether remote model access is a “release” of technology · CRS R46814; Zhao

Defense Production Act, Title I · Require priority performance of contracts; allocate materials, services and facilities · Aimed at mandating production more than preventing it (Rosenzweig) · Major questions doctrine; firms may reject orders for items they do not supply · CRS R43767; Rozenshtein; Fox News

Defense Production Act, Title VII · Collect information from industry; sponsor voluntary agreements with antitrust protection · Supports reporting; used for AI developer reports under President Biden · Most authorities lapse December 11, 2026 unless renewed · CRS R43767; Rozenshtein; Fox News

International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) · After a declared emergency, prohibit transactions involving foreign-interest property · Doubtful fit for domestic AI restrictions (Zhao; Frazier and Ball) · Informational-materials exemption; held not to authorize tariffs on February 20, 2026 · CRS R45618; Supreme Court; Cato

uses-of-authority-in-2026
Uses of Authority in 2026

February, Defense Production Act threat. On February 24, 2026 Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth threatened to invoke the Act against Anthropic (Rozenshtein). He demanded that it drop usage restrictions on autonomous weapons and mass surveillance by February 27 or 28 (sources differ; the D.C. Circuit gives February 27). Anthropic refused on February 26. On February 27 the President and the Secretary denounced the decision, and the Secretary began removing Claude from the Defense Department’s supply chain (D.C. Circuit opinion).

May and June, testing agreements and order. On May 5, 2026 CAISI announced agreements with Google DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI (NIST/CAISI). Executive Order 14409 of June 2, 2026 directs agencies to design a voluntary framework for pre-release government access of up to 30 days. Its Section 3 authorizes no mandatory licensing, preclearance or permitting requirement (see the Pace: Slowdowns and Gates tab). Earlier, Axios reported talk of pre-clearance requirements for new models (Axios).

June, export controls. A June 12, 2026 Commerce Department directive applied export controls to Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all foreign nationals, wherever located (Anthropic). Legal commentary reads the letter as an “is informed” license requirement that cited 15 C.F.R. § 744.22 and 50 U.S.C. § 4817(b)(1) (Harvard Law Review Blog; Mayer Brown). Anthropic removed access for every user, and the Commerce Secretary withdrew the controls on June 30 (his statement, via Fox Business; The Next Web). The directive covered foreign nationals only, yet U.S. users lost access too. After government approval on June 26, Mythos 5 returned for a set of U.S. organizations. Fable 5 returned on July 1, 202…

June, court challenge. Legion LegalTech Corp. sued on June 23, 2026 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (MLex). The complaint alleges the directive exceeded the export control statute, IEEPA and the Administrative Procedure Act. Legion dropped the suit in early July 2026, after the controls were withdrawn, and no court ruled on the directive (Law360 via MLex). The case was No. 1:26-cv-02225, before Judge Richard J. Leon (Law360 case page).

March, supply-chain-risk designation. The Defense Secretary made a formal determination against Anthropic on March 3, 2026 under 41 U.S.C. § 4713 (D.C. Circuit opinion). The notice reached Anthropic on March 4, and a Department memo of March 6 ordered its products removed within 180 days (same opinion). Anthropic’s statement of March 5 says the letter cited 10 U.S.C. § 3252 (Anthropic).

August and September, court rulings on the designation. The Northern District of California set aside the § 3252 designation on August 27, 2026, as the D.C. Circuit’s opinion describes it. The D.C. Circuit upheld the § 4713 exclusion on September 25, 2026, by 2 to 1 (opinion).
commentary
Commentary

Export law. Greenberg Traurig calls the directive the first known export control action against a particular frontier model (client alert). Alex Zhao finds the directive’s legal basis novel and uncertain (Harvard Law Review Blog). Mayer Brown also reports that Commerce relied on 15 C.F.R. § 744.22 and 50 U.S.C. § 4817(b)(1) (client alert, June 30, 2026). The letter itself was not opened.

Defense Production Act. Alan Rozenshtein writes that Title I maps awkwardly onto AI. Kevin Frazier and Dean Ball doubt it supports mandatory pre-deployment vetting and call the Communications Act implausible (Cato). James Lewis of CSIS said the authorities could be clearer but a solution could probably be assembled from existing law (Fox News).
Negotiated conditions. Commerce lifted the controls after Anthropic made commitments; sources differ on which (The Next Web; Startup Fortune).

Authority to operate private facilities. Three statutes pair government operation of private facilities with compensation. They are Atomic Energy Act § 108, Communications Act § 706 and Military Selective Service Act § 18. The first covers licensed nuclear facilities once Congress declares war or a national emergency. The second covers communications stations after a presidential proclamation of war or emergency. The third lets the President take over a plant that refuses a defense order.

Across the families. Stop proposals need a power to halt domestic training, which no listed authority was written to give. Pace and Contain and Channel proposals can build on testing agreements and federal contracts. Continue positions rely on voluntary cooperation, as Frazier and Ball do.
constitutional-constraints
Constitutional Constraints
The constitutional questions are open and mostly untested for frontier AI. No court has ruled on whether model weights or training decisions are speech, and no AI-specific takings analysis was found.

Speech: model weights. Alan Rozenshtein argues there is no general First Amendment right to distribute model weights (Lawfare, April 4, 2024). He reads Bernstein, Junger and Corley as protecting source code that people read, and treats weights as machine-readable parameters. A civil-society comment he cites argues the opposite by analogy to source code.

Speech: training choices. Rozenshtein writes that compelled retraining raises unsettled questions about whether training choices are protected editorial expression (Lawfare, February 25, 2026). Moody v. NetChoice recognized some algorithmic curation as protected, and the justices voiced doubts about its scope.

Speech: disclosure mandates. Bahrad Sokhansanj and Mackenzie Arnold conclude that laws such as California SB 53 remain viable and face more First Amendment risk than before (analysis). In xAI v. Bonta a district judge denied a preliminary injunction against California AB 2013 on March 4, 2026. The judge applied the stricter Central Hudson test and said xAI could prevail; an appeal is pending in the Ninth Circuit (No. 26-1591).

Speech: prior restraint. Alex Mark and Aaron Scher write that an administrative prior restraint must put on the government the burden of justifying a denial (arXiv 2509.05361, September 2025). They cite Freedman v. Maryland. They judge model algorithms likely protected speech and model weights likely unprotected. They treat limits on open release or API access as an administrative prior restraint.
Statutory speech limits. Export regulations exclude published information and fundamental research, and IEEPA exempts informational materials (CRS R46814; CRS R45618).

Major questions. The doctrine demands clear congressional authorization for agency action on questions of vast economic and political significance (CRS IF12077). In Learning Resources v. Trump, decided February 20, 2026, three justices applied it to presidential action under an emergency statute (opinion). Three concurring justices called it unnecessary, and three dissenters favored broader readings of national security delegations.

Due process. Anthropic said the June 2026 directive gave it hours to comply and rested on verbal evidence (Anthropic; NBC News). The FRONTIER Act would require written findings, notice where imminence allows, an expedited hearing with the burden on the Secretary and judicial review (section-by-section). The Sanders and Casar bill pairs charter revocation with appellate review and forfeiture of intellectual property and assets (bill text).

Takings. No analysis applying the Takings Clause to chips, weights or a training moratorium was found. CRS notes that courts have heard takings and due process challenges to IEEPA actions (CRS R45618). The Hardwired Pause working paper (October 2026, unpublished draft) proposes an insurance fund that pays book value for stranded model-specific chips (§§ 5 and 6).

Searches and inspections. The working paper points to U.S. rules implementing the Chemical Weapons Convention as a template (footnote 9). Those rules allow inspection by consent, by administrative warrant or by criminal warrant on probable cause. The Sanders and Casar bill makes full government access a charter condition, and the FRONTIER Act gives private verifiers unrestricted access.

Separation of powers and federalism. Executive Order 14365 directs the Justice Department to challenge state AI laws (White House). The GUARDRAILS Act (H.R. 8031) would declare that order void (Covington). No opened source treats nondelegation or the dormant Commerce Clause in depth.

Inferences for design. A statute that expressly authorizes a pause would answer the major questions objection that an executive order would invite. Limits on conduct, such as compute thresholds, sit on firmer speech ground under Rozenshtein’s analysis than rules dictating outputs. Both points are inferences, the speech point is contested, and no court has ruled.

Across the families. Stop proposals that strand chips or forfeit assets raise the takings question most directly. Pace proposals turn on the process attached to gates and emergency orders, and Contain and Channel proposals on inspection law. Continue positions invoke speech protections, as Executive Order 14365 does against state mandates on model outputs.

Preemption
Established. Congress has enacted no preemption of state AI law. The House passed a broad moratorium in May 2025, and the Senate stripped it 99 to 1 (Bullock).

Executive branch. Executive Order 14365 of December 11, 2025 directs suits against state AI laws and conditions some broadband funds (White House). The White House framework of March 20, 2026 would bar states from regulating AI development (Gibson Dunn).

Pending bills. The Great American AI Act draft would preempt state model-development laws for three years. The FRONTIER Act would bar new state frontier duties; the Sanders and Casar bill has no preemption clause.

Contested. In a July 23, 2026 statement, Americans for Responsible Innovation objects that FRONTIER’s preemption starts at once and has no sunset. It adds that drafting issues create a risk that the preemption is applied more broadly than intended (ARI). Charlie Bullock favors narrow preemption matched to the federal rules enacted (Bullock).

Across the families. The Sanders and Casar bill is the only Stop text found. FRONTIER and S. 2938 are Pace texts, and S. 2938 asks for options up to nationalization. The White House framework states the Continue position.

Regulatory Models

Bills and proposals of 2025 and 2026 borrow from older regulatory regimes. The mapping below is this document’s reading; the reference regimes and named scholarly proposals were not opened (Not confirmed).

Drug approval (pre-market approval) · Sanders and Casar bill: no advanced system deployed without final federal approval · Sanders; Casar; 22 leaders (31 signers by September 30, 2026) ask for mandatory pre-deployment testing · Frazier and Ball favor voluntary vetting

Aviation (certification, third-party audit) · FRONTIER Act: licensed “independent verification organizations” for very large developers · Obernolte; Trahan; Bullock backs a federal audit regime · ARI: release decisions stay with developers; no whistleblower channel
Nuclear licensing · Sanders and Casar charter with 20-year penalties; S. 2938 Energy Department program · Sanders; Casar; Hawley; Blumenthal · No critique of the model opened: Not confirmed

Self-regulatory body · No named proposal opened; nearest is Amodei on common lab standards and checkpoints · Amodei, with government mediation of antitrust concerns · Voluntary arrangements cannot block a release (Cloud Security Alliance, on CAISI)

Embedded examiners (bank supervision) · Amodei’s outside evaluators with access like employees; “whole-lab inspection”; the Two-Lane Plan’s resident examiners · Amodei; Choussat and Khoja; Brad Carson (unpublished) · No critique opened; warrant questions appear under Constitutional Constraints

Emergency orders in FRONTIER. Section 8 would let the Secretary of Commerce suspend development, deployment or internal use on written findings of imminent catastrophic risk. Provisional orders expire after 45 days and final orders after 90 days, renewable in periods of up to 90 days on a new finding. At a hearing the Secretary must show that adequate evidence supports the order (§ 8(j)(2)). Section 8(l) makes the section the exclusive means for any federal actor, the President included, to restrict a frontier developer on those grounds (introduced text).

Shutdown in the Sanders and Casar bill. The Secretary must disconnect systems showing “superintelligence precursor characteristics” and disable them within 30 days unless the Secretary verifies that the characteristics are gone (bill text, § 10).

Access terms. Sanders and Casar charter holders must give full access to systems, processes, staff and physical infrastructure. S. 2938 requires code, training data, weights and architecture details on request. FRONTIER verifiers get unrestricted access and must refer imminent catastrophic risk within 72 hours.

Existing practice. CAISI already tests unreleased models, some in classified settings, under voluntary agreements (NIST/CAISI). Defense Production Act Title VII allows voluntary industry agreements with antitrust protection (CRS R43767). For prior art on embedded oversight, see the Two-Lane Plan: Full Design tab.

Who holds the gate. The Sanders and Casar bill gives a new department approval over every advanced model. S. 2938 conditions deployment on federal evaluation. FRONTIER leaves release decisions with developers outside an emergency order, the point ARI criticizes.
Thresholds. Bill texts use 10^25 operations (Sanders and Casar) and 10^26 operations (S. 2938 and FRONTIER). FRONTIER adds revenue and spending tiers.

Insurance. The Hardwired Pause working paper proposes mandatory insurance for operators of model-specific chips (footnote 76). It notes that nuclear plant operators must buy insurance as a license condition.

Not adopted. No pending bill opened uses “born secret” classification or secrecy orders on the Invention Secrecy Act model. The UN scientific panel reviewed aviation, nuclear and cybersecurity safety regimes and made no recommendation (thematic brief).

Established and contested. The bill provisions are established, from bill texts and, for FRONTIER, the introduced text and the sponsor’s section-by-section summary. The mapping to older regimes is a reading of those texts, and sponsors do not all name the analogies.

Across the families. Stop proposals pair a charter with approval before any deployment. Pace proposals use audits, evaluation gates and bounded emergency orders, and Contain and Channel proposals rely on embedded examiners. Continue positions favor sector regulators with no new agency, as the White House framework does (Gibson Dunn).

The Call. Finland’s President Alexander Stubb and Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre initiated it (Norway). The text lists 31 signers: 22 at launch and nine more by September 28, France among them (text).

Legal form. The Hardwired Pause working paper expects informal agreements first and a treaty later (§ 3). U.S. law on treaties, executive agreements and political commitments was not opened for AI: Not confirmed.

Proposed agreements. Dario Amodei ranks deals with China from narrow bans to mutual testing, caps on recursive self-improvement and a full pause (essay). He considers a full pause unlikely in the near term. Machine Intelligence Research Institute researchers propose compute thresholds, chip tracking, verification and limits on research toward superintelligence (arXiv 2511.10783).

Control points. James N. Baker judges compute the most workable target for hard controls and compares such controls to COCOM and Wassenaar (survey). He adds that private-sector dominance makes domestic implementing law necessary.

Verification (contested). Mauricio Baker concludes that preparation can cut verification problems to levels managed in nuclear agreements (arXiv 2304.04123). Felix Choussat and Adam Khoja argue a slowdown is verifiable now by on-site lab inspection and supplier audits (AI Frontiers). The Machine Intelligence Research Institute authors write that political will does not yet exist.

Institutional design. The working paper cites ICAO for updating standards and the test-ban monitoring system for a compute ledger (§§ 2.2 and 3.6). It contrasts inspected chemical and nuclear regimes with the Biological Weapons Convention, which has no verification mechanism. Lewis Ho and co-authors list four functions: expert consensus, standard setting, access sharing and safety research (arXiv 2307.04699).

United States and China. Neither appears on the Call’s signatory list on the Dutch page. The working paper reports that China set up the World AI Cooperation Organization in July 2026, mainly as a capacity-building body (§ 7.5.2). Its quotation of Xi Jinping on human control has no citation; the Timeline tab sources his September 24, 2026 remarks.
At the United Nations. Politico reported sharply different U.S. and Chinese visions for AI regulation at a UN meeting (September 23, 2026). The working paper cites it; the page was not opened.

Domestic asks. The lab employees’ statement asks the U.S. government to support an international effort on tools for pacing (Pacing the Frontier). The Sanders and Casar bill would make pursuit of international agreements U.S. policy.

Across the families. Stop proposals that bind China mostly assume a treaty with verification. Pace proposals can begin with informal or staged agreements. The Two-Lane Plan assumes no deal and keeps an off-ramp to a verified agreement; Continue positions require no agreement.

what-the-polls-show
What the Polls Show
Slowing has broad support. The pause option led 48 to 31 in the Politico poll. In the CBS poll, 55 percent chose to slow down or stop development.

The tilt is partisan. Harris voters backed a pause 58 to 28, and Trump voters 44 to 40. In Pew’s data, Democratic concern rose from 46 percent in 2023 to 56 percent. Republican concern fell from 59 percent to 49 percent.

The China race also has majority support. Republicans back developing AI faster than China at 74 percent, and Democrats at 45 percent. Self-described liberals are at 36 percent (CBS News/YouGov topline).

Trust in institutions is low. In the CBS poll, 61 percent doubt AI companies will ensure appropriate use. Pew finds 67 percent lack confidence in government regulation, while CBS finds 63 percent think government is able to regulate. One question asks about confidence and the other about ability.

A trend. Polls on a pause from 2023 to 2025 were not opened: Not confirmed. Politico’s own page stayed blocked on October 7, 2026. Yahoo quotes the two statements at greater length than the working paper does, so the exact wording is unsettled.
A link to the U.S. network. The pollster Public First is a London firm unrelated to the U.S. political network of that name.

money
Money

Pledges. Leading the Future pledged more than $100 million and opposes restrictive regulation (NOTUS). Former Representatives Chris Stewart, a Utah Republican, and Brad Carson, an Oklahoma Democrat, announced Public First on November 25, 2025 (Public First). They said they expected to raise $50 million for a nonprofit and two super PACs, one Republican and one Democratic.

Self-reported totals. In February 2026 Public First said it had raised $50 million and planned to raise $25 million more (The American Prospect). Axios reported that month that Leading the Future had raised more than $125 million (Axios). Both figures exceed the super PAC receipts on the FEC pages, and the sources opened do not explain the gap.

Cash on hand. FEC pages show $31.0 million at Leading the Future and $493,550 at Public First PAC on June 30, 2026. Anthropic announced $20 million for Public First Action, a 501(c)(4) nonprofit, on February 12, 2026 (Axios). It announced $20 million more on July 21, 2026 (Anthropic). Anthropic says those gifts fund public education and policy work and cannot be used to influence any candidate’s election.

A test race. Before the primary, NBC News reported that Think Big had spent more than $1.5 million against Alex Bores, a RAISE Act sponsor (NBC News). He lost the New York 12th District primary to Micah Lasher (Leicht).

Both sides. OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman backs Leading the Future. Anthropic funds the nonprofit Public First Action. Amodei gave Public First PAC $1 million, and employees of Anthropic, Google and OpenAI gave more than $2 million (Axios).

Totals. The working paper cites about $265 million pledged by AI firms this cycle (Wall Street Journal). Leading the Future reported $75.8 million in receipts through June 30, 2026 (FEC). Third-quarter totals are Not confirmed; the Timeline tab records later reported figures.

Spending so far. Think Big and American Mission reported $17.2 million and $10.9 million of independent expenditures through August 31, 2026 (Think Big; American Mission). Jobs and Democracy PAC reported $17.9 million through June 30, and Defending Our Values PAC $7.1 million through July 29 (FEC; FEC). The four reports end on different dates, so the totals are not directly comparable.
